The router places the internal NotificationPageNotFoundStatus (MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/NotificationPageNotFoundStatus.cs:11) beside that not-found page; it renders nothing and calls NavigationManager.NotFound() on initialization, so a server render answers 404 rather than 200 (:5-10, :18). The pages themselves declare the mmca:notification-pages policy instead of a bare [Authorize], because [Authorize] is endpoint metadata and the authorization middleware would challenge a signed-out visitor to sign in before the router's gate ever ran, for a page that does not exist on this host (NotificationPageRequirement, MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/NotificationPageRequirement.cs:18, :23, rationale at :14-19). NotificationPageAuthorizationHandler (MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/NotificationPageAuthorizationHandler.cs:16) passes an authenticated caller, and every caller while the host hides the pages, reusing the gate's own predicate so the two cannot disagree (:26-30); AddUIShared registers the policy and the handler for every host (MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:78-85).

    Administration screens ship as components, not pages. Identity administration is the second finished feature in the package (ADR-116), and it is delivered as components an app routes itself: UserAdminList<TUser> (MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/UserAdminList.razor.cs:44), RoleAdminList (MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/RoleAdminList.razor.cs:28) and RoleAdminEdit (MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs:36) carry no @page directive, so the route, the authorization attribute and the links between them stay the app's decision (UserAdminList.razor.cs:17-22, RoleAdminList.razor.cs:12-14, RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs:13-14). The account roster is the one shipped screen that derives from the list-page base itself (MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/UserAdminList.razor:4) and it is generic over the app's own DTO, constrained only to IUserAdminDTO (UserAdminList.razor.cs:47-48). It has two data paths: by default it reads through IUserAdminUIService<TUserDto> (MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/IUserAdminUIService.cs:17), whose endpoint takes a search term and a role rather than the grid's per-column filter syntax (IUserAdminUIService.cs:11-16, :27-32), while an app whose roster lives on its own filtered endpoint passes a FetchPage delegate instead and the service is never resolved for reads, with the free-text box injected under the SearchFilterKey filter key (UserAdminList.razor.cs:32-39, :50-55). The three account actions always go through IUserAdminActionsUIService (MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/IUserAdminActionsUIService.cs:16), the non-generic half so a component that only acts on an account never names the DTO, and they are hidden on the signed-in operator's own row: an operator who locked or demoted themselves would lose the very capability needed to undo it, and the API has no notion of "the caller" (UserAdminList.razor.cs:40-44). SetRoleAsync is its own member rather than a default interface implementation over SetRolesAsync, because a default implementation is not virtual on the interface a mock proxies, so a test could neither stub nor verify it (IUserAdminActionsUIService.cs:40-54).

    Role administration is non-generic throughout, since a role and a permission are both strings the framework already owns (IRoleAdminUIService, MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/IRoleAdminUIService.cs:22, rationale at :11-15). The roster reports the permissions a role's code grants and the permissions stored rows grant as two separate counts, because only the stored half is editable and a single total would hide that removing a compiled permission is a code change (RoleAdminList.razor.cs:16-20). The editor offers only what the server's catalog declares, so nothing it can submit is a permission no endpoint checks, and it locks two kinds of checkbox: one the host compiled in for this role, and ManageRoles itself, which guards this very screen and which the server refuses to store, so offering it would be offering an action guaranteed to fail (RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs:17-29). The rest are grouped by the area before the first colon of an area:capability name through the private PermissionGroup record, with un-prefixed permissions filed under a localized "General" (RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs:39, :245-247, :338-340). Wording stays the app's: every string these three render is looked up in an app-supplied IStringLocalizer first and falls back to the framework's UserAdminListResources, RoleAdminListResources and RoleAdminEditResources markers, so "Deactivate" instead of "Lock" costs no parameter per word (UserAdminList.razor.cs:24-31, MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/RoleAdminListResources.cs:9-14). Both implementations, UserAdminService<TUserDto> (MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/UserAdminService.cs:26) and RoleAdminService (MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/RoleAdminService.cs:24), derive from AuthenticatedServiceBase rather than the entity-service base, because these endpoints are not CRUD over an entity resource, and they read every answer back through ProblemDetailsResultReader inside HttpResultExecutor so only the caller's own cancellation still propagates (UserAdminService.cs:15-22, RoleAdminService.cs:64-78, :89-101). [Rubric §18, UI Architecture & Component Design] again: the framework ships the screen, the app keeps the route, the vocabulary and the DTO.

    Two-factor and permission-gated pages follow the same opt-in shape. Two-factor authentication ships on the notification pattern. TwoFactorUIModule (MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/TwoFactorUIModule.cs:16), registered by AddTwoFactorUI(), contributes the account page's navigation item and the layout listener that sends a session refused for want of a second factor to that page, and a host that never registers it has no page, no nav item and no listener (TwoFactorUIModule.cs:10-15). TwoFactorPageGate (MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/TwoFactorPageGate.cs:12) has the router answer the page with the not-found page whenever the module is absent, because the page needs a client and API endpoints such a host does not have (:6-11), and the page declares the policy behind TwoFactorPageRequirement (MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:14) instead of a bare [Authorize], so on such a host every caller reaches the router and gets a 404 rather than a sign-in challenge for a page that does not exist, the same rule the notification pages follow (:5-13), evaluated by TwoFactorPageAuthorizationHandler. A permission-gated page needs no registration at all: HasPagePermissionAttribute (MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:19) requires a signed-in caller whose token carries the named permission claim, in every head, and checks it with the same HasPermissionClaim as NavItem.RequiredPermission, so a menu entry and the page it opens cannot disagree; it reads the claim only, since a UI head has no permission registry, so a role-only token never passes (:5-17). PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator (MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:16) registers one policy per permission declared in MMCA.Common.UI or in a registered UI module's assembly when the authorization options are first built, after the host has registered its modules, and keeps any policy the host already registered under the same name (:8-14). [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] and [Rubric §18, UI Architecture].

    Writes made offline, and a log the app can show. IOfflineWriteQueue (MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/IOfflineWriteQueue.cs:11), registered scoped by AddOfflineWriteQueue (MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:417), is a durable queue in the device's local store: each entry belongs to the user signed in when it was queued and is replayed through the IOfflineWriteHandler registered for its kind, matched ordinally (IOfflineWriteQueue.cs:5-10, MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/IOfflineWriteHandler.cs:5-9). OfflineWriteQueue (MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:47) keeps the whole queue as one list under one semaphore, so concurrent callers of one instance never lose a write, while two tabs or two circuits over one store are not coordinated (:14-20). A replay walks the user's entries oldest first: an entry older than MaxAge is discarded as Expired without being sent, an entry with no handler is skipped and kept, a transport failure, a timeout, or an unexpected, too-many-requests or unauthorized answer keeps the entry with one more attempt and stops the pass, a conflict discards it as Conflict and any other failure as Rejected (:22-29, the outcomes being OfflineWriteOutcome). A replay starts when the device comes back online, on the notifier component's first interactive render, and from a single retry timer on the injected TimeProvider whose delay doubles after each pass that settled nothing; the timer is removed when nothing is left to retry, when the device goes offline and on dispose (:30-42). Signing out clears the local store and the queue with it (:43-45; the clear is the optional ILocalCacheStore in AuthUIService, MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs:54, :599). Separately, AddInAppDiagnostics registers InAppLogBuffer (MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Diagnostics/InAppLogBuffer.cs:11), a bounded, thread-safe in-memory ring buffer filled by InAppLoggerProvider and read by the InAppDiagnosticsLog component, held only in process memory so nothing is written to disk or sent anywhere and the entries are gone on restart (:5-10); its size and lowest recorded level are InAppDiagnosticsOptions (MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Diagnostics/InAppDiagnosticsOptions.cs:6-10). [Rubric §29, Resilience] and [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability].

    One composed Blazor web host. The registration list, the request pipeline and the additional-assembly list every Blazor Server plus WebAssembly head repeats are three calls on BlazorWebHostExtensions (MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Hosting/BlazorWebHostExtensions.cs:44, :32-39). AddMmcaBlazorWebHost(options) registers, in a fixed order, the service defaults, Razor components with interactive server components, bounded circuits and the UI rate limiter, MudBlazor, the shared UI services, the session cookie pair, the trusted-caller header, session-cookie authentication, server token storage, the same-origin proxy, the web form factor, the Blazor CSP and finally the security headers (:50-61, :75). UseMmcaBlazorWebPipeline puts the UI rate limiter ahead of the exception handler and the not-found re-execute, so a throttled request answers 429 without re-rendering a page, adds the authenticated no-store header, and maps the client-config, session-cookie, same-origin proxy, culture, static-asset and service-worker endpoints (:166-173, :181, :203), and GetMmcaRazorComponentAssemblies supplies the head's additional assemblies (:225). What differs between heads arrives through MmcaBlazorWebHostOptions and MmcaBlazorWebPipelineOptions; render-mode registration stays per head, so the package takes no WebAssembly server dependency (:35-38), and a head must not register ITokenRefresher or ISessionCookieSync after the call, because the same-origin proxy replaces both and fails the boot when displaced (:62-67).

    How it wires up at startup. A host's Program.cs calls AddUIShared(configuration) once, a C# extension(IServiceCollection) member (see primer §4) on DependencyInjection (MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:35, :43). In order it binds and validates on start ApiSettings, so a missing endpoint fails the host rather than the first request (:42-45; the read-only face of those options is IApiSettings, whose WasmApiEndpoint lets the server call an internal URL while the browser is handed an external one, MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Settings/IApiSettings.cs:11-17); binds LayoutSettings, LegalSettings, RegistrationSettings, SignInSettings and NotificationBellOptions without validation, deliberately optional so a host that configures none of them keeps the compiled-in defaults; TryAdds TimeProvider.System as the clock those staleness policies are measured against; registers the notification pages' authorization policy and its handler (:81-85); sets up localization, the pseudo/Mud localizer decorators and the MudBlazor localization interceptor (:88-110); registers the auth and culture delegating handlers and the named "APIClient" whose base address comes from ApiSettings and whose timeout is pinned to HttpResilienceDefaults.TotalRequestTimeout rather than the BCL's arbitrary 100s, so the transport never pre-empts the resilience budget (:118-147; when Api:SameOriginApiEndpoint is configured the base address is that proxy endpoint and SameOriginProxyRequestHandler joins as the innermost handler, :120-121, :136, :149-154); calls AddCommonUiFacades() for the toast and dialog pair (:159); then TryAdds AuthUIService, the email-confirmation client (:166), the terms-acceptance client (:170), the OAuthFlowStateStore (:174), the two list-page state services, NavigationHistoryService, ThemeService, EndpointCultureApplier, ViewerTimeZone (:190), NavigationPublicLinkBuilder behind IPublicLinkBuilder (share-sheet and QR links resolved against the browser origin, which a MAUI head replaces because its WebView origin is a virtual host nobody else can open, MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/IPublicLinkBuilder.cs:9, MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/NavigationPublicLinkBuilder.cs:11), the preference reader and writer, and a default IOAuthUISettings (DefaultOAuthUISettings) that downstream apps override with ConfigurationOAuthUISettings, which reads provider availability from the OAuth section for a server host and from pre-computed Enabled flags for a WASM client (:161-204, MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/ConfigurationOAuthUISettings.cs:19, :24-30); and finally calls AddDeviceCapabilityDefaults() so every capability contract resolves on every head (:208, ADR-042, chapter 26). The TryAdd* discipline is what lets a consumer pre-register its own implementation and win. Browser hosts add AddClientAuthSessionCookieSync() (:240-242) and AddWasmFormFactor() (:252); a Blazor Server head adds AddCommonServerTokenStorage(), AddCommonBlazorCsp() (before AddCommonSecurityHeaders, so it beats the TryAdded static provider) and AddCommonWebFormFactor() from MMCA.Common.UI.Web (MMCA.Common.UI.Web/DependencyInjection.cs:41, :67, :85; the first also registers BrowserOriginHandler, :47-48) plus the UseAuthenticatedNoStore() middleware. A Blazor Web host that should install as a web app with an offline page also maps MapCommonServiceWorker() from ServiceWorkerEndpointExtensions (MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Pwa/ServiceWorkerEndpointExtensions.cs:15, :60-70): an anonymous GET /service-worker.js at the root so the worker's scope covers the whole site, excluded from the OpenAPI description and served no-cache (:17-18, :34-37), while the host supplies the app identity (manifest, icons, theme-color, :10-14). The worker never caches pages or data, because a server-rendered page carries the signed-in user's data: it sends every GET navigation to the network and falls back to the offline page only when the network fails, leaving every other request to the browser (:40-46). The package version is written into the embedded script, so each framework release is a byte change the browser installs on its next update check (:48-51, :73-84), and setting Pwa:ServiceWorker:Enabled to false serves a retired worker with no fetch handler that deletes the offline cache, so retiring a bad worker is a configuration change rather than a release (:24, :52-57, :64-66). The administration screens are opt-in on the same pattern: AddUserAdministrationUI<TUserDto>() registers the generic service and forwards the non-generic actions contract to that same instance, so the roster and the actions it performs go through one object and one substitute in a test (MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:321-328), and AddRoleAdministrationUI() registers the role client (:295-297); nothing in the framework calls either, so an app serving no administration endpoints registers nothing and the components are simply never rendered. An SSR host behind the gateway also calls AddTrustedCallerHeader(configuration), which composes TrustedCallerHandler (MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Security/TrustedCallerHandler.cs:35) onto every HttpClient the host creates, inserted at index 0 so the origin gate judges the authority the caller wrote rather than one Aspire's service-discovery handler has already rewritten (MMCA.Common.UI.Web/DependencyInjection.cs:121, :143-156), and registers nothing at all when no secret, header name or parseable gateway origin is configured (the early return at :137). The breadth is the point: the call that suffers most from the gateway's per-IP limiter partition, the cookie-session token refresh, is created by the framework under a name a host cannot reach, while the handler itself stays narrow, stamping the secret only on a request whose scheme, host and port match the gateway origin and replacing rather than appending the header, because the gateway compares one single-valued header in constant time (TrustedCallerHandler.cs:9-27, :67-79). UISharedAssemblyReference (MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:502) is the marker other assemblies scan against.

    How a WebAssembly client learns its API address. The WASM bundle is static, so the API base address is fetched at runtime rather than baked in. On the server side, ClientConfigEndpointExtensions (MMCA.Common.UI.Web/ClientConfig/ClientConfigEndpointExtensions.cs:19) adds MapClientConfigEndpoint, an anonymous GET /client-config excluded from the OpenAPI description whose framework-owned Api section carries Api:WasmApiEndpoint (:17, :52-81). It fails closed: with that key missing it throws rather than fall back to Api:ApiEndpoint, which is the server head's service-discovery name a browser cannot resolve, so the client fails to start instead of pointing at the wrong API (:32-38, :53-59). When the host runs the same-origin proxy, the same api section also carries sameOriginApiEndpoint, the proxy prefix with a trailing slash, which is what moves the client's "APIClient" onto it (:84-99). The endpoint declares AllowAnonymous itself, because the client fetches the document before it can hold a session and a host's fallback policy would otherwise gate it (:40-44, :80). A host adds its own sections through a per-request ClientConfigBuilder (MMCA.Common.UI.Web/ClientConfig/ClientConfigBuilder.cs:19), whose Add refuses a blank name, the reserved Api section and a duplicate, and whose remarks warn that everything added is served to every browser before sign-in, so only public values belong there (:12-16, :45-62). The client half is MmcaClientConfigBootstrap (MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Settings/MmcaClientConfigBootstrap.cs:28), whose LoadAsync fetches the document from the app's own origin with a 15-second per-attempt timeout and a single retry after one second (for the cold-start case where the Server host is still warming), then rethrows a second failure on purpose, and returns a buffered stream because browser fetch streams do not support the synchronous reads AddJsonStream performs (:12-22, :30, :33, :44-85). Only the timeout it did not ask for is retried, never the caller's own cancellation (:87-90). ADC wires both halves, the server half through the ClientConfig callback it hands UseMmcaBlazorWebPipeline (MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web/Program.cs:128, MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web/Program.cs:170, MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:31).

    The small Level-0 supporting cast fills in the rest: NotificationRoutePaths (MMCA.Common.UI/Common/NotificationRoutePaths.cs:8), whose deep-link builder formats invariantly because the route's :int constraint is the validation boundary (:14-20); QrErrorCorrectionLevel, the framework's own enum for QrCodeImage so the component's public API does not pin consumers to QRCoder's ECCLevel (MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Sharing/QrErrorCorrectionLevel.cs:9); RatingStars (MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Ratings/RatingStars.razor.cs:13), five read-only stars out of a MaxValue of 5 rendered as one role="img" element whose required AriaLabel carries the numeric figure, so the stars stay decorative rounding (whole stars fill, a half star shows at .5 and above, :6-11, :16, :31-33, :46-54), which the ADC feedback and speaker dashboards render (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/Pages/Feedback/OrganizerSessionFeedback.razor:67); ApiFileDownloadButton (MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Forms/ApiFileDownloadButton.razor.cs:16), which gives browsers a plain download link and native heads a fetch-stage-share flow, stripping directory segments from the supplied file name so a value built from entity data cannot steer the write out of the temp directory (:21-30); and MauiBackNavigationBridge with its BackNavigationResult for MAUI hardware-back handling, which reports both whether history.back() fired and whether the WebView is at the root of its stack so a host can decide to exit (MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/MauiBackNavigationBridge.cs:19, :28). Form-factor detection has graduated into its own device-capability layer (IFormFactor and friends, chapter 26). The presentational helper MoneyExtensions formats Money for display, grouping a mixed collection by currency so unrelated amounts never collapse under whichever symbol came first (MMCA.Common.UI/Extensions/MoneyExtensions.cs:14, the single-price form at :29-30 and the collection form at :33), keeping a display concern out of the domain value object, exactly where Clean Architecture wants it.

    Read the per-type sections that follow for the mechanics. The consumer-side module UIs live in the ADC module-UI chapter (chapter 21), and the bUnit component tests plus the Playwright/axe-core E2E suite that exercise this package are covered in the testing chapter (chapter 27), which is where [Rubric §28, Front-End Testing] lives.

    PagePermissionPolicy

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Authorization · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionPolicy.cs:9 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: the naming rule for the page permission policies. It turns a permission name such as conference:sessions:manage into the policy name a HasPagePermissionAttribute asks for.
    • Depends on: nothing.
    • Concept introduced, a policy name as a shared contract. ASP.NET Core authorization looks a policy up by string, so the attribute that names a policy and the code that registers it must agree on the exact string. Putting the format in one static class makes that agreement a compile-time reference rather than two copies of a literal. [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] assesses whether client-side route guards are consistent and hard to get wrong; one builder used by both sides is how this code keeps the guard and its registration from drifting.
    • Walkthrough: Prefix = "page-perm:" (PagePermissionPolicy.cs:12) and NameFor(string permission) => Prefix + permission (PagePermissionPolicy.cs:17). Nothing else.
    • Why it's built this way: the class doc comment (PagePermissionPolicy.cs:3-8) records why the prefix differs from the API's perm:: the API's policy provider, which a web host may install by replacement, intercepts every perm: name, while a page-perm: name falls through to the default provider and so reaches the policy AddUIShared registered. A distinct prefix is what lets the page guard coexist with ADR-020's API policies on a Blazor Web head that hosts both.
    • Where it's used: the HasPagePermissionAttribute constructor passes NameFor(permission) to its base (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:24), and PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator registers under the same name (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:35). The permission-coverage fitness rule strips the same prefix to recover the permission from an [Authorize(Policy = ...)] (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Api/ArchitectureRules.PermissionCoverage.cs:16, :140-142).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the fitness rule keeps its own "page-perm:" literal (ArchitectureRules.PermissionCoverage.cs:16) rather than referencing Prefix, so the two strings agree by convention, not by the compiler.

    PagePermissionRequirement

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Authorization · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionRequirement.cs:11 · Level 0 · record (internal, sealed)

    • What it is: the authorization requirement behind every page permission policy: the caller's token carries a permission claim equal to Permission.
    • Depends on: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.IAuthorizationRequirement (PagePermissionRequirement.cs:1).
    • Concept: the requirement/handler split of ASP.NET Core authorization, the same shape as NotificationPageRequirement in this group: a requirement is pure data, and a separate handler decides whether it is met.
    • Walkthrough: one positional record, internal sealed record PagePermissionRequirement(string Permission) : IAuthorizationRequirement; (PagePermissionRequirement.cs:11). The doc comment (PagePermissionRequirement.cs:5-10) names its evaluator, PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler.
    • Why it's built this way: internal, because nothing outside the framework constructs one; a host only writes the attribute. A record gives value equality for free, which is all a requirement needs.
    • Where it's used: constructed once per declared permission by PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:40). The shipped nav-guard contract base recognizes it by type name to model what a guarded page demands (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.UI/Navigation/NavItemGuardContractTestsBase.cs:50, :313-315), which is why it can stay internal.

    UISharedAssemblyReference

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:502 · Level 0 · class

    • What it is: an empty marker class whose only job is to give code a compile-checked typeof(...).Assembly handle on the shared UI assembly.
    • Depends on: nothing.
    • Concept introduced, the assembly-marker type. Reflection over an assembly needs an Assembly instance, and there are two ways to get one: a string (Assembly.Load("MMCA.Common.UI"), which fails at run time when someone renames the project) or a type reference (typeof(UISharedAssemblyReference).Assembly, which fails at compile time and is carried along by a rename refactoring). Every layer of the framework ships an equivalent marker; this is the UI layer's. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses exactly this kind of refactor-safety over stringly-typed lookups.
    • Walkthrough: a single declaration using the semicolon type body, public class UISharedAssemblyReference; (DependencyInjection.cs:502), with its doc comment on line 217. It shares a file with DependencyInjection but is declared at namespace scope beneath it, outside that static class, because a type nested inside a static class could not serve as a public marker the same way. It carries no members, so nothing can accidentally depend on state it does not have.
    • Why it's built this way: type-only, public and empty is the whole point. It is the assembly's identity expressed as a symbol the compiler tracks.
    • Where it's used: the architecture fitness suite is the real consumer. CommonArchitectureMap registers the assembly as the framework's UI layer with Framework(Layer.Ui, typeof(Common.UI.UISharedAssemblyReference).Assembly) (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/CommonArchitectureMap.cs:27), which is what lets the shared layer-dependency rules know which assembly is the UI layer; AnonymousEndpointTests includes it in the assemblies it scans (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Api/AnonymousEndpointTests.cs:19); and NavigationContractTests enumerates its types with typeof(UI.UISharedAssemblyReference).Assembly.GetTypes() (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Ui/NavigationContractTests.cs:105). [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance & Documentation] applies: this one-line type is what makes a layer boundary machine-checkable.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the doc comment (DependencyInjection.cs:346) offers "e.g., for Scrutor scanning" as the motivating case, but no Scrutor registration in this repo takes its scan root from this marker. AddUIModule<TModule>() scans FromAssemblyOf<TModule>() (DependencyInjection.cs:491), taking the root from the module descriptor's own assembly instead. Trust the call sites: the current consumers are the architecture tests.

    HasPagePermissionAttribute

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Authorization · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:19 · Level 1 · class (sealed attribute)

    • What it is: the attribute a Blazor page puts on itself to require a signed-in caller whose token carries a given permission claim, in every UI head (web, WebAssembly and MAUI), for example @attribute [HasPagePermission(ConferencePermissions.ActivitiesManage)] (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/Pages/Activities/ActivityList.razor:2).
    • Depends on: PagePermissionPolicy; Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.AuthorizeAttribute (HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:1, :19).
    • Concept introduced, the page-side twin of a menu permission. The doc comment (HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:5-10) states the design goal: the attribute and NavItem's RequiredPermission check the claim with the same HasPermissionClaim (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:95), so a menu entry gated on a permission and the page it opens cannot disagree; the menu runs that check at MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Layout/NavMenu.razor.cs:127. [Rubric §25, Navigation & IA] assesses whether navigation and route access are consistent; here the two derive from one predicate. [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] assesses route guards: the attribute derives from AuthorizeAttribute, so the Blazor router's standard [Authorize] handling applies it, rather than each page checking in code. The server-side counterpart is ADR-020's API permission policy; this attribute is a UI guard only, and the API still authorizes every call itself.
    • Walkthrough: [AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class, AllowMultiple = true, Inherited = true)] (HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:18). The constructor passes PagePermissionPolicy.NameFor(permission) to the base as the policy name and keeps the raw permission (HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:23-24), exposed as Permission (HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:27) so the configurator can read it back by reflection.
    • Why it's built this way: the second paragraph of the doc comment (HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:11-16) gives the two decisions. No registration is needed, because AddUIShared registers one policy per permission declared on a component in MMCA.Common.UI or in any registered UI module's assembly (see PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator). And the check reads the claim only, because a UI head has no permission registry, so it suits a host whose token issuer stamps permission claims; a role-only token never passes.
    • Where it's used: ADC's Conference management pages (for example the activity, category and event list, create and detail pages, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/Pages/Events/EventList.razor:2); the module descriptor notes that its nav items require the same permissions so an editor sees exactly the entries its grant opens (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/ConferenceUIModule.cs:27). The permission-coverage fitness rule reads the attribute by full name and its Permission value (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Api/ArchitectureRules.PermissionCoverage.cs:9, :120).

    PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Authorization · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:12 · Level 1 · class (internal, sealed)

    • What it is: the handler that decides a PagePermissionRequirement: it succeeds when the principal carries the permission claim.
    • Depends on: PagePermissionRequirement, HasPermissionClaim from ClaimsPrincipalExtensions (PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:2); AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement>.
    • Concept: cross-reference NotificationPageAuthorizationHandler, which uses the same HasPermissionClaim for its optional permission (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/NotificationPageAuthorizationHandler.cs:39).
    • Walkthrough: HandleRequirementAsync (PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:15-28) guards both arguments (:19-20), calls context.Succeed(requirement) only when context.User.HasPermissionClaim(requirement.Permission) (:22-25), and returns Task.CompletedTask (:27). It never calls Fail, so a missing claim simply leaves the requirement unmet.
    • Why it's built this way: the doc comment (PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:6-11) calls HasPermissionClaim the framework's single definition of a token-granted permission and the same check the nav menu runs, so page and menu entry cannot disagree. The handler does not test authentication itself: the policy adds RequireAuthenticatedUser() (PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:39), so an unauthenticated principal never passes.
    • Where it's used: registered by AddUIShared through TryAddEnumerable as a transient IAuthorizationHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:112-113).

    PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Authorization · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:16 · Level 3 · class (internal, sealed)

    • What it is: an IConfigureOptions<AuthorizationOptions> that discovers every permission a HasPagePermissionAttribute declares and registers one policy for each, so a host adds a guarded page with no registration call of its own.
    • Depends on: IUIModule (primary constructor, PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:16), PagePermissionPolicy, HasPagePermissionAttribute, PagePermissionRequirement; System.Reflection and Microsoft.Extensions.Options (PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:1-3).
    • Concept introduced, options configuration as late discovery. An IConfigureOptions<T> runs when the options instance is first built, not when it is registered. The doc comment (PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:8-14) relies on exactly that: it runs after the host has registered its modules, so the module list it scans is complete regardless of whether AddUIShared was called before or after the Add{Module}UI() calls. [Rubric §33, Developer Experience] assesses how many steps a common change takes; adding a guarded page here is one attribute.
    • Walkthrough: Configure (PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:20-43) builds the permission set as one LINQ pipeline (:24-31): every module's Assembly (:25), plus the framework's own UI assembly (:26), deduplicated (:27), flattened to their types through LoadableTypes (:28), each type's HasPagePermissionAttributes read with inherit: true (:29), projected to Permission (:30) and deduplicated ordinally (:31). For each permission it computes the policy name (:35) and, only when options.GetPolicy(name) is null (:36), adds a policy that requires an authenticated user and a PagePermissionRequirement (:38-40). LoadableTypes (:47-57) returns assembly.GetTypes() and, on a ReflectionTypeLoadException, the types that did load (:53-55); its comment (:45-46) explains that a module assembly referencing something the head does not load would otherwise fail the whole scan.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping an existing policy of the same name (:36) leaves the host the last word, consistent with the TryAdd convention of DependencyInjection. Scanning the registered modules, rather than every loaded assembly, bounds the reflection to the assemblies that can contribute routable pages.
    • Where it's used: registered by AddUIShared through TryAddEnumerable as a transient IConfigureOptions<AuthorizationOptions> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:110-111); its module list comes from the AddSingleton<IUIModule, TModule>() that AddUIModule<TModule>() performs (DependencyInjection.cs:496).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the framework assembly is scanned too (:26), but no .razor or .cs file under MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation applies the attribute today, so in practice the policies come from module assemblies.

    DependencyInjection

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:35 · Level 10 · class (static, with one extension(IServiceCollection) block)

    • What it is: the composition root of the UI layer. One AddUIShared(configuration) call wires the shared UI infrastructure every head needs (Blazor Server, WebAssembly, MAUI), and twelve smaller methods cover the per-head, per-module and per-opt-in registrations.
    • Depends on: nearly the whole group. Settings: ApiSettings / ApiSettingsValidator, LayoutSettings, LegalSettings, RegistrationSettings, SignInSettings, NotificationBellOptions. Authorization: NotificationPageRequirement / NotificationPageAuthorizationHandler, TwoFactorPageRequirement / TwoFactorPageAuthorizationHandler, PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator / PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler. Localization: PseudoStringLocalizerFactory, ResxMudLocalizer, InvariantMudLocalizationInterceptor. HTTP: AuthDelegatingHandler, CultureDelegatingHandler, SameOriginProxyRequestHandler, HttpResilienceDefaults. Facades: IToastService / MudToastService, IAppDialogService / MudAppDialogService, IPendingToastService / PendingToastService. Services: IAuthUIService / AuthUIService (which also backs ISignInLinkUIService and IPasskeyUIService), IEmailConfirmationUIService / EmailConfirmationUIService, IOidcDiscoveryUIService / OidcDiscoveryUIService, ILegalAcceptanceUIService / LegalAcceptanceUIService, OAuthFlowStateStore, ListPageStateService, ListPageQueryStateService, NavigationHistoryService, ThemeService, ICultureApplier / EndpointCultureApplier, ViewerTimeZone, IPublicLinkBuilder / NavigationPublicLinkBuilder, IUserPreferenceWriter / ApiUserPreferenceWriter, IUserPreferenceReader / ApiUserPreferenceReader, IOAuthUISettings / DefaultOAuthUISettings, IForbiddenReExecutionDetector / NoForbiddenReExecutionDetector, ISessionCookieSync / JsFetchSessionCookieSync. Opt-ins: IUserAdminUIService<TUserDto> / UserAdminService<TUserDto>, IUserAdminActionsUIService, IRoleAdminUIService / RoleAdminService, IMachineClientAdminUIService / MachineClientAdminService, IViewAsGrantsUIService / ViewAsGrantsService, IAuditHistoryUIService / AuditHistoryService, IOfflineWriteQueue / OfflineWriteQueue / OfflineWriteQueueOptions / IOfflineWriteHandler, IFeatureFlagAdminUIService / FeatureFlagAdminService / FeatureFlagAdminUIOptions. Capabilities: IFormFactor / WasmFormFactor. Composition: IUIModule, IEntityService<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType>. Externals: Scrutor (Decorate, Scan), MudBlazor, and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization plus Microsoft.Extensions.{Configuration, DependencyInjection, Localization, Options} (DependencyInjection.cs:1-27).
    • Concept introduced, the composition root written as an extension(T) block. The whole registration surface lives inside extension(IServiceCollection services) (DependencyInjection.cs:37) rather than as classic this-parameter extension methods; the class doc comment calls them C# extension members (DependencyInjection.cs:31-34). See primer, C# extension(T) types for the language mechanics, taught once. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses one consistent idiom across layers, and this file matches the other DependencyInjection classes in every layer of the workspace. [Rubric §33, Developer Experience] assesses fail-fast startup and a small number of calls per host. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether concerns are wired once, centrally: localization, culture forwarding, authentication, page authorization and the HTTP time limit are all configured here rather than per page.
    • Walkthrough: thirteen methods in the extension block.
      • AddUIShared(IConfiguration configuration) (:43-257), in order:
        • Options. ApiSettings binds with .ValidateOnStart() (:48-50) and TryAddEnumerable registers the source-generated ApiSettingsValidator as its IValidateOptions<ApiSettings> (:51); the comment (:45-47) records why: the validator checks the data annotations with no reflection and no Options.DataAnnotations package on a WebAssembly client. A missing ApiEndpoint therefore fails the host at startup rather than at the first HTTP call. LayoutSettings binds without validation because empty defaults are acceptable (:54-55), and so do LegalSettings (:59-60, the footer, registration-checkbox and terms-dialog links; an absent section leaves every URL empty, which renders none of them, per :57-58), RegistrationSettings (:64-65, the optional blocks of the shared register page; an absent section keeps every block), SignInSettings (:69-70, the optional actions of the shared sign-in pages such as sign-in links under ADR-116; an absent section offers nothing new, per :67-68) and NotificationBellOptions (:73-74, an absent section leaving the compiled-in defaults, per :72).
        • Clock. TryAddSingleton(TimeProvider.System) (:79), the clock the notification bell and the stale-toast sweep measure against, with a comment explaining both directions of the TryAdd (:76-78): a host that already registered one, as AddInfrastructure does, keeps it, and a test substitutes a FakeTimeProvider.
        • Page policies. One AddAuthorizationCore call (:85-101) registers three policies: NotificationPageRequirement.PolicyName carrying a plain NotificationPageRequirement (:87-89), NotificationPageRequirement.ManagePolicyName carrying one built with NotificationPermissions.Manage (:90-92), the policy for the history and compose pages, and TwoFactorPageRequirement.PolicyName carrying a TwoFactorPageRequirement (:98-100). TryAddEnumerable adds the transient NotificationPageAuthorizationHandler and TwoFactorPageAuthorizationHandler (:102-105). The comments state the shared rule: [Authorize] semantics (plus notifications:manage for the history and compose pages), except that a host without the notification UI (no AddNotificationUI) lets the request reach the router, which answers 404 instead of the sign-in challenge or Access Denied (:81-84); the two-factor account page follows the same rule for a host without AddTwoFactorUI, and its policy is registered unconditionally so the page's attribute resolves in every host (:94-97). Then the page permission guards: TryAddEnumerable registers PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator as a transient IConfigureOptions<AuthorizationOptions> (:110-111) and PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler as a transient IAuthorizationHandler (:112-113). The comment (:107-109, ADR-020) explains that there is one policy per permission a page declares through HasPagePermissionAttribute, discovered from the registered UI modules when the options are first built, so a host adds a guarded page without a registration call of its own [Rubric §26, Front-End Security].
        • Localization (ADR-027). AddLocalization() (:116) for IStringLocalizer<T>, then Decorate<IStringLocalizerFactory, PseudoStringLocalizerFactory>() (:123), registered unconditionally because the pseudo-locale transform is inert under every other culture and the pseudo locale is only ever activatable in Development (:118-122). TryAddTransient<MudBlazor.MudLocalizer, ResxMudLocalizer>() (:129) localizes MudBlazor's own component text; the comment (:125-128) records why TryAdd is authoritative regardless of host registration order, namely that AddMudServices registers no MudLocalizer of its own and a DI resolution test guards that assumption. AddLocalizationInterceptor<InvariantMudLocalizationInterceptor>() (:138) follows immediately: MudBlazor's own default interceptor reads its built-in English strings by assigning CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture (invariant, then the previous value back), which writes an AsyncLocal culture into the calling context; on a MAUI hybrid head, where that is the main thread, nothing resets it and the app pins to its launch language even after a culture switch reloads the thread defaults. InvariantMudLocalizationInterceptor reads the same resource under an explicit invariant culture instead, and registers with replace semantics so it wins whether AddMudServices ran before or after this call (ADR-027 Decision 10) (:131-137).
        • The one HTTP client. Both delegating handlers register transient (:142-143). Before the client itself, usesSameOriginProxy is computed from the raw configuration (:148-149): it is true only when Api:SameOriginApiEndpoint carries a value, which per the comment (:145-147) happens only on a WebAssembly client whose Server host opted into the same-origin API proxy (ADR-131) and handed that value down through /client-config; every other host (Server, MAUI, a WASM client of a host that did not opt in) keeps the pipeline unchanged. Then the named "APIClient" (:152-175), whose builder is kept in apiClient (:152) so a handler can be appended afterwards. Its factory resolves IOptions<ApiSettings> (:159) and sets client.BaseAddress = new Uri(apiSettings.SameOriginApiEndpoint ?? apiSettings.ApiEndpoint!, UriKind.Absolute) (:164): the same-origin proxy base, when present, replaces the gateway URL for data calls, and the comment (:161-163) notes the bootstrap has already resolved it to an absolute address. There is deliberately no hand-written endpoint guard, and the comment says why (:154-158): resolving .Value runs the ApiSettingsValidator registered above, so a missing [Required] endpoint already fails as an OptionsValidationException, and a second check would only give the same failure a different, less informative exception. client.Timeout is pinned to HttpResilienceDefaults.TotalRequestTimeout (:170), and the comment (:166-169) says why it matters: this is the one time limit on the client in every render mode, because WebAssembly and MAUI add no resilience handler and the Blazor web host (AddMmcaBlazorWebHost) removes the one AddServiceDefaults() puts on every factory client; it is the shared 90-second total-request timeout rather than the BCL's 100-second default [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity]. Default headers are cleared and Accept: application/json added (:171-172), and the two handlers chain in order (:174-175) so every outgoing call carries both the bearer token and the active UI culture as Accept-Language (:140-141). When usesSameOriginProxy is true, SameOriginProxyRequestHandler is registered transient and appended as the innermost handler (:177-183); the comment (:179-180) gives the reason for that position: it must see, and strip, every Authorization header the outer handlers or a service's DefaultRequestHeaders attached, and it stamps the proxy's CSRF header [Rubric §26, Front-End Security].
        • Facades. services.AddCommonUiFacades() (:187), factored out so a bUnit harness can register exactly these three without pulling in the whole shared-UI surface (:185-186).
        • Scoped services, all via TryAdd so several composing hosts cannot double-register: IAuthUIService to AuthUIService (:190); IEmailConfirmationUIService to EmailConfirmationUIService (:194, the /confirm-email page's client per ADR-116; a separate interface rather than new IAuthUIService members, so a consumer's own IAuthUIService implementation keeps compiling, per the comment at :192-193); ISignInLinkUIService (:198) and IPasskeyUIService (:203, ADR-139), both mapped onto the framework's AuthUIService so a redeemed link or a passkey sign-in stores its tokens through the same path a password sign-in does (:196-197, :200-202; the passkey client is inert until a host offers passkeys through SignIn:OfferPasskeys or renders the passkeys panel); IOidcDiscoveryUIService to OidcDiscoveryUIService (:207, home-realm discovery for the sign-in page's "Sign in with your organization" step, inert until the host configures an OIDC provider that declares email domains, per :205-206); ILegalAcceptanceUIService to LegalAcceptanceUIService (:211, the terms-acceptance client behind TermsAcceptanceGate, registered for every host and inert until a host renders the gate, per :209-210); OAuthFlowStateStore (:215, binding an OAuth completion to the flow this client started so a deep-linked completion code from someone else's provider round trip is dropped instead of exchanged, per :213-214); ListPageStateService (:216), ListPageQueryStateService (:217), NavigationHistoryService (:218); ThemeService (:221, ADR-028); ICultureApplier defaulting to EndpointCultureApplier (:227); ViewerTimeZone (:231, the viewer's browser time zone, so UTC instants such as notification and session times render on the clock the person reads, per :229-230); IPublicLinkBuilder defaulting to NavigationPublicLinkBuilder (:237); and the per-user preference writer and reader, ApiUserPreferenceWriter and ApiUserPreferenceReader (:240-241), documented as best-effort and a no-op for an anonymous user (:239). Two singletons close the list: TryAddSingleton<IOAuthUISettings, DefaultOAuthUISettings>() (:245), a no-op default that a downstream app replaces, and TryAddSingleton<IForbiddenReExecutionDetector, NoForbiddenReExecutionDetector>() (:250), the not-found page's "is this a 403 re-execution" question, which always answers false because a WebAssembly or MAUI head has no request to read; the Blazor Web host replaces it with the request-reading one (:247-249).
        • Capabilities. AddDeviceCapabilityDefaults() (:254, ADR-042) so every capability contract resolves on every head, registered here specifically so MAUI and browser hosts can override afterwards under last-registration-wins (:252-253).
      • AddCommonUiFacades() (:278-284): three TryAddScoped calls, IToastService to MudToastService (:280), IAppDialogService to MudAppDialogService (:281) and IPendingToastService to PendingToastService (:282), the toast that survives a forceLoad navigation and is injected by the shared layout's PendingToastHost. Its doc comment (:259-277) is the clearest statement of the facade rule anywhere in the codebase: apart from the two Mud-backed implementations (and the ConfirmationDialog they open), the only framework types that name MudBlazor's ISnackbar / IDialogService are the DeleteConfirmation component, which injects IDialogService directly to show its typed dialog, and StaleToastSweeper, which injects ISnackbar to remove toasts a navigation left behind (pages, other components and the Result helpers depend on the contracts); they are scoped to match the MudBlazor services they wrap, and the method is called both by AddUIShared and by the shipped bUnit base so a component test resolves the facades without the rest of the shared-UI surface.
      • AddClientAuthSessionCookieSync() (:291-295): one TryAddScoped<ISessionCookieSync, JsFetchSessionCookieSync>() (:293), the bridge that mirrors the client's in-memory tokens into the HttpOnly cookie read during server-side SSR prerender. Called from both the Blazor Server host and the WebAssembly client (:286-290).
      • AddWasmFormFactor() (:303-304): registers IFormFactor to WasmFormFactor as a singleton. The doc comment names the two alternatives (:297-302): AddCommonWebFormFactor() from MMCA.Common.UI.Web on the Blazor Server head, AddMauiFormFactor() from MMCA.Common.UI.Maui on the MAUI head.
      • AddUserAdministrationUI<TUserDto>() (:321-331), the ADR-116 UI opt-in for user administration: registers IUserAdminUIService<TUserDto> to UserAdminService<TUserDto> (:323), then forwards IUserAdminActionsUIService to the same instance rather than registering it a second time (:327-328), so the actions the component performs and the reads the app makes go through one instance (and one substitute, in a test), per the comment at :325-326. The doc comment (:306-320) states the call convention (once per app, after AddUIShared, with the app's own administration DTO) and that an app which serves no administration endpoints registers nothing and the component the service backs is simply never rendered.
      • AddRoleAdministrationUI() (:347-352): the non-generic ADR-116 sibling, registering IRoleAdminUIService to RoleAdminService (:349). Its doc comment (:333-346) explains why it takes no type parameter unlike AddUserAdministrationUI<TUserDto>(): roles and permissions are strings the framework already owns, so there is no app DTO to name (:340-341).
      • AddMachineClientAdministrationUI() (:362-367), the ADR-140 opt-in: IMachineClientAdminUIService to MachineClientAdminService (:364), the client the MachineClientAdmin page reads and writes the app's Admin/MachineClients endpoints through (:354-361).
      • AddSupportAccessLogUI() (:380-385), the ADR-137 opt-in: IViewAsGrantsUIService to ViewAsGrantsService (:382), the client the SupportAccessLog page reads the app's Admin/ViewAsGrants endpoint through (:369-379).
      • AddAuditHistoryUI() (:399-404), the ADR-075 opt-in: IAuditHistoryUIService to AuditHistoryService (:401), the HTTP client an AuditHistoryPanel's FetchPage delegate reads an AuditHistoryControllerBase endpoint through; the doc comment (:387-398) adds that calling it again changes nothing and an app's own registration made first is kept.
      • AddOfflineWriteQueue(Action<OfflineWriteQueueOptions>? configure = null) (:417-429): the opt-in durable offline write queue (ADR-144). It registers IOfflineWriteQueue to OfflineWriteQueue scoped (:419), because the browser connectivity service and local store it reads are scoped (:407-408), TimeProvider.System unless one is registered (:420), and OfflineWriteQueueOptions with the optional callback applied (:422-426). The doc comment (:406-414) notes that Common's MainLayout already hosts the OfflineWriteNotifier that drains and reports the queue.
      • AddOfflineWriteHandler<THandler>() (:437-443), constrained to THandler : class, IOfflineWriteHandler (:438): one TryAddEnumerable of a scoped IOfflineWriteHandler (:440), the replay handler for one write kind, so registering the same handler type again adds nothing (:431-434).
      • AddFeatureFlagAdministrationUI(params string[] sources) (:458-467), the ADR-031 opt-in: guards sources (:460), registers IFeatureFlagAdminUIService to FeatureFlagAdminService (:462) and appends the sources to FeatureFlagAdminUIOptions.Sources (:463-464). Each source is the API route prefix of one service's FeatureFlagsControllerBase (for example Admin/Conference/FeatureFlags), so a multi-service host lists every service's flags in one table (:451-453).
      • AddUIModule<TModule>() (:487-497), constrained to TModule : class, IUIModule (:488): a Scrutor scan FromAssemblyOf<TModule>() registering every IEntityService<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> implementation scoped as its implemented interfaces (:490-494), then AddSingleton<IUIModule, TModule>() (:496). The doc comment (:469-482) records the deliberate boundary: this is the two-step prologue every module's Add{Module}UI() opens with, and module-specific services stay with the caller afterwards, so a module whose service must beat a shared default still controls its own registration order. The type-parameter doc (:483-486) states the constraint that follows from using the descriptor's assembly as the scan root: it must live alongside the module's entity services and Razor pages. That same IUIModule registration is what PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator enumerates to find guarded pages.
    • Why it's built this way: TryAdd throughout is both a safety property (several composing hosts calling AddUIShared cannot double-register) and the override mechanism (a host that registers its own implementation before the call wins). Several ordering choices push in the opposite direction and are called out in comments because they are load-bearing: ICultureApplier's default round-trips a server /culture/set endpoint that a MAUI hybrid head does not have, so hybrids override it after AddUIShared (:223-226); IPublicLinkBuilder's default resolves against the browser origin, which is wrong for a MAUI WebView whose origin is a virtual host nobody else can open, so that is overridden after as well (:233-236); and IForbiddenReExecutionDetector's default answers false everywhere until the Blazor Web host replaces it (:247-249). InvariantMudLocalizationInterceptor follows the same head-dependent pattern one layer down: MudBlazor's own interceptor is correct everywhere except the MAUI hybrid main thread, so the replacement is registered unconditionally here rather than left to the affected head to override, because replace semantics make the registration order irrelevant (:131-138). SameOriginProxyRequestHandler is the one registration decided by configuration rather than by order: it is added only when Api:SameOriginApiEndpoint is present (:148-149, :177-183), so a host that never opts in carries no trace of it in its pipeline. The page permission policies avoid ordering altogether by deferring discovery to options build time (:107-111). Read together, the file encodes a rule worth carrying into any new registration: a contract whose correct implementation depends on the head is defaulted here and replaced later (or, where replace semantics make order irrelevant, registered outright), while a contract that is the same everywhere is TryAdded and left alone. The opt-ins follow the same principle one level up: nothing else in the framework calls any of them (:315-316, :342-343, :358-359, :375-376, :394-395, :413, :453), so an app that serves none of those endpoints registers nothing and the corresponding component is simply never rendered.
    • Where it's used: called once at startup by all six consuming UI hosts (ADC's MMCA.ADC.UI.Web, MMCA.ADC.UI.Web.Client and MAUI MMCA.ADC.UI, plus the three Store equivalents), each followed by the per-module Add{Module}UI() calls, which are usually one-liners over AddUIModule<TModule>(), for example MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:24 and MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:19. AddCommonUiFacades() has a second caller outside any host, the shipped bUnit base (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.UI/Infrastructure/BunitComponentTestBase.cs:54). The administration, audit, offline and feature-flag opt-ins are each meant to be called once per app, after AddUIShared (for example :311, :338), by an app that opts into the corresponding surface; nothing inside the framework itself calls any of them. The "APIClient" configured here is the client every EntityServiceBase<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType>-derived service resolves. The assembly this class lives in is also the one UISharedAssemblyReference names for the architecture fitness suite.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the Store citation (MMCA.Store/.../MMCA.Store.Identity.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:19) is carried over from the prior section and was not re-read in this pass; MMCA.Store is outside this guide's verified scope.

    BreakpointConstants

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Common · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/BreakpointConstants.cs:9 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: a one-method static helper that answers "is this viewport a mobile viewport?", so C# viewport detection and the CSS media-query boundary agree on one number.
    • Depends on: MudBlazor.Breakpoint (NuGet, imported at BreakpointConstants.cs:1). Nothing first-party.
    • Concept introduced, the single authoritative breakpoint. [Rubric §22, Responsive & Cross-Browser] assesses whether a codebase has one definition of "small screen" rather than a magic number re-chosen per component; this class embodies it by making the mobile/desktop split a named predicate. The doc comment (BreakpointConstants.cs:11-15) pins the threshold as MudBlazor's Xs or Sm breakpoint (< 960 px) and states plainly that this is not the sidebar boundary: the layout's sidebar collapses separately, below 1024 px. So this class is the one definition of "mobile" for the data-grid-versus-cards switch, not for every responsive decision. [Rubric §20, Design System & Theming] applies for the same reason: one named threshold keeps every list page switching modes at the same width instead of at slightly different ones.
    • Walkthrough: the type has exactly one member. IsMobileBreakpoint(Breakpoint breakpoint) (BreakpointConstants.cs:16-17) is expression-bodied and returns breakpoint is Breakpoint.Xs or Breakpoint.Sm. That pattern is the whole rule: Md and wider is desktop, and there is no third state.
    • Why it's built this way: static and dependency-free, so a component can call it without injecting anything, and moving the mobile threshold is a one-line edit rather than a hunt through component code.
    • Where it's used: exactly one production call site, DataGridListPageBase<TDto>'s viewport-change handler NotifyBrowserViewportChangeAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Common/DataGridListPageBase.cs:410), which sets IsMobile from it at line 414 and, on a desktop-to-mobile transition, resets MobileCurrentPage to 1 and re-requests the mobile data (DataGridListPageBase.cs:416-420). That single assignment is what swaps a desktop MudDataGrid for the MobileInfiniteScrollList<TItem> card layout on every list page in both consumer apps.

    ComponentLifetimeExtensions

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Common · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/ComponentLifetimeExtensions.cs:18 · Level 0 · class (static, extension methods)

    • What it is: one extension method, LifetimeToken(this CancellationTokenSource?), that gives a component a cancellation token it can read at any point of its lifetime without risking an exception.
    • Depends on: System.Threading.CancellationTokenSource, CancellationToken and ObjectDisposedException (BCL). Nothing first-party.
    • Concept introduced, the always-safe lifetime token. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether a recurring hazard has one shared answer. Reading CancellationTokenSource.Token after Dispose() throws ObjectDisposedException, and a Blazor component's async continuation can easily run after the component is gone. The extension converts that failure mode into the correct behavior: a component that has ended gets a token that is already cancelled, so the in-flight call stops instead of throwing out of a dead render tree.
    • Walkthrough: LifetimeToken (ComponentLifetimeExtensions.cs:26-42) has three outcomes. A null source, or one whose IsCancellationRequested is already true, returns new CancellationToken(canceled: true) (:28-31). Otherwise it returns source.Token (:35) inside a try; an ObjectDisposedException (a source disposed without being cancelled first) is caught and also returns a cancelled token (:37-41), with the comment that the component is gone all the same.
    • Why it's built this way: an extension on the nullable source, rather than a wrapper type, so a component keeps its familiar _cts field and writes _cts.LifetimeToken() where it used to write _cts.Token. null is treated as ended (:28), which covers a component whose source was never created.
    • Where it's used: LatestLoadGuard reads its token through it (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/LatestLoadGuard.cs:58), and the ResultUiExtensions examples show _cts.LifetimeToken() as the call-site shape (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/ResultUiExtensions.cs:47, :63). The convention is enforced by ArchitectureRules.ComponentsReadTheirTokenThroughLifetimeToken (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Ui/ArchitectureRules.LifetimeTokens.cs:28), which fails the build on a direct _cts.Token read, wrapped for subclassing by LifetimeTokenConventionTestsBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Ui/LifetimeTokenConventionTestsBase.cs:13). It is on the shipped public surface (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/PublicAPI.Shipped.txt:1391).

    LatestLoadGuard

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Common · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/LatestLoadGuard.cs:38 · Level 0 · class (sealed, IDisposable)

    • What it is: a small per-page helper that keeps a routed component showing the load it asked for last, by giving every load a generation number and a cancellation token and cancelling the previous one as the next begins.
    • Depends on: System.Threading.CancellationTokenSource and ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf (BCL), and ComponentLifetimeExtensions for the token it hands out.
    • Concept introduced, generation-guarded supersession. [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] assesses the correctness of in-flight asynchronous state, and this is the canonical bug it looks for. The doc comment states it precisely (LatestLoadGuard.cs:5-10): Blazor reuses a routed component instance across route-parameter changes, so a page that opens entity 100 (slow response) and then navigates to entity 101 (fast response) receives 100's late answer after 101 has already rendered. Assigning it unconditionally leaves the URL on 101 while the page holds 100, and any action bound to the loaded entity then fires against the wrong record. Cancellation alone does not fix this, because a fetch that ignores its token still completes; the integer generation is the authoritative check. The same pattern appears at component scope inside MobileInfiniteScrollList<TItem>, which snapshots a generation before awaiting and drops the result if the world moved; LatestLoadGuard is that idea extracted into a reusable object so a detail page gets it in three lines. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] applies: the alternative is every page hand-rolling a token source, a counter and a dispose path.
    • Walkthrough: three private fields (LatestLoadGuard.cs:40-42): the current CancellationTokenSource?, the int _generation, and a _disposed flag.
      • Begin() (:50-59) is the entry point. It throws if the guard is disposed (:52), cancels and disposes the previous load through the private CancelAndDisposeCurrent() (:54), publishes a fresh token source (:55), increments the generation (:56), and returns the pair (CancellationToken Token, int Generation) (:58), with the token read as _cts.LifetimeToken() rather than _cts.Token (:58) so it is the always-safe token of ComponentLifetimeExtensions. Returning a tuple rather than exposing two properties is what makes the generation a snapshot: the caller holds the value it started with, so a later Begin() cannot retroactively change what it compares against.
      • IsCurrent(int generation) (:67) is the check after the await: !_disposed && generation == _generation. Disposal counts as not-current, so a component torn down mid-fetch also drops its answer instead of assigning into a dead render tree.
      • Dispose() (:70-79) is idempotent via the _disposed early return (:72-75) and cancels the in-flight load on the way out.
      • CancelAndDisposeCurrent() (:81-91) null-guards, then cancels, disposes and nulls the source, so the guard never double-disposes a token source and never leaks one.
      • The usage shape is spelled out as a <code> block in the doc comment (:15-31): a private readonly LatestLoadGuard _load = new(); field, var (token, generation) = _load.Begin(); at the top of OnParametersSetAsync, an if (!_load.IsCurrent(generation)) { return; } immediately after the await, and public void Dispose() => _load.Dispose();.
    • Why it's built this way: deliberately not thread-safe, and the doc comment says so in bold (:32-36). It is built for the renderer's synchronization context, where component lifecycle methods and event callbacks are already serialized, so the fields need no interlocking and the type stays allocation-cheap. That is a contract, not an oversight: sharing one instance across threads is documented as unsupported.
    • Where it's used: the framework's DetailPageBase exposes one as protected LatestLoadGuard LoadGuard { get; } = new(); and disposes it (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Common/DetailPageBase.cs:34, :95), so every detail page derived from it inherits the guard. RoleAdminEdit holds its own _load and runs the Begin() / IsCurrent(generation) shape directly (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs:42, :162, :174, :187), and ADC's public event, session and speaker detail pages and SessionCreate also call it (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/Pages/Public/Events/PublicEventDetail.razor.cs, Pages/Public/Sessions/PublicSessionDetail.razor.cs, Pages/Public/Speakers/PublicSpeakerDetail.razor.cs, Pages/Sessions/SessionCreate.razor.cs). It is on the shipped public surface (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/PublicAPI.Shipped.txt:37-41). It is also exercised by LatestLoadGuardTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Common/LatestLoadGuardTests.cs:11, six test methods covering Begin cancelling the prior token, generation advance, IsCurrent after supersession, and behavior after disposal) [Rubric §28, Front-End Testing]; DetailPageBaseTests covers the base-class wiring (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Pages/Common/DetailPageBaseTests.cs).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the guard is not thread-safe by contract, and a page that bypasses it (assigning a fetch result unconditionally) is not caught by any analyzer; adoption is by DetailPageBase inheritance or by hand, as RoleAdminEdit does.

    NavGroup

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Common · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/NavGroup.cs:23 · Level 0 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: the optional rendering description of one collapsible sidebar group, keyed by the NavItem Group string: its icon, whether it starts expanded, and its position within its section.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party at compile time (its doc comment cross-references NavItem and IUIModule).
    • Concept introduced, describing a group by key rather than by ownership. [Rubric §25, Navigation & Information Architecture] assesses whether a menu's structure is declared rather than hard-coded. A group has no owner: it exists because items carry the same Group key, and the doc comment (NavGroup.cs:8-12) makes the consequence explicit. A module may describe a group whose items another module contributes (for example a framework-owned entry an app wants to place), the first registered description of a key wins, and a group nobody describes renders as before: the folder icon, collapsed, in the order its first item appears. [Rubric §27, Internationalization] applies through what the record deliberately does not carry: no display text. The heading is still the Key resolved against the first item's TitleResource (NavGroup.cs:14-17, ADR-027).
    • Walkthrough: a positional record on one line (NavGroup.cs:23) with four parameters, three optional.
      • string Key: the NavItem.Group value the description applies to.
      • string? Icon = null: null keeps the folder icon.
      • bool Expanded = false: whether the group starts expanded.
      • int Order = 0: the group's position among the units of its section, where each group and the section's ungrouped items (which count as order 0) are units; ties keep first-appearance order (NavGroup.cs:4-6, :22).
    • Why it's built this way: a separate record rather than more parameters on NavItem, so group metadata is stated once per group instead of repeated on every item, and so an app can arrange a group it does not own. Every member defaults to the old behavior, so a host that declares no group renders exactly as it did. The menu realizes it in two steps: NavMenu.OnInitializedAsync collects every module's NavGroups with TryAdd, which is the first-registered-wins rule (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Layout/NavMenu.razor.cs:79-83), and the private Arrange groups a section by key in first-appearance order, applies the description's Icon ?? Icons.Material.Filled.Folder, Expanded ?? false and Order ?? 0 to each NavUnit, then stable-sorts the units by Order (NavMenu.razor.cs:51-66).
    • Where it's used: declared through the defaulted IReadOnlyList<NavGroup> NavGroups => [] member of IUIModule (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Interfaces/IUIModule.cs:22) and consumed by NavMenu. ADC's ConferenceUIModule is the consumer example: it describes its organizer layout, with Conference Day and Program starting expanded and the framework's Notifications group placed last (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/ConferenceUIModule.cs:95-99). Covered by NavMenuOrderingTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Layout/NavMenuOrderingTests.cs:39, :82, :101, :124), which pins the undescribed default, a described icon and expanded state, group ordering with ties, and the first-declaration-wins rule across modules [Rubric §28, Front-End Testing]. ADR-067 records the UI shell composition it belongs to.

    NavSection

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Common · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/NavSection.cs:7 · Level 0 · enum

    • What it is: classifies a sidebar entry into one of three audience groups: everyone, signed-in users, or administrators.
    • Depends on: nothing. Consumed by NavItem and by the shared nav menu.
    • Concept introduced, audience as a first-class navigation axis. [Rubric §25, Navigation & Information Architecture] assesses whether the menu structure is declarative and audience-aware rather than a hand-maintained pile of conditionals. [Rubric §11, Security] touches it too, but with an important distinction worth internalizing early: the section is a grouping hint, not an authorization check. What actually hides a link is RequiredRole / RequiredClaim on NavItem, evaluated by the menu (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Layout/NavMenu.razor.cs:125-126), and what actually protects the destination is page-level and API-level authorization.
    • Walkthrough: three values in declaration order, and the order is itself a contract because the doc comment states sections render in enum declaration order (NavSection.cs:5). General (:10) is for items visible to everyone, anonymous and authenticated alike. User (:13) is for signed-in non-admin items. Admin (:16) is for administrator items.
    • Why it's built this way: an enum rather than a string gives the renderer exhaustive, typo-proof matching, which is exactly what NavMenu.razor.cs relies on when it partitions the flattened item list into three sections with i.Section is NavSection.General / User / Admin, arranging each one into its units (NavMenu.razor.cs:130-132). It is a plain C# enum rather than a smart enumeration because no member needs to carry data or behavior, which is the default this codebase commits to (ADR-104).
    • Where it's used: the Section parameter of NavItem (NavItem.cs:16, defaulting to General), and the three-way partition at NavMenu.razor.cs:130-132. NotificationUIModule shows both non-default values in one file: its inbox item is Section: NavSection.User (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/NotificationUIModule.cs:19) and its push-management item is Section: NavSection.Admin (:20).

    PersistedTally

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Common · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/PrerenderStateBudget.cs:104 · Level 0 · class (private sealed, nested in PrerenderStateBudget)

    • What it is: the per-state running total behind PrerenderStateBudget's page-wide cap: the set of keys already persisted into one PersistentComponentState and the UTF-8 JSON bytes they add up to.
    • Depends on: HashSet<string> and StringComparer.Ordinal (BCL). Nothing first-party.
    • Concept introduced: none of its own; the budget concept is taught at PrerenderStateBudget. What this type adds is how a pass boundary is detected without any hook from the framework.
    • Walkthrough: two fields, _keys (an ordinal HashSet<string>, PrerenderStateBudget.cs:106) and _totalBytes (:107).
      • Fits(string key, int bytes, int budget) (:113-122): if key is already in the set, the tally clears both fields first (:115-119), because one persistence pass cannot persist a key twice, so a repeat marks a later pass over the same state instance (:110-111). It then returns _totalBytes + bytes <= budget (:121).
      • Add(string key, int bytes) (:124-128) records the key and adds its bytes.
    • Why it's built this way: split into a check and a commit so the caller can count a key only after PersistAsJson has accepted it (PrerenderStateBudget.cs:95-98), leaving the tally untouched if the write throws. It holds no lock itself; the caller locks the instance around both calls (:86).
    • Where it's used: only inside PrerenderStateBudget, which keeps one per state in a ConditionalWeakTable<PersistentComponentState, PersistedTally> (PrerenderStateBudget.cs:51) and creates it on first use (:85). Exercised indirectly through PrerenderStateBudgetTests (see PrerenderStateBudget).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the restart-on-repeated-key rule has no dedicated test: no call in PrerenderStateBudgetTests.cs persists the same key twice into one state (its calls at :33-34, :56-58, :83, :90 all use distinct keys per state).

    RoutePaths

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Common · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/RoutePaths.cs:7 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: the route-path constants owned by the shared UI package itself. Module-specific routes live in their own *RoutePaths classes.
    • Depends on: nothing.
    • Concept introduced, one source of truth for route strings. [Rubric §25, Navigation & Information Architecture] also covers URL hygiene: a literal "/profile/sessions" typed into four components is four places to get a rename wrong. The class comment (RoutePaths.cs:3-6) states both halves of the convention: centralized paths shared across all UI modules and hosts live here, and module-specific paths live in their own class. That convention is followed consistently across the workspace, by NotificationRoutePaths in this package and by ConferenceRoutePaths, EngagementRoutePaths and IdentityRoutePaths in the consumer modules.
    • Walkthrough: two public static readonly string members.
      • Home = "/" (RoutePaths.cs:9).
      • Sessions = "/profile/sessions" (:16), the signed-in-devices page. Its doc comment (:11-15) records why it belongs to the framework rather than to an app: the page is framework-owned (MMCA.Common.UI.Pages.Auth.Sessions), lists the user's live refresh sessions with per-device and account-wide sign-out, and is reachable from the shared nav menu's authenticated section, so a consuming app gets it without doing any routing work.
