    ListPageQueryStateService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/ListPageQueryStateService.cs:28 · Level 2 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the two-way translator between a ListPageState and the browser address bar, so browser back/forward, a refresh and a link pasted into chat all restore the same filtered, sorted, paged view.
    • Depends on: ListPageState, ColumnFilterState and QueryStringCodec, which parses and appends query strings, so the UI package takes no query-helper dependency; externals NavigationManager and StringValues.
    • Concept introduced, the URL as shareable state. [Rubric §25, Navigation & Information Architecture] assesses whether the address bar reflects what the user is looking at; this class is that contract for every list page. The remarks (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:13-27) document the reserved keys and why they are terse (they end up in shareable links): p (0-indexed desktop page), ps (page size), mp (1-indexed mobile page), s (sort column), sd (desc only, since ascending is the default), d (1 only, since comfortable density is the default), q (free-text search), f:<name> for any other named filter and c:<property> for a grid column filter, written <operator>:<value> because MudDataGrid operators never contain a colon (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:24). Defaults are omitted entirely, so a pristine list page has a clean URL. [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] applies because this is the second of the three transports the same record travels over.
    • Walkthrough
      • The key names are private constants (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:30-42), including the "search" filter name that maps to q by convention, the c: prefix and its : separator (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:38-39), and the desc/1 markers. A separate MaxPageSize constant of 1000 (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:47) caps the page size a URL may ask for; its summary (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:44-46) ties it to the same ceiling KeysetPageRequest.MaxPageSize states.
      • ReadCurrent() (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:52-56) is the instance entry point: it resolves the absolute URI from the injected NavigationManager and hands the query to the parser.
      • ParseQueryString (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:63) is deliberately static and public, documented as a pure helper exposed for unit testing without a NavigationManager (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:58-62). It parses through QueryStringCodec.Parse (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:65), then reads the three integers through TryGetInt (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:273-283, which parses with CultureInfo.InvariantCulture and falls back to the supplied default rather than throwing). Out-of-range values get the same fallback as unparsable ones (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:67-71): the page is floored at 0, the mobile page at 1, and a page size outside 1..1000 collapses to 0, the page default, through ClampPageSize (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:271). The inline comment states the reason: a hand-edited or stale link with p=-3 or ps=5000 must not leave the list stuck on a failing fetch. It then treats a blank sort value as no sort (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:74-81), matches desc case-insensitively (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:86) but the dense marker 1 ordinally (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:92), then hands the rest to ParseFilters (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:95, body at ListPageQueryStateService.cs:191-220), which skips empty values, folds q into the search filter, strips the f: prefix off named filters and turns each c: key into a ColumnFilterState (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:212-216). Both dictionaries land on the returned state (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:105-106).
      • TryParseColumnFilter (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:256-268) splits the value at its first colon. A value with no colon or no operator (separator <= 0, ListPageQueryStateService.cs:259) is a hand-edited link and is ignored, and an empty value after the colon becomes a null value for an operator that takes none, such as is empty (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:251-255).
      • BuildPath (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:115) is the inverse, and the omission rules are visible one by one: page only when > 0 (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:122), page size only when > 0 (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:127), mobile page only when > 1 (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:132), sd only when a sort column exists and is descending (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:137-144), d only when dense (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:146-149). Filters go through AddFilterParameters (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:151, body at ListPageQueryStateService.cs:223-249), which writes q, the f: keys and one c:<property> key per column filter that has an operator (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:242-248). With no parameters at all it returns the bare base path, otherwise it appends them with QueryStringCodec.AddQueryString (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:153-155).
      • ReplaceState (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:174) writes the URL back using NavigationOptions { ReplaceHistoryEntry = true } (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:187) so filter changes do not pollute the back stack.
    • Why it's built this way: the most instructive part is the guard in ReplaceState (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:179-184), which drops the write when the current path no longer matches the owning basePath. The remarks (ListPageQueryStateService.cs:164-173) record the diagnosed defect: a grid-state write is inherently deferred (a debounced search, a late ServerData completion), so it can land after the user has already navigated away. Building from the then-current URI used to stamp grid parameters onto the next page's URL and issue a spurious navigation that disposed it mid-load, and detail pages reached by clicking a list row had their first data fetch canceled about 66ms in, leaving them stuck on their loading state.
    • Where it's used: registered TryAddScoped (DependencyInjection.cs:217) and injected into DataGridListPageBase<TDto> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Common/DataGridListPageBase.cs:30), which reads the URL on initialization and on parameter changes (DataGridListPageBase.cs:266 and DataGridListPageBase.cs:337) and writes it back after a grid or filter change (DataGridListPageBase.cs:1720 and DataGridListPageBase.cs:1797).

    ListPageStateService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/ListPageStateService.cs:70 · Level 2 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the per-circuit memory of list-page state, keyed by route, with an optional write-through to sessionStorage so the state survives things a circuit-scoped dictionary cannot.
    • Depends on: ListPageState and LazyJsModule; externals IJSRuntime, IJSObjectReference and the nav-interop.js module shipped in the package's wwwroot.
    • Concept introduced, a synchronous fast path with an asynchronous durable path. [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] assesses how state survives lifecycle boundaries; this class answers with two tiers. The class comment (ListPageStateService.cs:62-69) names exactly what the durable tier buys: state survives circuit teardowns, forceLoad: true navigations and the SSR to WASM render-mode transition. The synchronous dictionary matters just as much, because it is safe to read from OnInitialized during prerender, when JS interop does not exist yet.
    • Walkthrough
      • Two constants set the contract: the module path ./_content/MMCA.Common.UI/nav-interop.js (ListPageStateService.cs:72) and the mmca.lps: session-key prefix (ListPageStateService.cs:73). State is a plain Dictionary<string, ListPageState> (ListPageStateService.cs:75) plus one LazyJsModule (ListPageStateService.cs:76).
      • GetState (ListPageStateService.cs:83-84) is a GetValueOrDefault and is documented as safe to call during SSR prerender (ListPageStateService.cs:78-82). SaveState (ListPageStateService.cs:91-92) stores in memory only.
      • UpdateScrollPosition (ListPageStateService.cs:99-102) is the fast path for scroll events: it uses a with expression to preserve every other field, and creates a minimal entry when none exists yet, for the case where the user scrolls before the grid has fired its first save.
      • HydrateFromSessionAsync (ListPageStateService.cs:110) invokes sessionGet on the JS module (ListPageStateService.cs:120, the export at MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/wwwroot/nav-interop.js:12) and adopts any persisted snapshot (ListPageStateService.cs:121-124).
      • PersistToSessionAsync (ListPageStateService.cs:137) does the reverse through sessionSet (ListPageStateService.cs:152, nav-interop.js:24), returning early when there is nothing in memory to write (ListPageStateService.cs:139-142).
      • ClearAsync (ListPageStateService.cs:169) forgets every list page's state: it clears the in-memory dictionary first (ListPageStateService.cs:171), then calls sessionRemoveByPrefix with the mmca.lps: prefix (ListPageStateService.cs:181, the export at nav-interop.js:45), leaving the tab's other sessionStorage keys alone. Its summary (ListPageStateService.cs:161-168) gives the reason: the search and filters belong to the account that typed them, sessionStorage outlives the session in the same tab, and clearing memory before the first await means a caller that cannot await still drops it at once.
      • All three interop methods share one exception filter, catch (Exception ex) when (IsInteropUnavailable(ex)) (ListPageStateService.cs:126, ListPageStateService.cs:154 and ListPageStateService.cs:183). IsInteropUnavailable (ListPageStateService.cs:212-213) matches InvalidOperationException (prerender), JSDisconnectedException (a torn-down circuit), JSException (a browser-side failure such as Safari Private mode or an exceeded quota) and TaskCanceledException (an interop timeout or cancellation); the comment above it (ListPageStateService.cs:209-211) notes it is the same set PendingToastService swallows. The catch in PersistToSessionAsync (ListPageStateService.cs:156-157) records why it matters there: the call is fire-and-forget from the grid page, so an escaping exception would be an unobserved fault.
      • The private GetModuleAsync (ListPageStateService.cs:190-204) converts an unavailable runtime into a null module rather than an exception, which is what makes the public methods' early returns read cleanly. DisposeAsync (ListPageStateService.cs:207) simply forwards to the module wrapper.
    • Why it's built this way: the degradation contract here is "never let storage failures break the calling page", which is why this class swallows what LazyJsModule deliberately does not. Scoped registration means one instance per circuit, so the in-memory dictionary is naturally per-user without any keying by identity.
    • Where it's used: registered TryAddScoped (DependencyInjection.cs:216) and injected into DataGridListPageBase<TDto> (DataGridListPageBase.cs:29), which reads it during state restore (DataGridListPageBase.cs:268), hydrates from session on first render (DataGridListPageBase.cs:503), records scroll offsets (DataGridListPageBase.cs:688), and saves plus persists after grid and density changes (DataGridListPageBase.cs:1699-1726 and DataGridListPageBase.cs:1792-1801). JwtAuthenticationStateProvider takes it as an optional dependency (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:43) and calls ClearAsync on sign-in and sign-out (JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:141, JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:149 and JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:153-154); the session-ended handler cannot await, so it relies on the synchronous in-memory clear (JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:147-148).

    MudToastService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/MudToastService.cs:33 · Level 2 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the MudBlazor-backed IToastService. It is one of only two types in the framework that name a component-library service, the other being its sibling MudAppDialogService.
    • Depends on: IToastService (the contract implemented at MudToastService.cs:33) and ToastSeverity (the vendor-neutral level, taken as a Show parameter at line 56 and switched over at lines 180-186); MudBlazor's ISnackbar (held in a private field, line 35), Snackbar, Severity, Variant, Color and SnackbarOptions, and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Rendering.RenderTreeBuilder (ASP.NET Core) for the one method that renders markup (lines 63-69).
    • Concept introduced, the vendor boundary. [Rubric §20, Design System, Theming & UI Consistency] assesses whether the app depends on its own design vocabulary rather than on a specific component library's API. Every page, component and Result helper in both applications depends on IToastService; only this class and MudAppDialogService know that MudBlazor exists, and the DI comment says so outright (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:225-230). [Rubric §14, Testability & Test Strategy] is the practical payoff: a test records toasts against the interface without rendering a snackbar host, which is how ResultUiExtensions.NotifyOnFailure can be tested at all (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/ResultUiExtensions.cs:255,267). [Rubric §1, SOLID Principles] covers the shape: an internal implementation behind a public interface means no consumer can name the concrete type even by accident. The class doc comment also states why toast text is not duplicated into a second screen-reader channel: MmcaThemeProviders hosts MudBlazor's MudSnackbarProvider inside a role="status" aria-live="polite" element, so the rendered toast is itself the live-region content, and pushing the same sentence through a second channel would announce it twice and make every text locator ambiguous.
    • Walkthrough
      • The class holds ISnackbar in a private field (_snackbar, line 35) set by an explicit constructor (line 41) rather than a primary-constructor parameter; the two are behaviorally identical, only the field-access syntax changed. Beside it sit the pinned-toast bookkeeping, a List<Snackbar> (_pinned, line 38) and a Lock (_pinnedSync, line 39).
      • Four one-liners cover the common levels: Success, Info, Warning and Error (lines 44, 47, 50, 53), each a direct _snackbar.Add(message, Severity.X). Show(message, severity) (line 56) is the same call with the level chosen at runtime. None of these is pinned, so they never touch the tracking list.
      • ShowPersistent(title, body, severity) (line 59) is the push-notification shape. It renders a two-line body through a RenderTreeBuilder (a bolded title, a line break, then the body, lines 63-69) and sets RequireInteraction = true with Variant.Filled (lines 75-76). The comment states the rule (lines 73-74): the message arrived unprompted, so it must survive until the user has actually looked at the screen rather than expiring on the default timer. The whole Add call is wrapped in AddPinned(...) (line 60) so the toast is tracked and capped.
      • ShowAction(message, actionText, onAction, severity, requireInteraction) (line 80) is the undo-style toast. A local Configure function (line 96) sets Action and ActionColor (lines 98-99) and adapts MudBlazor's click signature to the caller's parameterless delegate by discarding the Snackbar instance MudBlazor passes (line 103). requireInteraction is opt-in: when false the toast goes straight to _snackbar.Add (line 93) so the host's own snackbar timing applies and the toast is not tracked; when true it goes through AddPinned (line 89) and Configure states both RequireInteraction and Variant.Filled outright rather than relying on MudBlazor's null default (comment at lines 107-110, values at lines 111-112).
      • AddPinned(Func<Snackbar?> add) (line 122) is the pinned-toast cap. MudBlazor shows at most SnackbarConfiguration.MaxDisplayedSnackbars at once and queues the rest out of sight, and a pinned toast never expires, so a burst of pushes would fill every slot and each newer toast would wait invisibly. Under the lock (line 124), when tracked toasts have reached the cap (_snackbar.Configuration.MaxDisplayedSnackbars, line 130) it removes the oldest one this service raised (lines 131-136), then adds the new one and subscribes ForgetPinned to its OnClose (lines 141-146). The newest is therefore always the one on screen. The class comment states the scope: only toasts this service added are ever removed, timed toasts and snackbars raised elsewhere are untouched (MudToastService.cs:18-27), and the tracking is per circuit or per app because the service is scoped, with a lock because close events arrive on timer threads (lines 28-31). A null return from add() means the host's duplicate prevention suppressed the toast, so there is nothing to track (comment at line 140).
      • Two helpers keep the list honest. ForgetPinned (line 165) drops a toast from the list when its OnClose fires, under the same lock. ForgetRemovedPinned (line 156) catches removals that raise no event (ISnackbar.Remove, RemoveByKey, Clear): when fewer snackbars are shown than the cap, nothing is queued, so any tracked toast absent from ShownSnackbars is gone and is pruned (lines 158-161).
      • Map(ToastSeverity) (line 178) projects the neutral enum onto MudBlazor's with an explicit switch over all five members plus a Normal default (lines 180-186). It is written out rather than cast on purpose: the two enums agree numerically today, and an implicit dependency on that would break silently the day either side gains a member (comment at lines 173-177).
      • The cap behavior is pinned by MudToastServicePinnedCapTests, which builds the service over a SnackbarConfiguration with MaxDisplayedSnackbars = Cap (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/MudToastServicePinnedCapTests.cs:124).
      • Nothing wraps onAction. The absence is a documented contract, pinned by a test that asserts a throwing callback propagates (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/MudToastServiceTests.cs:49-59): a caller whose work can fail guards it instead of discovering the failure as a swallowed no-op.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the vendor type behind a facade is what makes the component library swappable in principle and mockable in practice, and it is the reason the framework ships AddCommonUiFacades() as its own registration (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:278-284), factored out so a bUnit harness can register exactly these three services (toast, dialog and pending toast) without pulling in the whole shared-UI surface (comment at lines 165-166). Every method returns void: a toast is fire-and-forget by design, and MudBlazor's ISnackbar.Add is synchronous. The pinned-toast eviction exists because a notification burst is the one case where fire-and-forget silently loses the newest message.
    • Where it's used: registered by AddCommonUiFacades with TryAddScoped (DependencyInjection.cs:280), which AddUIShared calls for every host (DependencyInjection.cs:187). Consumers resolve IToastService, never this type: the framework's NotificationListener raises an incoming push as a persistent toast (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Notifications/NotificationListener.razor:49), ResultUiExtensions.NotifyOnFailure turns a failed Result into one (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/ResultUiExtensions.cs:267), and ADC's LiveEventListener uses the action shape for its reconnect prompt (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Components/LiveEventListener.razor.cs:191,332). Its own behavior is pinned by MudToastServiceTests, which captures the options lambda and applies it to a fresh SnackbarOptions carrying MudBlazor's defaults, so the assertions see exactly what a rendered snackbar would (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/MudToastServiceTests.cs:163).
    • Caveats: ShowPersistent renders the title and body as content in a render fragment, so both are escaped by the renderer, but neither string is length-bounded in source: a long push body produces a correspondingly tall toast. Show, Success and the rest pass the caller's string straight to MudBlazor, so any localization has to happen before the call; the facade does not touch IStringLocalizer. The pinned-toast cap evicts only toasts this class raised and tracks them per scope, so two scopes (two circuits) never evict each other's toasts.

    PendingToastService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/PendingToastService.cs:13 · Level 2 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the sessionStorage-backed IPendingToastService, the toast that survives a full page reload. A toast raised through MudToastService lives in the current circuit or WebAssembly runtime, so one raised just before NavigateTo(url, forceLoad: true) dies with the page; this service parks it instead.
    • Depends on: IPendingToastService (implemented) and IAsyncDisposable (PendingToastService.cs:13), IJSRuntime via the primary constructor, a LazyJsModule over ./_content/MMCA.Common.UI/nav-interop.js (lines 18, 20), ToastSeverity, and the nested PendingToast payload.
    • Concept introduced, best-effort persistence across a reload. [Rubric §20, Design System, Theming & UI Consistency] covers consistent user feedback: a confirmation that vanishes because the page reloaded reads as silence. The service reuses the nav-interop.js module (sessionSet, sessionGet, sessionRemove) that ListPageStateService already uses (class comment, lines 6-12), under one fixed key, mmca.pendingToast (StorageKey, line 16). One toast is held at a time: queueing again overwrites it (IPendingToastService.cs:11).
    • Walkthrough
      • QueueAsync(severity, message, ct) (line 23) returns early for a blank message (lines 25-28), otherwise imports the module lazily and calls sessionSet with a new PendingToast (lines 32-33).
      • TakeAsync(ct) (line 42) reads with sessionGet (line 47), returns null when nothing is parked, and removes the entry with sessionRemove before returning it (line 55). The comment (lines 53-54) gives the reason: removing first means a second render, or a second tab restoring the session, cannot show the same toast twice. A blank message or an undefined severity is discarded as null (lines 57-59), so a tampered entry cannot reach the toast host.
      • Both methods swallow interop failure through IsInteropUnavailable (lines 72-73): prerender (InvalidOperationException), a torn-down circuit (JSDisconnectedException), a browser-side failure (JSException) and an interop timeout or cancellation (TaskCanceledException). The comment at line 37 of the queue path says why: the toast is a courtesy and must not fail the action that raised it.
      • DisposeAsync (line 68) forwards to the lazy module.
    • Why it's built this way: parking in sessionStorage rather than a cookie or server state keeps it per tab and off the wire. The interface also warns callers not to pass the page's lifetime token when the same action signs the user out of an [Authorize] page, because the re-render disposes the page and cancels that token, silently dropping the toast (IPendingToastService.cs:24-29).
    • Where it's used: registered by AddCommonUiFacades with TryAddScoped<IPendingToastService, PendingToastService>() (DependencyInjection.cs:282). The shared layout renders PendingToastHost (Layout/MainLayout.razor:19), which calls TakeAsync on its first interactive render (Components/Notifications/PendingToastHost.razor:18) and shows the result through IToastService. ADC's Profile page queues through it before a forced reload (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI/Pages/Users/Profile/Profile.razor.cs). Tests: MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/PendingToastServiceTests.cs.

    • What it is: the typed client contract for the machine-client admin page: list every client (revoked ones included), create one, rotate, promote and revoke its secret.

CreateAsync and RotateAsync return MachineClientSecretResponse and their docs say the secret comes back once (lines 17, 23); every other member returns the secret-free MachineClientResponse. Rotation is two-step: RotateAsync issues a secondary secret and PromoteAsync makes it the primary, so a caller can deploy the new secret before the old one stops working. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses credential handling; the return types keep a secret off every read path after the one that minted it.

    • Why it's built this way: the UI opt-in of machine clients (ADR-140), registered only by AddMachineClientAdministrationUI (DependencyInjection.cs:354-367).

(lines 54-57) replaces the complete stored permission set for one role in a single PUT, not an incremental add/remove, so the caller always sends the full desired set.

The roster is deliberately not a member: it is the app's generic paged entity endpoint, read through the standard entity service and handed to UserAdminList as its FetchPage delegate (type doc comment).

Implemented by UserAdminService<TUserDto>.

ADC and Store each ship their own user row shape (different columns for the admin grid), so the interface is generic rather than fixed to one DTO, and only the single-account read needs the parameter (the sessions and sign-ins reads return fixed framework responses): the write half in IUserAdminActionsUIService takes only an id and never returns a DTO, so it carries no type parameter of its own. [Rubric §1, SOLID Principles] reads the split as interface segregation again: a caller that only needs to lock or re-role an account depends on the narrower, non-generic interface.

(lines 32-34) reads the account's live (signed-in) sessions, newest first, from GET Admin/Users/{userId}/sessions; it is view only (doc comment, lines 25-28). GetSignInsAsync(userId, ...) (lines 43-45) reads the account's sign-in history from GET Admin/Users/{userId}/sign-ins: one row per sign-in, ended ones included, newest first, at most 50, also view only (doc comment, lines 36-39). The cap of 50 is stated by the doc comment; the client passes no limit, so it is the server's to enforce.

GetAllAsync, GetAsync(role, ...) and GetCatalogAsync are each a one-line call into it with a different URL and response type (lines 33-35, 38-47, 50-51). Only the write, SetStoredPermissionsAsync, needs its own method, because it is the one call whose response reader differs (a RolePermissionsResponse rather than a bare success) and whose HTTP verb is PUT.

(lines 38-47) null-checks role then appends Uri.EscapeDataString(role), so a role name with reserved URL characters still round-trips. GetCatalogAsync (lines 50-51) appends /catalog. SetStoredPermissionsAsync (lines 54-79) null-checks both arguments, builds {Endpoint}/{role}/permissions, and PUTs a SetRolePermissionsRequest wrapping the complete permission list (line 71), inside the same authenticate-retry-read wrapper as the private read helper but written out separately because it POSTs (in fact PUTs) rather than GETs. It is a plain AuthenticatedServiceBase subclass rather than an EntityServiceBase<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> one because roles are not a CRUD resource with create/delete: only read and one full-replace write exist.

(lines 105-109) wraps the single role in a one-element array and calls SetRolesAsync, the concrete implementation of the convenience member IUserAdminActionsUIService declares.     ISessionCookieSync

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/ISessionCookieSync.cs:8 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: a two-method contract for mirroring the client's in-memory tokens into the browser's HttpOnly auth cookies, and for clearing them again on logout. Both methods report whether the cookie jar was actually updated.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party. Implemented by JsFetchSessionCookieSync and, on a Blazor Server host that enabled the same-origin proxy, by HandoffSessionCookieSync (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/SameOriginProxy/HandoffSessionServices.cs:52); consumed by WasmTokenStorageService and by ServerTokenStorageService (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Services/ServerTokenStorageService.cs:51).
    • Concept introduced, the prerender visibility gap. A Blazor Web App renders a server-side pass before the interactive circuit exists. During that pass there is no Authorization header and no way to read the interactive client's in-memory access token, so an [Authorize] page opened by a deep link, an F5, or right-click "open in new tab" would bounce to /login even for a signed-in user. The interface doc says exactly that (ISessionCookieSync.cs:3-7). The cookie is the one thing both sides can see, so keeping it in step with the in-memory token is what makes fresh GETs work.
      • [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] assesses where browser credentials live. The target is an HttpOnly cookie, unreadable from JS, rather than localStorage.
      • [Rubric §25, Navigation, Routing & Information Architecture] assesses whether deep links behave. This contract is the reason a bookmarked authorized route renders instead of redirecting.
    • Walkthrough: two members, both returning Task<bool>: true when the cookie jar was updated, false when the write failed or could not be attempted (a non-2xx answer, a dropped connection, JS interop unavailable). SyncAsync(accessToken, refreshToken) writes the pair (ISessionCookieSync.cs:15) and ClearAsync() removes it (line 20). The two callers treat the answers differently on purpose. A failed sync is surfaced: WasmTokenStorageService throws InvalidOperationException when SyncAsync returns false (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/WasmTokenStorageService.cs:153-156), so AuthUIService reports Auth.TokenStorageUnavailable instead of a sign-in that silently ends at the first access-token expiry, when no cookie exists to refresh from (comment at lines 64-67; ServerTokenStorageService does the same at ServerTokenStorageService.cs:216). A failed clear is discarded (_ = await sessionCookieSync.ClearAsync(), WasmTokenStorageService.cs:167), because sign-out proceeds locally whatever the cookie endpoint answered.
    • Why it's built this way: the shape is the client half of ADR-022, which decided the BFF-style mmca_auth_access / mmca_auth_refresh HttpOnly cookie pair and the /auth/session/token hydration endpoint. Keeping it an interface (rather than calling JS interop inline from token storage) is what lets a bUnit or unit test drive the storage services with a mock and no browser, which WasmTokenStorageServiceTests does (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/WasmTokenStorageServiceTests.cs:30).
    • Where it's used: registered by the dedicated extension AddClientAuthSessionCookieSync(), which TryAddScopeds JsFetchSessionCookieSync (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:291-295); the doc there records that both the Blazor Server host and the WebAssembly client call it (lines 165-169).

    SameOriginProxyHeaders

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/SameOriginProxyHeaders.cs:11 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: two constants naming the fixed CSRF request header the same-origin API proxy requires on every state-changing request: CsrfHeaderName = "X-CSRF" (SameOriginProxyHeaders.cs:14) and CsrfHeaderValue = "1" (line 17).
    • Depends on: nothing. It lives in MMCA.Common.UI rather than MMCA.Common.UI.Web so the client that stamps the header and the server that checks it share one definition.
    • Concept introduced, a custom header as a CSRF signal. A cross-site page can make a browser send a simple POST carrying the user's cookies, but it cannot add a custom header without a CORS preflight. The proxy answers OPTIONS itself with no CORS grant and refuses any request whose Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site names another origin, so the header is defense in depth behind that origin check; the value carries no secret (SameOriginProxyHeaders.cs:3-10).
      • [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] assesses cookie-borne credentials against cross-site request forgery. Once the bearer moves into an HttpOnly cookie, a header the browser will not attach on a cross-site request is what distinguishes the app's own calls.
    • Walkthrough: two const string members and no behavior. Being const, both values are baked into each caller at compile time.
    • Why it's built this way: one shared type instead of a literal per call site keeps the stamp and the check from drifting apart. The proxy design is ADR-131.
    • Where it's used: stamped by SameOriginProxyRequestHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/SameOriginProxyRequestHandler.cs:19-20) and by NotificationHubService on the SignalR connection options (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Notifications/NotificationHubService.cs:374); checked by SameOriginApiProxyEndpoint in HasCsrfHeader, which demands exactly one value equal to CsrfHeaderValue (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/SameOriginProxy/SameOriginApiProxyEndpoint.cs:125-128); stripped before forwarding by SameOriginProxyTransformer (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/SameOriginProxy/SameOriginProxyTransformer.cs:78). Covered by SameOriginProxyClientTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/SameOriginProxyClientTests.cs:27).

    JsFetchSessionCookieSync

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/JsFetchSessionCookieSync.cs:13 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the ISessionCookieSync implementation. It calls two small JS helpers that issue a browser-side fetch, so the resulting Set-Cookie lands in the user's cookie jar on both Blazor Server and WebAssembly.
    • Depends on: ISessionCookieSync (the contract) and IJSRuntime (Microsoft.JSInterop), plus the mmcaAuthCookie object defined in the package's static web asset MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/wwwroot/mmca-auth-cookie.js:4.
    • Concept introduced, why the fetch has to come from the browser. On Blazor Server the code runs on the server, so a server-issued HTTP call would put the cookie in the server's own handler, not the user's browser. Routing the call through JS interop makes the browser the one issuing the request, which is the only way the Set-Cookie reaches the right cookie jar (JsFetchSessionCookieSync.cs:6-8).
      • [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] again: the tokens transit JS only for this one same-origin POST and are never persisted anywhere JS can read afterwards.
      • [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses degradation. Every interop failure is caught and turned into a false answer, so a prerender pass or a disconnected circuit cannot throw out of a cookie write, yet the caller still learns the write did not happen.
    • Walkthrough:
      • IsInteropUnavailable(ex) (JsFetchSessionCookieSync.cs:15-16) is the shared exception filter, naming the four types that mean "there is no live JS runtime right now": InvalidOperationException, JSDisconnectedException, JSException and OperationCanceledException.
      • SyncAsync(accessToken, refreshToken) (line 19) returns InvokeAsync<bool>("mmcaAuthCookie.set", accessToken, refreshToken) (line 23): the script itself reports whether the endpoint answered 2xx. An interop failure returns false, the comment noting nothing was written (lines 25-29).
      • ClearAsync() (line 33) returns InvokeAsync<bool>("mmcaAuthCookie.clear") (line 37) under the same filter, and an interop failure again returns false because the cookie was not cleared by this call (lines 39-43). The class doc records that the script tries the clear twice (JsFetchSessionCookieSync.cs:9-11).
    • Why it's built this way: a shared static filter rather than two duplicated when clauses keeps the definition of "interop unavailable" in one place. Reporting rather than swallowing silently is what lets the token storage services refuse a sign-in whose cookie never landed (see ISessionCookieSync). The cookie contract itself belongs to ADR-022.
    • Where it's used: TryAddScoped behind ISessionCookieSync by AddClientAuthSessionCookieSync() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:293); consumed by WasmTokenStorageService and ServerTokenStorageService.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the mmcaAuthCookie.set / .clear JS implementations live in mmca-auth-cookie.js, outside this unit; only the C# side is described here.

    SameOriginProxyRequestHandler

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/SameOriginProxyRequestHandler.cs:11 · Level 1 · class (internal, sealed)

    • What it is: the innermost handler of the "APIClient" pipeline on a WebAssembly client whose host runs the same-origin API proxy. It removes any Authorization header and stamps the proxy's CSRF header on every request (SameOriginProxyRequestHandler.cs:3-10).
    • Depends on: SameOriginProxyHeaders for the header name and value; external DelegatingHandler.
    • Concept introduced, the browser holds no usable bearer. Behind the proxy the client only ever holds a claims-only token; the proxy attaches the real bearer server-side from the HttpOnly session cookie. Any Authorization header the outer handlers (such as AuthDelegatingHandler) or a service's DefaultRequestHeaders attached is therefore noise at best, so this handler clears it rather than trusting every caller to know.
      • [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] assesses whether a usable credential is reachable from browser code. Here it is not, and the transport enforces that for every request.
    • Walkthrough: one override. SendAsync(request, cancellationToken) (SameOriginProxyRequestHandler.cs:14) guards request with ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull (line 16), sets request.Headers.Authorization = null (line 18), removes any existing CSRF header and adds exactly one with TryAddWithoutValidation (lines 19-20), then delegates to base.SendAsync (line 21). Removing first guarantees a single value, which is what the proxy's check demands.
    • Why it's built this way: registering it innermost means it sees the request after every other handler and service has had its say, so one place decides what reaches the proxy. It is registered only when Api:SameOriginApiEndpoint is configured, so every other client (Blazor Server, MAUI, a WebAssembly client of a host that did not opt in) keeps its pipeline unchanged (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:144-149). The proxy design is ADR-131.
    • Where it's used: AddTransient and AddHttpMessageHandler inside AddUIShared() behind the usesSameOriginProxy check (DependencyInjection.cs:178-183), after the auth and culture handlers (lines 124-125). The proxy side that reads the CSRF header is SameOriginApiProxyEndpoint.

    JwtAuthenticationStateProvider

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:24 · Level 2 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the custom AuthenticationStateProvider that turns the stored JWT into the ClaimsPrincipal Blazor's AuthorizeView and [Authorize] read, pushes a new state immediately on login and logout, signs the shell out when the token storage reports that the session ended on the server, and forgets the list pages' persisted search and filters on every sign-in and sign-out.
    • Depends on: ITokenStorageService (required constructor parameter), ListPageStateService (optional constructor parameter, defaulted to null) and ISessionAwareTokenStorage (an optional capability it probes the storage for); externals Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Authorization.AuthenticationStateProvider, System.Security.Claims and JwtSecurityTokenHandler.
    • Concept introduced, Blazor's auth-state contract. Blazor does not know about JWTs; it asks an AuthenticationStateProvider for an AuthenticationState and re-renders every CascadingAuthenticationState consumer when the provider says the state changed. This class is the adapter between "there is a token in storage" and that framework contract.
      • [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] assesses how a cross-cutting piece of UI state propagates. Notifying rather than reloading is the whole point: a sign-in updates the navbar and every guarded fragment without a page refresh (lines 96-99). The class doc also makes this the one place per-tab list state is forgotten, because every sign-out passes through it (JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:18-22).
      • [Rubric §11, Security] assesses the trust boundary, and the class doc draws it: claims are extracted client-side without server validation to keep the UI responsive, and the WebAPI performs full token validation on every request (lines 9-11). The same doc records the second half of that boundary (lines 12-17): a session revoked from another device, or ended by account deletion, flips the shell to anonymous instead of leaving it signed in behind 401s (A-34).
    • Walkthrough:
      • AnonymousState, a single static AuthenticationState over an empty ClaimsIdentity (JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:26-27). Because a ClaimsIdentity with no authentication type reports IsAuthenticated == false, this one shared instance is the "signed out" answer.
      • One constructor, (ITokenStorageService tokenStorageService, ListPageStateService? listPageState = null) (line 41). It null-guards the storage (line 45), stores both into _tokenStorageService and _listPageState (fields at lines 29-30), and, when the storage is an ISessionAwareTokenStorage, subscribes OnSessionEnded to its SessionEnded event (lines 50-53). The comment at line 49 explains why no unsubscribe is needed: the provider shares the storage's DI scope and lifetime, so the subscription never outlives either. The parameter doc gives the reason the list state is taken at all: it is mirrored to sessionStorage, which outlives the session in the same tab, so without the clear the next account signing in on that tab saw the previous account's search applied (lines 36-40).
      • GetAuthenticationStateAsync() (line 61) reads the token (line 65) and returns the anonymous state on a blank token (lines 66-69), an unreadable token (lines 72-75), or an expired one (ValidTo < DateTime.UtcNow, lines 78-81). On success it builds a ClaimsIdentity from the token's claims with the authentication type "jwt", and the comment at line 83 records why that string matters: naming an authentication type is what makes the identity IsAuthenticated. A bare catch under an annotated CA1031 suppression ("an unreadable token is an anonymous user, never a broken authentication state", lines 88-93) turns any remaining failure, including JS interop being unavailable, into anonymous rather than an exception inside a render.
      • NotifyUserAuthentication(token) (line 100) rebuilds the principal the same way and calls the base NotifyAuthenticationStateChanged (line 106). It does not consult storage, because the caller has just been handed the token.
      • NotifyUserLogout() (lines 112-113) pushes AnonymousState back out.
      • SignOutAsync() (line 121, internal) is the sign-out every AuthUIService path ends in: it awaits the list-state clear, then calls NotifyUserLogout(). It is awaited so the sessionStorage removal lands before the caller's forceLoad navigation to the sign-in page tears the page down (doc at lines 115-120).
      • SignInAsync(token) (line 139, internal) is the sign-in counterpart: it awaits the list-state clear, then calls NotifyUserAuthentication(token). The doc (lines 127-137) records why it clears on EVERY sign-in, the same account's included: in WebAssembly a session revoked from another device while the tab was not running ends without SessionEnded, so a different account can sign in over a tab that still looks signed in, and telling accounts apart would need an identity that case no longer has. A token refresh is not a sign-in and keeps the state.
      • OnSessionEnded (lines 145-151), the private event handler, starts the list-state clear without awaiting it (_ = ForgetListPageStateAsync(), line 149), because an event handler cannot await and the in-memory state clears synchronously inside the call (comment at lines 147-148), then calls NotifyUserLogout() (line 150). Per MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/ISessionAwareTokenStorage.cs:3-10,14-18 the event fires once, only on a definitive "no session" refresh answer (never on a transient failure), and the stored access token is already cleared when it does.
      • ForgetListPageStateAsync() (lines 153-154) is Task.CompletedTask when no list state was supplied, otherwise _listPageState.ClearAsync().AsTask().
    • Why it's built this way: falling back to anonymous on every failure is the safe direction for a UI gate, since the API rejects anything the client wrongly let through. Keeping the notify methods public and adding the internal SignInAsync / SignOutAsync pair is what lets AuthUIService drive the state transition at the exact moment tokens change; it does so behind an is JwtAuthenticationStateProvider type test (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs:201,483,544), so a host that registered a different provider still works. Putting the list-state clear here rather than in each sign-out path means the server-ended session (driven by the storage event) and the client-driven sign-outs cannot disagree about what is forgotten. Both the list state and the session-aware capability are optional (a defaulted parameter and a type test), so a storage that does not implement ISessionAwareTokenStorage behaves exactly as before.
    • Where it's used: registered with AddScoped<AuthenticationStateProvider, JwtAuthenticationStateProvider>() by the shared Blazor Server host wiring (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Hosting/BlazorWebHostExtensions.cs:144) and by the WebAssembly and MAUI heads (MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:54, MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI/MauiProgram.cs:130, MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:53, MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/MauiProgram.cs:178). Covered by JwtAuthenticationStateProviderTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/JwtAuthenticationStateProviderTests.cs:16), whose WhenTheStorageReportsTheSessionEnded_NotifiesAnonymous (line 137) and WhenTheStorageReportsTheSessionEnded_ForgetsTheListPageStateAndNotifiesAnonymous (line 152) drive the session-ended path through a fake session-aware storage (its EndSession, line 178). AuthUIServiceTests constructs a real one rather than a double, precisely because the type test above would not match a mock (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/AuthUIServiceTests.cs:80, and with a list state at line 609); the shared token-storage tests do the same (MMCA.Common/Tests/Shared/UI/TokenStorageServiceTestsBase.cs:316). ADR-051 (client auth token lifecycle) mentions it.

    TokenOwner

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:344 · Level 2 · record (private, sealed, nested in AuthDelegatingHandler)

    • What it is: the value type of the handler's owner map: which storage attached a bearer, and when (AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:343-344). Two positional members, WeakReference<ISessionAwareTokenStorage> Storage and long TrackedAt.
    • Depends on: ISessionAwareTokenStorage (the storage it points at); externals WeakReference<T> and Environment.TickCount64 (the clock TrackedAt is stamped from).
    • Concept reinforced, a weak back-reference keyed by token. The map routes a 401 to the storage instance that attached the refused bearer, but it is static, so a strong reference would keep every ended circuit or scope alive. Holding the storage weakly means the map never extends a session's lifetime (doc at AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:61-64).
      • [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses whether a long-lived process degrades: the entry carries its own timestamp, so a sweep can drop it on age as well as on a dead owner.
    • Walkthrough: no members beyond the two positional properties. Entries are created by TrackTokenOwnerAt (AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:84-88) and stored in the static Owners dictionary (line 56). They are read three ways: HasLiveOwner (lines 102-103) and the two report paths resolve Storage.TryGetTarget to find a live owner (lines 237, 318), and IsStale (lines 178-179) treats an entry as droppable when TrackedAt is older than RetentionMs or the target is gone.
    • Why it's built this way: a private nested record keeps the map's shape out of the public surface; only the handler and its internal test hooks touch it.
    • Where it's used: only inside AuthDelegatingHandler; no usage outside the defining file.

    AuthDelegatingHandler

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:36 · Level 3 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the DelegatingHandler that attaches the stored JWT as a Bearer header on every outgoing API request, so no UI service ever sets an Authorization header by hand, and that reports a refused bearer back to the storage that holds it: a 401 triggers one renewal attempt, and a coded 403 raises the "second factor required" signal. One request can opt out through the SkipBearer request option.
    • Depends on: ITokenStorageService (its only constructor parameter), ISessionAwareTokenStorage (the renewal capability a 401 is reported to), TokenOwner (its owner-map entry), MultiFactorRequiredSignal and AuthErrorCodes (the coded 403 path), and AuthenticatedServiceBase (replay-safety marking); externals System.Net.Http.Headers.AuthenticationHeaderValue, DelegatingHandler, ConcurrentDictionary and System.Text.Json.JsonDocument.
    • Concept introduced, the HTTP message-handler pipeline. HttpClient composes handlers into a chain, each free to inspect or mutate a request before passing it to the next. Registering this one on the named "APIClient" client means auth is applied once, at the transport, for every typed service built on top of it.
      • [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven Design] assesses whether concerns like auth are centralized rather than repeated per call. This is the client-side twin of the server's middleware pipeline: one registration covers every request, and the same place sees every refusal.
      • [Rubric §11, Security] assesses session handling: a 401 to a bearer makes one refresh attempt, and a refused refresh ends the session so a protected page lands on the sign-in page. A token acquired that way is remembered and a 401 to it is not reported again, so an API that keeps refusing a freshly issued token cannot drive a refresh per request (class doc at AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:19-26).
    • Walkthrough:
      • SkipBearer (AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:44) is a public static HttpRequestOptionsKey<bool> named "MMCA.Common.UI.Auth.SkipBearer". The token refresh POST sets it: that endpoint is anonymous, and reading token storage from inside a refresh would re-enter the very acquisition that is waiting for the request to complete (doc at lines 39-43).
      • Three private constants: SweepThreshold = 1024 (line 47), RetentionMs = 24L * 60 * 60 * 1000, 24 hours, longer than any access token lives (line 50), and ProblemJsonMediaType = "application/problem+json" (line 53). Two static ordinal ConcurrentDictionary maps hold the cross-request state: Owners (token to TokenOwner, line 56) and RenewedTokens (token to the tick it was renewed at, line 59).
      • TrackTokenOwner(accessToken, owner) (line 68, internal static) records which storage attached a bearer. It ignores a blank token or a storage that is not an ISessionAwareTokenStorage (lines 70-73) and otherwise stores a weak reference stamped with Environment.TickCount64 (line 75). The reason is in the class doc: the handler resolves its own storage in the IHttpClientFactory handler scope, which in a browser host is not the instance the component holds, so without this a service's 401 would go to the wrong storage (lines 27-34). TrackTokenOwnerAt (line 84) and MarkRenewedAt (line 93) write the maps directly and are the hooks tests use to age entries; HasLiveOwner (line 102), IsTrackedOwner (line 108) and IsMarkedRenewed (line 113) read them.
      • SweepIfLarge() (line 119) runs after every write. SweepOwners (line 151) and SweepRenewed (line 165) do nothing until a map holds more than SweepThreshold entries, then drop the owner entries that are stale (older than RetentionMs or whose storage is gone, IsStale, lines 178-179) and the renewal entries older than RetentionMs (IsExpired, line 181).
      • SendAsync(request, cancellationToken) (line 127) is a thin wrapper: it awaits the private SendWithBearerAsync inside a try, and on an HttpRequestException calls AuthenticatedServiceBase.MarkReplaySafety(ex, request) before rethrowing (lines 131-141). The shared retry policy sees only the exception, not the request, so this is where it is told whether the request may be resent: a keyless POST or PATCH may not, once sent (comment at lines 137-138).
      • SendWithBearerAsync (line 183) holds the bearer logic. When SkipBearer is set to true the request passes straight to base.SendAsync without touching token storage at all (lines 187-190). A request that already carries an Authorization header also gets no stored token (the Authorization is null check at line 192): the forced-refresh replay sets the token it just acquired, and replacing it with the stored one would resend the token the server just rejected. Otherwise it awaits GetAccessTokenAsync() (line 194), and only when the result is non-blank sets request.Headers.Authorization = new AuthenticationHeaderValue("Bearer", token) (lines 195-198). It then reads the bearer it is about to send with BearerOf (line 202; the helper at lines 144-149 accepts only a non-blank Bearer scheme), before the call, because the same-origin proxy handler further in strips the header (comment at line 201). After base.SendAsync (line 203) a 401 to a request that carried a bearer goes to ReportRejectedAsync (lines 205-208) and a 403 goes to ReportMultiFactorRequiredAsync (lines 209-212). The response is returned unchanged either way (line 214): it is never replayed.
      • ReportMultiFactorRequiredAsync (line 231) resolves the live owner of the token, falling back to the handler's own storage (lines 237-239), and returns early unless that owner has a MultiFactorRequiredSignal subscriber and the body is application/problem+json (lines 240-244), so a host that never called AddTwoFactorUI() never has its 403 bodies read (doc at lines 217-224). It buffers the content first so the caller still reads the same response (line 246), and raises the signal when CarriesMultiFactorRequired (line 257) finds AuthErrorCodes.MultiFactorRequired under errors[*].code; a body that is not valid JSON is ignored (lines 274-277). PropertyOf (line 284) matches property names ignoring case.
      • ReportRejectedAsync(rejectedToken, fallbackOwner) (line 310, internal static) is the 401 path. A token already in RenewedTokens is skipped, since refreshing again would loop (lines 312-316). Otherwise it resolves the live owner or the fallback as an ISessionAwareTokenStorage (lines 318-324) and awaits RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync(rejectedToken) (line 328). A renewed token that differs from the refused one is tracked to the same owner and marked renewed (lines 329-333). Any exception other than cancellation is swallowed under an annotated CA1031 suppression (lines 335-340): the caller still receives the server's 401, which is the answer that matters. The doc records it is also the 401 handling for a bearer attached outside this pipeline, the notification hub's WebSocket handshake (lines 297-302). Note the freshness work happens inside the token service: by the time this handler sees a token, a stale one has already been re-acquired. The 401 path is the backstop for a token the server refuses anyway.
    • Why it's built this way: a handler rather than a base-class helper, because the pipeline applies to everything the named client sends, including calls made by code that never inherits from a framework base. The owner and renewal maps are static because a handler instance is per handler scope, not per component, and the map has to bridge the two; holding owners weakly and sweeping on age keeps that static state bounded. It is registered AddTransient (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:142), the lifetime AddHttpMessageHandler expects.
    • Where it's used: added to the "APIClient" pipeline alongside the culture handler (DependencyInjection.cs:174-175). Services that attach their own bearer register its owner: AuthenticatedServiceBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Api/AuthenticatedServiceBase.cs:84), AuthUIService (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs:567), and the preference reader and writer (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceReader.cs:52, MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:117). NotificationHubService calls ReportRejectedAsync for a refused hub handshake (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Notifications/NotificationHubService.cs:671). The SkipBearer option is set by DirectApiTokenRefresher on its refresh request (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/DirectApiTokenRefresher.cs:66). On a WebAssembly client of a host running the same-origin proxy, SameOriginProxyRequestHandler sits inside this handler and strips whatever header it attached (DependencyInjection.cs:181-182). Covered by AuthDelegatingHandlerTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandlerTests.cs:18), by SessionBearerRenewalTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Api/SessionBearerRenewalTests.cs:32) and by a DI resolution test that exists because the pipeline must be able to construct it (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/ApiClientRegistrationTests.cs:33).

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/IPasskeyUIService.cs:14 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the client of the API's passkey endpoints under auth/passkeys: register a passkey for the signed-in user, list, rename and delete them, and sign in with one (IPasskeyUIService.cs:7-13).
    • Depends on: Result and the passkey contracts PasskeyOptionsResponse, PasskeyResponse, PasskeyRegisterRequest and PasskeySignInRequest, plus AuthenticationResponse. Implemented by AuthUIService.
    • Concept reinforced, the bespoke UI service contract (introduced at IAuthUIService). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses extension without breakage: the doc states this is a separate interface rather than new IAuthUIService members, so a consumer's own IAuthUIService implementation keeps compiling, following the ISignInLinkUIService precedent (lines 8-11). [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] shows in the split between the authenticated management members and the anonymous sign-in pair.
    • Walkthrough: seven members, every one returning a Result, in two halves.
      • Registration is a two-step WebAuthn ceremony: BeginRegistrationAsync (line 19, POST auth/passkeys/register/options) returns the flow and creation options, and CompleteRegistrationAsync(PasskeyRegisterRequest, ct) (line 25, POST auth/passkeys/register) sends the browser's attestation and a name back and returns the stored passkey.
      • Management: ListAsync (line 30, GET auth/passkeys), RenameAsync(id, name, ct) (line 37, PATCH auth/passkeys/{id}) and DeleteAsync(id, ct) (line 43, DELETE auth/passkeys/{id}), whose doc names the refusal a page must expect: the last passkey of a password-less account (line 42).
      • Sign-in is the same two steps, anonymous: BeginSignInAsync (line 48, POST auth/passkeys/signin/options) and SignInAsync(PasskeySignInRequest, ct) (line 57, POST auth/passkeys/signin), which stores the token pair and notifies the auth state like a password sign-in (lines 50-53).
    • Why it's built this way: implementing it on AuthUIService means a passkey sign-in stores its tokens through the password sign-in's path (lines 11-12, and the registration comment at MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:200-202). The registration is inert until a host offers passkeys (SignIn:OfferPasskeys) or renders the passkeys panel. The design is ADR-139.
    • Where it's used: registered TryAddScoped<IPasskeyUIService, AuthUIService>() in AddUIShared() (DependencyInjection.cs:203); injected by PasskeySignInButton (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/PasskeySignInButton.razor.cs:40) and PasskeysPanel (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/PasskeysPanel.razor.cs:39), and probed by Login to decide whether to offer passkeys (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor.cs:203).

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/ISignInLinkUIService.cs:16 · Level 3 · interface

    • Depends on: Result and AuthenticationResponse. Implemented by AuthUIService.
    • Concept reinforced, the bespoke UI service contract (introduced at IAuthUIService). [Rubric §11, Security] shows twice in two members: the request side is anti-enumeration and the redeem side is single-use. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]: a separate interface rather than new IAuthUIService members, so a consumer's own IAuthUIService implementation keeps compiling, the IEmailConfirmationUIService precedent (remarks at lines 10-15).

      • RequestSignInLinkAsync(email, ct) (line 25) asks the API to email a link. The endpoint answers 202 for every well-formed address, so a success says nothing about whether the address holds an account; a failure is a malformed request or an outage (lines 18-24).

    IEmailConfirmationUIService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/IEmailConfirmationUIService.cs:21 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the client-side contract for the email-confirmation flow: redeeming a confirmation link's token, and asking for a fresh one when the first has expired or was never received.
    • Depends on: Result; externals: BCL (Task, CancellationToken, string).
    • Concept reinforced, the bespoke UI service contract (introduced at IAuthUIService). [Rubric §18, UI Architecture & Component Design] and [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] (assesses that a resend cannot be used to enumerate registered addresses). Two members, both returning Result so a page branches on the outcome instead of catching. ResendEmailConfirmationAsync's own doc comment states the anti-enumeration rule directly, that the endpoint answers 202 whether or not the address holds an account, so a success means "accepted", never "this address exists" (IEmailConfirmationUIService.cs:31-33). The class-level remarks also record why there is no retry: the token is single-use and the resend spends a per-address request budget, so a repeat is a second request rather than a replayed response (IEmailConfirmationUIService.cs:16-19).
    • Walkthrough: two methods.
      • ConfirmEmailAsync(string email, string token, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (IEmailConfirmationUIService.cs:28) redeems a single-use token via POST auth/confirm-email; the doc comment records that the endpoint returns the same generic rejection for every bad token (IEmailConfirmationUIService.cs:23-27).
      • ResendEmailConfirmationAsync(string email, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (IEmailConfirmationUIService.cs:38) requests a fresh link via POST auth/send-email-confirmation, always reported as success at this layer regardless of whether the address is known.
    • Why it's built this way: a narrow interface here, rather than the generic IEntityService<,>, matches the same reasoning IAuthUIService documents: confirming an email is not a CRUD operation on a resource with an identity, so it gets its own contract instead of being bent to fit one ([Rubric §14, Testability]).
    • Where it's used: implemented by EmailConfirmationUIService; injected by MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/ConfirmEmail.razor.cs and by MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.UI/Pages/ConfirmEmailPageTestsBase.cs; registered in AddUIShared() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs).
