    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/EmailConfirmationUIService.cs:22 · Level 4 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the IEmailConfirmationUIService implementation. It posts to the two confirmation endpoints and translates the response through the shared HttpResultExecutor / ProblemDetailsResultReader path used across the auth services.
    • Depends on: IEmailConfirmationUIService (the contract it implements); IHttpClientFactory (its only constructor parameter, EmailConfirmationUIService.cs:22); HttpResultExecutor and ProblemDetailsResultReader (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Http/ProblemDetailsResultReader.cs) for the transport and response-translation work.
    • Concept reinforced, one shared execution path for every anonymous auth POST. Both members funnel through the private PostOnceAsync<TRequest> helper, so the retry policy and response translation are written once rather than duplicated per endpoint.
      • [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses duplication; the two public methods are each a single expression forwarding to the shared helper, without its own async state machine (EmailConfirmationUIService.cs:27-32).
      • [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] is answered by what the helper deliberately does not do: no retry, because a repeat here is a second request (a spent token, a second email), never a replayed response (EmailConfirmationUIService.cs:40-41).
    • Walkthrough:
      • ApiClientName = "APIClient" (EmailConfirmationUIService.cs:24) names the shared named client.
      • ConfirmEmailAsync (line 28) posts a ConfirmEmailRequest to auth/confirm-email.
      • ResendEmailConfirmationAsync (line 32) posts a SendEmailConfirmationRequest to auth/send-email-confirmation.
      • PostOnceAsync<TRequest>(relativeUrl, body, cancellationToken) (line 35) creates a fresh HttpClient from the factory (line 39), posts the body with PostAsJsonAsync (lines 43-44) and reads the result with ProblemDetailsResultReader.ReadAsync (line 46), all wrapped in HttpResultExecutor.ExecuteAsync for the shared transport-fault translation.
    • Why it's built this way: a fresh HttpClient per call (rather than a stored field) matches how the other anonymous auth services in this package are built, since the client is cheap to create from the factory and this service holds no other per-call state.
    • Where it's used: covered by EmailConfirmationUIServiceTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/EmailConfirmationUIServiceTests.cs); registered against IEmailConfirmationUIService in AddUIShared() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs).

    IAuthUIService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/IAuthUIService.cs:18 · Level 5 · interface

    • What it is: the single client-side authentication contract: login, register, OAuth code exchange, sign-out of this device, refresh, the three password flows, the signed-in-devices list with revoke, the sign-in history, and sign-out of every device. The password-based auth pages in the framework talk to this; the sign-in-link, passkey and email-confirmation flows have their own narrow contracts beside it (ISignInLinkUIService, IPasskeyUIService, IEmailConfirmationUIService).
    • Depends on: Result and its generic form from MMCA.Common.Shared.Abstractions; the MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth contracts LoginRequest, RegisterRequest, AuthenticationResponse, RefreshSessionSummaryResponse and SignInSummaryResponse; and ErrorType for the failure kinds it documents. Implemented by AuthUIService.
    • Concept introduced, the failure travels with the call. The interface doc states the rule (IAuthUIService.cs:11-16): every call that talks to the API returns a Result carrying the server's own errors, so the failure arrives with the call rather than on a LastError property that the next call would overwrite. Pages render it through MMCA.Common.UI.Common.ResultUiExtensions (ResultUiExtensions).
      • [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether return types carry meaning. Three different shapes appear here on purpose, and each deviation is argued in source rather than assumed.
      • [Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] assesses whether a form can show the server's real message. Because the failure is the return value, a login page can bind the error next to the field without a second lookup.
      • [Rubric §11, Security] shows in two documented behaviors: the anti-enumeration contract on password reset, and the OAuth exchange keeping tokens out of the address bar.
    • Walkthrough: twelve members, in the order they appear.
      • LoginAsync(LoginRequest, ct) and RegisterAsync(RegisterRequest, ct) both return Result<AuthenticationResponse> and both store tokens on success (IAuthUIService.cs:21,24).
      • ExchangeOAuthCodeAsync(code, ct) (line 31) trades a single-use completion code carried in the redirect URL for the token pair through auth/oauth/exchange, stores the tokens and notifies auth state; the doc's closing sentence names the reason for the indirection, keeping tokens out of the address bar (lines 26-30).
      • LogoutAsync() (line 40) is the deliberate no-Result member: it signs out this device only, revoking this device's server-side refresh session through auth/revoke/current and clearing local storage, so the account stays signed in on its other devices. It returns nothing because the local sign-out happens whatever the server answered: a user who asked to leave must never be kept signed in by a failed network call (lines 33-39).
      • TryRefreshTokenAsync(ct) (line 51) is the deliberate bool member: it makes no API call of its own, since the host's ITokenRefresher owns the exchange, and its two states ("session still live", "session gone") are not errors to render. A false is not always a sign-out: when an ISessionAwareTokenRefresher reports the attempt as transient (TokenAcquisition.IsUnavailable), the stored credential is kept and a later call tries again (lines 42-50).
      • ChangePasswordAsync(currentPassword, newPassword, ct) (line 54) hits auth/password.
      • RequestPasswordResetAsync(email, ct) (line 61) hits the anonymous auth/forgot-password. The doc pins the semantics: the endpoint answers 202 for every well-formed address as an anti-enumeration measure, so a success means "accepted", never "an account exists" (lines 56-60).
      • ResetPasswordAsync(email, token, newPassword, ct) (line 68) completes the reset via the anonymous auth/reset-password; an invalid, expired or already-consumed token comes back as a failure carrying the server's generic message (lines 63-67).
      • GetSessionsAsync(ct) (line 76) returns Result<IReadOnlyList<RefreshSessionSummaryResponse>> from auth/my-sessions, newest first, and documents that exactly one row can carry IsCurrent, resolved server-side from the access token's sid claim (lines 70-75).
      • GetSignInsAsync(ct) (line 85) returns Result<IReadOnlyList<SignInSummaryResponse>> from auth/my-sign-ins: one row per sign-in however often it refreshed, ended ones included with how they ended, newest first, at most 50, the caller's own carrying IsCurrent (lines 78-84).
      • RevokeSessionAsync(sessionId, ct) (line 94) signs one device out via auth/revoke/{sessionId}; another account's session id (or a nonexistent one) answers 404 and arrives as an ErrorType.NotFound failure, and revoking an already-revoked session answers the same 404 (lines 87-90).
      • RevokeAllSessionsAsync(ct) (line 104) signs out of every device via auth/revoke and, unlike LogoutAsync, returns the server's answer as a Result. A failed revoke is reported rather than hidden, and the local session is left in place so the caller can say so and let the user retry; on success it also performs the same local sign-out LogoutAsync does (lines 96-103). The pair is the clearest statement of the return-shape rule: two sign-outs with opposite failure policies, because "leave this device" must never fail while "end every session" must never claim success it did not get.
    • Why it's built this way: the interface is where the three return shapes are justified, and each justification is a behavior rule rather than a style preference. The twelve operations stay on one contract because they share one consumer set (the shipped auth and devices pages are framework types); newer flows were added as separate interfaces instead, so a consumer's own implementation of this one keeps compiling (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:192-193). The device-list and revoke members are the UI surface of ADR-097; the OAuth exchange is the client end of ADR-036 and ADR-043.
    • Where it's used: registered TryAddScoped against AuthUIService by AddUIShared() (DependencyInjection.cs:190, the comment at line 189 noting TryAdd prevents duplicate registration when several hosts call in); injected by the shipped auth pages, including Login (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor) and Sessions, which lists devices and sign-ins and whose sign-out-everywhere action calls RevokeAllSessionsAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Sessions.razor.cs:99,131,241).

    AuthUIService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs:48 · Level 6 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the one client-side service that owns a user's session on a Blazor or MAUI head. It calls the WebAPI auth/* endpoints (sign in, register, OAuth code exchange, sign-in links, passkeys, change password, forgot and reset password, list and revoke devices, sign-in history, sign out), persists the returned token pair, and tells Blazor's authentication state that something changed, so AuthorizeView and [Authorize] routes react without a page reload. It implements three contracts, IAuthUIService, ISignInLinkUIService and IPasskeyUIService (AuthUIService.cs:56), so every way of signing in stores its tokens through one path. Every method that talks to the API hands back a Result carrying the server's own error text, so no page has to interpret an HttpResponseMessage.
    • Depends on: first-party ITokenStorageService (token persistence, AuthUIService.cs:50), ITokenRefresher (the host-specific renewal path, AuthUIService.cs:51), JwtAuthenticationStateProvider (injected as the framework AuthenticationStateProvider base type at AuthUIService.cs:52 and pattern-matched back down), IPushRegistrationService (native push cleanup, AuthUIService.cs:53), ILocalCacheStore (optional device-local document cache, defaulted to null, AuthUIService.cs:54, wiped on sign-out), IDeviceMetadataReporter (optional per-session device reporter, AuthUIService.cs:55) run through DeviceMetadataReporting, an optional ILogger<AuthUIService> (AuthUIService.cs:56), AuthDelegatingHandler (owner tracking for the bearers it attaches), HttpResultExecutor (transport-fault translation), ProblemDetailsResultReader (response translation), and the shared auth contracts LoginRequest, RegisterRequest, OAuthCodeExchangeRequest, ChangePasswordRequest, ForgotPasswordRequest, ResetPasswordRequest, SendSignInLinkRequest, RedeemSignInLinkRequest, PasskeyRegisterRequest, PasskeySignInRequest, PasskeyOptionsResponse, PasskeyResponse, AuthenticationResponse, RegistrationOutcome, RefreshSessionSummaryResponse and SignInSummaryResponse. Externals: IHttpClientFactory, System.Net.Http.Json (PostAsJsonAsync, PutAsJsonAsync), System.Net.Http.Headers.AuthenticationHeaderValue, and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Authorization.AuthenticationStateProvider.
    • Concept introduced, the client-side session lifecycle as one service, with a sign-out that cannot fail. Everything a session needs on the client (acquire a token pair, hold it, renew it, publish the identity to the component tree, and tear all of that down) lives behind injectable interfaces with a single implementation, so no component ever touches localStorage, a Bearer header, or a token string. [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] assesses whether credentials are confined to a narrow, auditable surface in the browser: here the only code that reads or writes tokens is this service plus AuthDelegatingHandler, both of them going through ITokenStorageService rather than doing JS interop of their own. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses the end-to-end auth design. There are two sign-outs with opposite failure policies. LogoutAsync is deliberately local-first and ends this device only: the remote revoke of auth/revoke/current is best effort and bounded, and both the server call and the local clear are wrapped so a dropped connection can never strand a user inside a session they asked to leave (AuthUIService.cs:101-117, 125-140, 531-548). RevokeAllSessionsAsync is server-first: it reports a failed revoke and only signs out locally once the server confirmed, so "signed out everywhere" is never claimed when it did not happen (AuthUIService.cs:143-164). [Rubric §19, State Management] assesses who owns mutable client state and when it is invalidated: this service is the single writer of auth state, and every sign-out it performs also wipes the device-local document cache, whose plaintext snapshots survive restarts and are keyed by surface rather than by user (AuthUIService.cs:35-40), and, through the provider, the per-tab list-page state. [Rubric §18, UI Architecture] sees the same shape the entity services use, a typed service over the named "APIClient" returning Result, so pages render failures with ResultUiExtensions instead of catching exceptions. [Rubric §14, Testability] is served by taking every collaborator through the primary constructor with no statics of its own: AuthUIServiceTests drives the whole class through a stub HttpMessageHandler.
    • Walkthrough
      • Two public error codes head the class. TokenStorageUnavailableCode = "Auth.TokenStorageUnavailable" (AuthUIService.cs:62) is reported when authentication succeeded but the tokens could not be written because JS interop was unavailable (SSR prerender, or a render-mode transition), and MissingAccessTokenCode = "Auth.MissingAccessToken" (AuthUIService.cs:68) covers a 2xx whose body carried no access token, which means the response shape drifted. Both are const string, so tests and pages branch on them without duplicating literals. The private ApiClientName = "APIClient" (AuthUIService.cs:70) names the shared client, and LogoutRevokeTimeout (line 73) is 10 seconds.
      • LoginAsync (line 76) and RegisterAsync (lines 85-86) are one-liners over the private AuthenticateAsync, differing in the relative URL (auth/login, auth/register) and in RegisterAsync passing allowConfirmationPending: true: behind the email gate the API answers 202 Accepted (account created, confirmation pending, no session), which comes back as a success carrying RegistrationOutcome.ConfirmationPending with nothing stored and no sign-in (remarks at lines 80-84).
      • ExchangeOAuthCodeAsync (AuthUIService.cs:89) guards the code client-side first: a blank code returns Error.Validation("Auth.OAuth.MissingCode", ...) without a round trip (AuthUIService.cs:91-95), then it posts an OAuthCodeExchangeRequest to auth/oauth/exchange (AuthUIService.cs:97). The single-use code arrives in the redirect URL, which is what keeps the tokens themselves out of the address bar (ADR-036, Website/docs-src/adr/036-external-oauth-login.md).
      • AuthenticateAsync (AuthUIService.cs:419) is the shared body of every sign-in: login, register, OAuth exchange, sign-in-link redemption and passkey sign-in. It posts the credential on the plain factory client through HttpResultExecutor (lines 426-439); when a 202 is allowed it short-circuits to the confirmation-pending success (lines 431-435), otherwise it reads ProblemDetailsResultReader.ReadAsync<AuthenticationResponse> (line 437). It returns early on failure or confirmation-pending (lines 441-444), then checks the access token is actually present and fails with MissingAccessTokenCode if it is not (lines 447-451). Only then does it call tokenStorageService.SetTokensAsync (line 455) inside a try that converts an InvalidOperationException into a TokenStorageUnavailableCode failure carrying the exception message as detail (lines 457-479). The point of that branch is that valid credentials nothing can hold are a failure, not a silent no-op; on browser hosts it also fires when the HttpOnly cookie write reports failure, because the token storage services throw on a false from ISessionCookieSync. Before returning that failure it cleans up after itself: the server already minted a session and the storage took the access token in memory before the cookie write failed, so it revokes the session through TryRevokeAsync(authentication.AccessToken, ...) (line 464) and then clears the stored tokens (line 467, swallowing a second InvalidOperationException, lines 469-472), or the API client would behave signed in behind a page that reported failure (comment at lines 459-463). On success it pattern-matches the injected AuthenticationStateProvider down to JwtAuthenticationStateProvider and awaits its SignInAsync (lines 483-486), which forgets the previous account's list-page state before publishing the new identity (comment at lines 481-482). The is test rather than a cast is what lets a host register a different provider without breaking sign-in. Last it runs ReportDeviceAsync (line 489), after the tokens are stored so the report's bearer names the new session.
      • ReportDeviceAsync (lines 499-505) calls DeviceMetadataReporting.ReportAsync (line 503) only when a reporter was injected. The constructor doc records that the registered default is a no-op, the MAUI package replaces it, and its wait is bounded with failures logged and swallowed, so it can never fail or hold up a sign-in (lines 41-46).
      • LogoutAsync (AuthUIService.cs:101) runs three steps, each isolated so a failure cannot stop the next. First the private UnregisterPushAsync() (line 103). Second, if a token can be read (lines 105-106), it calls the private TryRevokeAsync under a CancellationTokenSource of LogoutRevokeTimeout (lines 112-113): the comment at lines 108-111 records that the revoke is awaited but never fails, and is bounded by 10 seconds rather than the client's 90 s HttpClient.Timeout, so a hung backend cannot hold the sign-out. TryRevokeAsync (line 125) is the shared best-effort revoke: it creates an APIClient, sets the Bearer header by hand (line 128) and posts auth/revoke/current (line 132) inside a bare catch that ignores every failure (lines 134-139). It ends only the session that token belongs to, so the account stays signed in on its other devices (doc at lines 119-124). The helper is shared with the login path that cannot store the session it was just issued, so the two revokes cannot drift. Third, the private SignOutLocallyAsync() (line 116).
      • RevokeAllSessionsAsync (AuthUIService.cs:143) posts auth/revoke through HttpResultExecutor on an authenticated client, reading it with the non-generic reader (lines 145-153). Only when the result is a success does it run UnregisterPushAsync() then SignOutLocallyAsync(), in the same order as LogoutAsync so the push unregister still holds a valid access token (lines 155-161); either way it returns the server's Result (line 163). A failure leaves the local session intact for the caller to report and retry.
      • TryRefreshTokenAsync (AuthUIService.cs:167) makes no HTTP call of its own. It asks the injected tokenRefresher for a token, through one of two paths. When the refresher is an ISessionAwareTokenRefresher (pattern-matched at line 178) it calls TryAcquireAccessTokenAsync and, if the answer IsUnavailable (a transient outcome that says nothing about the session, for the direct refresher a 409 refresh-superseded), returns false immediately (lines 180-184) without clearing anything: the stored credential is kept for the next attempt, because clearing it would stop this client from ever presenting a token someone else rotated, which is what lets the server's reuse detection (BR-206) revoke the other holder's session (comment at lines 172-176). Any other refresher falls back to AcquireAccessTokenAsync (line 190). Browser hosts renew through the same-origin cookie proxy so the refresh token never reaches JS (SameOriginProxyTokenRefresher) and MAUI renews straight from secure storage (DirectApiTokenRefresher). A null or blank answer means the session is gone, which this method treats exactly like a sign-out: it calls SignOutLocallyAsync() and returns false (lines 193-199). A token that comes back is published with NotifyUserAuthentication, not the provider's SignInAsync, because a refresh is not a sign-in and keeps the list-page state, and is answered with true (lines 201-206). The bool return is the honest type here, because neither outcome is an error a page would render (IAuthUIService.cs:42-51).
      • The password trio all wrap HttpResultExecutor. ChangePasswordAsync (line 210) is the only one that authenticates: it builds a ChangePasswordRequest and PUTs it to auth/password (line 220). RequestPasswordResetAsync (line 226) and ResetPasswordAsync (line 268) deliberately use the plain factory client with no Bearer header (line 232 for the first), because a reset must not be bound to whatever session happens to be open (comment at lines 230-231). The comment at lines 236-237 records the contract that matters: auth/forgot-password answers 202 for every well-formed address, so a success never means "this account exists".
      • The sign-in-link pair implements ISignInLinkUIService. RequestSignInLinkAsync (line 243) posts a SendSignInLinkRequest to the anonymous auth/sign-in-link (line 250) and reads it with the non-generic reader (line 252). RedeemSignInLinkAsync (line 257) hands a RedeemSignInLinkRequest to AuthenticateAsync against auth/sign-in-link/redeem, so a redeemed link is stored and signalled exactly like a password sign-in.
      • The session methods back the devices page. GetSessionsAsync (line 286) GETs auth/my-sessions and reads it with the generic reader into IReadOnlyList<RefreshSessionSummaryResponse> (lines 293-294); GetSignInsAsync (line 300) does the same for auth/my-sign-ins into IReadOnlyList<SignInSummaryResponse> (lines 307-308). RevokeSessionAsync (line 314) posts auth/revoke/{sessionId} and reads it with the non-generic reader (lines 319-324), because that endpoint answers 204 and ProblemDetailsResultReader's generic overload would turn an empty 2xx body into an "empty response" failure (comment at lines 321-322). Picking the wrong overload there would turn every successful revoke into an error.
      • The passkey members implement IPasskeyUIService, each on an authenticated client except the sign-in pair: BeginRegistrationAsync (line 329, auth/passkeys/register/options), CompleteRegistrationAsync (line 341, auth/passkeys/register), ListAsync (line 353), RenameAsync (line 364), DeleteAsync (line 376, the non-generic reader again because the endpoint answers 204, comment at line 382), BeginSignInAsync (line 389, auth/passkeys/signin/options) and SignInAsync (lines 402-403), which goes through AuthenticateAsync against auth/passkeys/signin.
      • Private helpers close the class. UnregisterPushAsync (line 512) calls pushRegistration.UnregisterAsync() (line 516) inside a bare catch (lines 518-523): the Devices DELETE is authenticated, so it has to happen while the access token is still valid, and it is a no-op on web heads (ADR-044, Website/docs-src/adr/044-native-push-delivery.md). SignOutLocallyAsync (line 531) is the local half of every sign-out, shared by Logout, Sign out everywhere and an unrefreshable session (doc at lines 526-530): tokenStorageService.ClearTokensAsync() under catch (InvalidOperationException) for the interop-unavailable case (lines 533-540), then ClearLocalCacheAsync() (line 542), then the provider's SignOutAsync() behind the type test (lines 544-547), which forgets the list-page state and notifies logout. The two #pragma warning disable CA1031 blocks (lines 134-136 in TryRevokeAsync, 518-520 in UnregisterPushAsync) are deliberate and annotated in place: catching everything is the correct policy for a best-effort cleanup step. CreateAuthenticatedClientAsync (line 556) creates the APIClient, sets DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization from the stored token (line 563) and registers that token's owner with AuthDelegatingHandler.TrackTokenOwner (line 567), so a 401 to it renews or ends the session this page holds rather than the handler's own storage (comment at lines 565-566); its doc comment states that it mirrors AuthenticatedServiceBase and cannot inherit it, because this is not an entity service and takes a different dependency set (lines 550-555). ReadAccessTokenAsync (line 573) swallows InvalidOperationException from the store and returns null, so an SSR prerender proceeds tokenless and lets the API answer 401 like any other failure (lines 579-584). ClearLocalCacheAsync (line 590) no-ops when localCache is null (lines 592-595), otherwise calls localCache.ClearAsync() (line 599) inside a catch (InvalidOperationException) for the same JS-interop-gone case the token clear guards against (lines 601-604), so a device-local offline snapshot never survives to be read by the next account on the same device.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-051 (Website/docs-src/adr/051-client-auth-token-lifecycle.md) is the record behind the split visible in the constructor: storage, renewal and orchestration are three different abstractions because each render mode (SSR prerender, Blazor Server, WebAssembly, MAUI) can hold and renew a credential differently, while the orchestration above them stays identical. The refresh path itself is server-side rotation with reuse detection (ADR-050, Website/docs-src/adr/050-jwt-refresh-token-rotation.md), generalized to one row per device by ADR-097 (Website/docs-src/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.md), which is what gives GetSessionsAsync, RevokeSessionAsync and the this-device-only auth/revoke/current something to list and revoke. Browser hosts keep the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie rather than in reachable storage (ADR-022, Website/docs-src/adr/022-browser-session-cookie-auth.md), which is exactly why TryRefreshTokenAsync delegates instead of calling a refresh endpoint itself. Implementing the sign-in-link and passkey contracts on this class rather than in their own services means every sign-in shares AuthenticateAsync, so token storage, the storage-failure revoke, the provider sign-in and the device report cannot drift between flows (registration comments at MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:196-202). Returning Result instead of throwing keeps every auth failure renderable: the API's Problem Details payload already carries the server's own wording and ErrorType, so the page shows that rather than a client-invented message.
    • Where it's used: registered three times in AddUIShared(), as TryAddScoped<IAuthUIService, AuthUIService>(), TryAddScoped<ISignInLinkUIService, AuthUIService>() and TryAddScoped<IPasskeyUIService, AuthUIService>() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:190,198,203), so every host that adds the shared UI gets it. Consumers inside the shared UI are the auth pages (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor:361, Pages/Auth/Register.razor:250, Pages/Auth/OAuthComplete.razor:86, Pages/Auth/ForgotPassword.razor:95, Pages/Auth/ResetPassword.razor:157), the devices page Sessions (Pages/Auth/Sessions.razor.cs:99, 131, 175, 241), the sign-in-link and passkey surfaces through their own interfaces, and the components that sign out (Layout/MainLayout.razor:219, Layout/NavMenu.razor.cs:70, Components/Capabilities/BiometricGate.razor.cs:266, Components/Legal/TermsAcceptanceGate.razor.cs:235, Pages/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAccount.razor.cs:311, all calling LogoutAsync). Downstream, the shared ChangePasswordCard calls ChangePasswordAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:149), and the consumer profile pages (Profile) host that card rather than calling the service themselves. ForgotPassword.razor discards the Result of its call (line 95), because the page must look identical whether or not the address exists. The component gallery substitutes NoOpAuthUIService, and AuthUIServiceTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/AuthUIServiceTests.cs:39) pins the behavior end to end.
    • Caveats: TryRefreshTokenAsync has no call site in MMCA.Common.UI outside its own declaration; renewal in a running app happens further down, inside the storage service, the refreshers and the AuthDelegatingHandler 401 path, so this method is a public entry point for hosts and tests. CreateAuthenticatedClientAsync sets a DefaultRequestHeaders Bearer while AuthDelegatingHandler would otherwise attach one to every APIClient request from storage (DependencyInjection.cs:174); the handler skips its own lookup when the request already carries an Authorization header (Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:192), so the stored token is read once here and the handler leaves that header alone. Behind the same-origin proxy both are then stripped by SameOriginProxyRequestHandler.

    AppUserAgent

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Devices · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Devices/AppUserAgent.cs:10 · Level 0 · class (public, static)

    • What it is: builds the User-Agent header value a native MMCA app sends, in the shape Name/Version (Platform OsVersion; MmcaApp), so the server can tell an app session from a browser session and the signed-in-devices page can label it.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; BCL only (string.Normalize, CharUnicodeInfo, StringBuilder).
    • Concept introduced, a header value built from untrusted text must be made header-safe. App name, version and OS version come from the device, and an HTTP header token cannot hold spaces, parentheses, slashes or non-ASCII. Build therefore sanitizes every part instead of trusting it.
      • [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether externally sourced text is neutralized before it reaches a protocol boundary. Comment text drops the delimiters (, ), the escape \ and the separator ; (AppUserAgent.cs:112), so a hostile or odd OS string cannot close the comment early or forge the MmcaApp marker.
      • [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] shows in the single Sanitize routine shared by both character classes (AppUserAgent.cs:79), parameterized by predicate and replacement character.
    • Walkthrough:
      • Marker = "MmcaApp" (AppUserAgent.cs:13) is the public token the reader side looks for; FallbackName = "App" (line 16) stands in when nothing of the app name survives sanitizing, and TokenSymbols (line 19) lists the punctuation an RFC 9110 token may hold.
      • Build(appName, appVersion, platform, osVersion) (line 29) rejects a blank appName with ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace (line 31), tokenizes the name (falling back to App, lines 33-37) and the version, joins them as name/version or just name (lines 39-40), then builds the comment from the normalized platform and OS version (lines 42-44). The result is product (system; MmcaApp), or product (MmcaApp) when both system parts are empty (lines 46-48).
      • NormalizePlatform (line 55) renames MAUI's UI-stack names to OS names: WinUI becomes Windows and MacCatalyst becomes macOS (lines 59-64).
      • ToToken (line 71) and ToCommentText (line 77) call Sanitize (line 79): it folds accents with FormD and drops non-spacing marks, then collapses each run of disallowed characters into one replacement (a hyphen for tokens, a space for comment text), never leading with one. IsTokenChar (line 110) is ASCII letters, digits and TokenSymbols; IsCommentChar (line 112) is visible ASCII minus the four reserved characters.
    • Why it's built this way: the writer and the reader are separate classes with one shared constant, so the marker cannot drift: UserAgentSummary matches on AppUserAgent.Marker rather than a literal. Sanitizing at the writer keeps the reader's parse trivially simple.
    • Where it's used: called once by MauiAppUserAgentHandler to build its cached header (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/Services/MauiAppUserAgentHandler.cs:21); read back by UserAgentSummary.ParseApp (UserAgentSummary.cs:185, 161). Pinned by AppUserAgentTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/Devices/AppUserAgentTests.cs).

    BackfillGate

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Devices · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Devices/DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:95 · Level 0 · class (private, sealed, nested)

    • What it is: the two-flag state DeviceMetadataReporting keeps per reporter instance, answering "is the refresh backfill done?" and "is one running right now?" so the backfill reports until one report succeeds and never runs twice at once.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; BCL Volatile and Interlocked only.
    • Walkthrough: two int fields, _reported and _running (DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:97-98). TryBegin (lines 100-101) returns true only when _reported still reads 0 and a CompareExchange flips _running from 0 to 1, so a concurrent refresh that loses the race skips rather than waits. End (line 103) releases _running; MarkReported (line 105) sets _reported for good, after which TryBegin always refuses.
    • Why it's built this way: an int pair with Volatile/Interlocked is the lock-free form of a one-shot gate: nothing blocks, and a joiner simply skips the backfill because another call is already doing it. The class doc states the two questions it answers (line 94).
    • Where it's used: only inside DeviceMetadataReporting, created on demand by Gates.GetValue (DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:47, 75), opened by TryBegin (line 76), released in a finally (line 87) and closed by MarkReported after any recorded report (line 47).

    IDeviceMetadataReporter

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Devices · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Devices/IDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:22 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the client-side contract that reports the device this app runs on to the server, which records it on the caller's current refresh session (PUT auth/sessions/current/device), so the signed-in devices list and the sign-in history name the device instead of describing its user-agent (IDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:3-6).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party in its signature. Implemented by NullDeviceMetadataReporter (the default on every head) and by MauiDeviceMetadataReporter on native heads; the metadata it sends is the server-side DeviceMetadata record.
    • Concept introduced, a best-effort side call with a boolean contract. The device report rides behind a sign-in or a refresh that already succeeded, so it must never be able to fail or delay either. The interface encodes that in two ways: the class doc makes "should not throw" part of the contract and says the callers bound the wait and swallow whatever escapes (IDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:14-20), and the single method returns bool instead of throwing, so "not recorded, try again later" is an ordinary answer.
      • [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether a contract states its failure semantics. ReportAsync documents both answers (IDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:28-32): true when the server recorded the report or there is nothing to report, false when it was not recorded, so the refresh backfill tries again on the next refresh.
    • Walkthrough: one member, Task<bool> ReportAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (IDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:33). The caller cancels the token after a short bound (line 27; the bound is DeviceMetadataReporting.Timeout).
    • Why it's built this way: the class doc (IDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:7-13) explains the two callers. The sign-in path reports every time; the native token storage also reports after a successful refresh until one report in the process has succeeded, so a session that began before the server stored device metadata gets described within one access-token lifetime without a new sign-in. Rotation then carries the metadata to every successor session. It must be registered as a singleton because the once-per-process state is tracked per reporter instance (lines 17-19). The device capability abstraction this sits in is ADR-042; the refresh lifecycle it piggybacks on is ADR-051.
    • Where it's used: registered as the no-op default with TryAddSingleton (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Capabilities/DependencyInjection.cs:71) and replaced on MAUI with AddSingleton (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/DependencyInjection.cs:80). Called through DeviceMetadataReporting by AuthUIService after each sign-in (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs:503) and by SecureStoreTokenStorageService after a refresh (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/SecureStoreTokenStorageService.cs:143). Pinned by AuthUIServiceDeviceReportTests and SecureStoreDeviceBackfillTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/Devices/).

    DeviceMetadataReporting

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Devices · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Devices/DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:14 · Level 1 · class (internal, static, partial)

    • What it is: the one place that runs an IDeviceMetadataReporter for its two callers, the sign-in path and the refresh backfill, under the same rules: the wait is capped, and any failure (cancellation included) is logged and swallowed, so a report never fails or holds up the call it follows (DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:6-13).
    • Depends on: IDeviceMetadataReporter and its own nested BackfillGate; externals ConditionalWeakTable, CancellationTokenSource, Task.WaitAsync and the [LoggerMessage] source generator.
    • Concept introduced, bounding a call you do not control. A cancellation token only works if the callee honors it. ReportAsync therefore applies the bound twice: it links the caller's token to a CancelAfter(Timeout) source and passes that to the reporter, and it also wraps the returned task in WaitAsync(Timeout, cancellationToken), so a reporter that ignores cancellation still cannot hold the caller past the bound (comment and call at DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:41-43).
      • [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether swallowed failures stay visible. The broad catch is deliberate (the CA1031 suppression at lines 52-54 names the reason, best-effort) and still logs through a generated LogReportFailed at Warning level (lines 58, 91-92).
    • Walkthrough:
      • Timeout = 3 seconds (DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:20): the report follows a request that just succeeded, so it normally takes a fraction of that; the bound only caps a hung connection (lines 16-19).
      • Gates (line 27) is a ConditionalWeakTable<IDeviceMetadataReporter, BackfillGate>: backfill state keyed by reporter instance rather than a static flag, so it lives and dies with the reporter it describes (lines 22-26).
      • ReportAsync(reporter, logger, cancellationToken) (line 34) runs one bounded report (lines 38-43). When the report was recorded it marks the reporter's gate reported, whoever the caller was, because a recorded device needs no backfill: rotation carries it forward (lines 44-48). Any exception is logged when a logger was supplied and turned into false (lines 53-62).
      • ReportOncePerProcessAsync(reporter, logger) (line 73) is the refresh backfill. It gets the gate, returns immediately when TryBegin refuses (lines 75-79: already reported, or a report is already running), otherwise runs ReportAsync with CancellationToken.None and releases the gate in a finally (lines 81-88). A failed report leaves the gate open, so the next successful refresh (one per access-token lifetime) tries again; nothing retries in between (doc at lines 65-69).
    • Why it's built this way: two callers with one rule set is a duplication risk; centralizing the bound, the swallow and the gate here keeps AuthUIService and SecureStoreTokenStorageService to a one-line call each. Keying the gate by instance is what makes the "register as a singleton" requirement on IDeviceMetadataReporter load-bearing.
    • Where it's used: ReportAsync from AuthUIService.ReportDeviceAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs:503); ReportOncePerProcessAsync from the native token storage after a refresh, deliberately after the hydrate slot is cleared because the report authenticates through the APIClient pipeline whose bearer read comes back to that storage (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/SecureStoreTokenStorageService.cs:139-144).

    IOAuthUISettings

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.OAuth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/IOAuthUISettings.cs:9 · Level 1 · interface

    • What it is: tells the shared login page which external identity providers this host can actually use: three booleans for the built-in providers plus the list of configured generic OIDC providers, so a sign-in button renders only where the provider is really wired up.
    • Depends on: OidcProviderOption (the element type of OidcProviders). Implemented in the framework by DefaultOAuthUISettings and ConfigurationOAuthUISettings; consumed by the shared Login page.
    • Concept introduced, default interface members as a safe-off baseline. All four members carry a body: the three flags return false and the provider list returns [] (IOAuthUISettings.cs:12,15,18,21), so an implementation can be an empty class and still compile with every provider hidden. That is what makes the framework's default a seven-line file rather than a stub with four properties.
      • [Rubric §18, UI Architecture & Component Design] assesses whether a component asks a typed contract rather than reaching into configuration. The login page injects this interface and never touches IConfiguration, so the same markup works on a host that has no OAuth at all.
      • [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] assesses what the client is told. The contract carries availability only: no client id, no secret, no redirect URI, and the OIDC entries carry a name, a display name and a domains flag. The class docs state the intent directly, that implementations declare availability so the login page can conditionally render social buttons (IOAuthUISettings.cs:3-8).
    • Walkthrough: three get-only flags, GoogleEnabled (IOAuthUISettings.cs:12), GitHubEnabled (line 15) and AppleEnabled (line 18), each declared as bool X => false, and IReadOnlyList<OidcProviderOption> OidcProviders => [] (line 21), documented as the providers configured under OAuth:Oidc:<Name>, one sign-in button each (line 20).
    • Why it's built this way: external login is optional per host, and the decision has to be readable from the render tree. Making the interface the question (rather than a settings object) lets the framework register a no-op default and lets a host swap in a real answer without any page change. Adding OIDC as a defaulted member kept every existing implementation compiling. The federated login flow the flags gate is recorded in ADR-036, and the mobile callback variant in ADR-043.
    • Where it's used: AddUIShared() registers the no-op default with TryAddSingleton (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:245, with the override instructions in the comment at lines 243-244). The shared login page injects it (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor:16), guards the Apple, Google and GitHub buttons on it (lines 192, 214, 236), renders one button per OIDC provider (line 260), and in OnInitialized folds everything into one _hasExternalProviders value (lines 305-306) that decides whether the whole external-login block renders (line 180). MMCA.ADC registers ConfigurationOAuthUISettings on all three heads (MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web/Program.cs:86, MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:38, MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/MauiProgram.cs:96).

    NullDeviceMetadataReporter

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Devices · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Devices/NullDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:8 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the no-op IDeviceMetadataReporter, the default on every head. A browser reports no device metadata; its sessions are described from the user-agent the server records at sign-in (NullDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:3-7).
    • Depends on: IDeviceMetadataReporter only.
    • Concept reinforced, the Null Object as a registration default (the same move DefaultOAuthUISettings makes). [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] assesses whether a pattern removes branching. The detail that matters is the answer: ReportAsync returns Task.FromResult(true) (NullDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:11), "nothing to report", so the first sign-in closes the backfill gate in DeviceMetadataReporting and no caller ever retries it.

    OAuthFlowStateStore

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.OAuth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:20 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: binds an OAuth authorize-redirect to the client that started it, by minting a random state value, persisting it with a start time, and later checking that the value the provider's callback returns matches. It is the anti-CSRF half of the flow described by ADR-036.
    • Depends on: ILocalCacheStore (device-local storage, injected, OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:20) for persistence, TimeProvider (injected, defaulted to TimeProvider.System, OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:20, 31) for the expiry check, System.Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator to mint the state value, and its own private record PendingAttempt as the stored shape.
    • Concept introduced, device-local state binding for a redirect-based flow. A browser or MAUI OAuth challenge leaves the app entirely and comes back on a different navigation, so nothing in memory survives the round trip; the only thing that can prove the callback belongs to the request this client made is a value written to durable storage before the redirect and checked after it. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses this exact class of defense: BeginAsync mints the value with RandomNumberGenerator.GetHexString(32, lowercase: true) (OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:57), a cryptographically strong source, not Guid.NewGuid() or a counter. It also fails closed: with no storage to bind against, a completion is refused rather than waved through.
    • Walkthrough:
      • StorageKey = "auth.oauth-flow" (OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:23) and AttemptLifetime = 10 minutes (OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:29, "comfortably longer than a provider round trip and far shorter than a session, so an abandoned attempt cannot be revived days later").
      • IsEnforced (OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:38) reports store.IsAvailable: false only on a host that registered neither the browser nor the native local-storage capability. There nothing durable can be written across the redirect, so every completion is refused (doc at 33-37).
      • BeginAsync (OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:50) returns null immediately when storage is unavailable (52-55), otherwise mints the state, stores a PendingAttempt under StorageKey (57-60), then reads the attempt back and compares its state ordinally (64-65). The read-back exists because the browser store swallows a failed write (comment at 62-63); if the attempt was not kept (storage full, site data blocked, private mode) it throws InvalidOperationException (67-68, documented at 45-49), so the failure surfaces before the redirect for the page to explain rather than one redirect later as an unexplained refusal. On success it returns the state for the caller to append to the challenge URL (71).
      • TryCompleteAsync (OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:85) returns false when storage is unavailable (87-92, "fail closed: with nowhere to keep the attempt, no completion can be shown to belong to this client"), otherwise reads and unconditionally removes the pending attempt (94-95, "removed either way, so a value is good for exactly one completion"), and fails if there was none or it expired (97-100). When a pending attempt exists, it accepts only a non-empty returnedState that matches exactly, ordinal comparison (105-106). An absent or empty value is refused: every legitimate flow round-trips the state, and accepting an omitted parameter would let a pasted link bypass the binding (comment at 102-104, doc at 74-81).
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-036 (Website/docs-src/adr/036-external-oauth-login.md) is the OAuth design this binds into; the single-use, time-boxed local record, together with refusing a completion that omits the state or cannot be bound at all, is what keeps a replayed, stale, or forged callback from being accepted.
    • Where it's used: registered in MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:215 (TryAddScoped). The web flow begins on the Login page (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor.cs:378) and completes on the OAuthComplete page (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/OAuthComplete.razor:75); the native callback path takes it in the constructor of MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/Capabilities/Auth/MauiExternalAuthBroker.cs:40. Pinned by OAuthFlowStateStoreTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/OAuthFlowStateStoreTests.cs), with the page wiring covered by LoginOAuthAttemptTests and OAuthCompleteTests.

    UserAgentSummary

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Devices · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Devices/UserAgentSummary.cs:21 · Level 1 · class (internal, static)

    • What it is: a deliberately tiny User-Agent reader that turns a session's header into the device label a person recognizes their own device by: the browser and the platform for a web session, or the app name and platform for a native MMCA app. When a native client reported device metadata, the label uses that instead. Shared by the signed-in-devices page, the administrator's sessions table and the sign-in history table.
    • Depends on: AppUserAgent (its Marker constant, UserAgentSummary.cs:185), DeviceMetadata (the reported name, model and platform); externals IStringLocalizer (for Describe) and string.Contains with StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase.
    • Concept introduced, scoping a parser to the question actually asked. The class doc argues the design rather than describing it (UserAgentSummary.cs:6-15): a device list only has to let someone answer "is that me?", so a full UA database buys precision nobody reads, while the browser-and-platform pair separates a phone from a work laptop. Anything unrecognized reports null from Parse, and Describe supplies its own "unknown device" wording rather than dumping the raw header, which is neither readable nor localizable.
      • [Rubric §27, Internationalization & Localization] assesses whether user-visible text survives translation. This is the sharpest example in the package: the parts are returned separately and never joined in code, because composing "Chrome on Windows" would hard-code English word order. Describe formats them through localizer resources (Auth.Sessions.Device.Format, Auth.Sessions.Device.AppFormat, Auth.Sessions.Device.Unknown, UserAgentSummary.cs:114-124, and Auth.Sessions.Device.NamedFormat, line 146; ADR-027 is named in the class doc, lines 16-19).
      • [Rubric §32, Dependency & Supply-Chain] applies to what is absent: no UA-parsing library and no data file to keep current, which is a real dependency avoided for a cosmetic feature.
    • Walkthrough:
      • Browsers, eleven (Token, Name) pairs in most-specific-first order (UserAgentSummary.cs:28-41). Order is load-bearing and the comment says why (lines 23-26): every Chromium browser also says "Chrome", and Chrome and Edge both say "Safari", so Edg/, EdgiOS/ and EdgA/ come before OPR/, which comes before CriOS/ and Chrome/, which come before Safari/.
      • Platforms, ten pairs with the same rule (UserAgentSummary.cs:47-59): Windows Phone before Windows, Mac OS X and Macintosh before Linux, because an iPad reports "Macintosh" in desktop mode and Android reports "Linux".
      • AppPlatforms, nine (Word, Name) pairs (UserAgentSummary.cs:65-76) for the one-word platform a native app header carries, including MAUI's desktop names (WinUI to Windows, MacCatalyst to macOS).
      • Parse(string? userAgent) (line 86) returns (null, null) for a missing or blank header (lines 88-91), otherwise runs the shared matcher over each table and returns the pair (line 93).
      • Describe(userAgent, localizer) (line 103) is the header-only label. It reads the native-app marker BEFORE the browser tokens, because an app header that also carries a WebView's Chrome/ token is still the app (lines 107-115). Otherwise a switch over the Parse pair covers all four null combinations: both present uses the Format resource, one present returns it bare, neither returns the localized unknown string (lines 117-125).
      • Describe(device, userAgent, localizer) (line 137) is the overload every view calls. It treats blank metadata values as absent through Blank (line 163), takes the device name, and builds a detail from the model and platform with DescribeHardware (line 154), which reuses the same Format resource so the word order stays a resource (comment at line 153). Name and detail together use NamedFormat (line 146), either one alone is returned bare, and with neither it falls back to the header-only Describe (line 149), which is every browser session.
      • ParseApp (line 169) finds the first ( and the ) after it (searching only from the ( on, through AsSpan(commentStart).IndexOf(')'), lines 182-183), splits the comment on ;, and returns (null, null) unless the parts contain AppUserAgent.Marker (lines 184-188). The app name is the product token before any / (lines 190-196); the platform is the first word of the first comment part, mapped by MatchAppPlatform (lines 198-201).
      • MatchAppPlatform (line 208) checks AppPlatforms case-insensitively, then falls back to the browser Platforms table, then to the raw word (lines 210-218).
      • Match(userAgent, candidates) (line 221) walks a table in order and returns the first name whose token appears case-insensitively, or null.
    • Why it's built this way: ordered tables plus one loop keep the whole implementation small, so adding a browser is one line and the ordering rule is visible at the point it matters. It is internal because nothing outside the package should treat it as a UA parser, and Describe lives here (rather than in each view) so the views cannot label the same session differently. Reported metadata wins over the header because a native app's header names only the app and the platform, while the metadata names the device itself.
    • Where it's used: three call sites of the metadata-aware Describe: Sessions.DescribeDevice (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Sessions.razor.cs:266), the admin UserSessionsTable.DescribeDevice (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/UserSessionsTable.razor.cs:69) and SignInHistoryTable (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/SignInHistoryTable.razor.cs:74). Pinned by UserAgentSummaryTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/Devices/UserAgentSummaryTests.cs). The devices page is the UI half of ADR-097.

    ConfigurationOAuthUISettings

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.OAuth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/ConfigurationOAuthUISettings.cs:19 · Level 2 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the real IOAuthUISettings: it computes provider availability and the generic OIDC provider list once at construction from the OAuth configuration section, and covers both a server host and a WASM client with a single class.
    • Depends on: IOAuthUISettings (the contract it implements) and OidcProviderOption (the list element); externally Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration (IConfiguration, IConfigurationSection).
    • Concept introduced, one class over two configuration shapes. A server host holds the actual OAuth client ids, so "is Google available" is answered by whether OAuth:Google:ClientId is populated. A WASM client must never receive a client id, so it is handed pre-computed OAuth:GoogleEnabled flags through its runtime configuration endpoint instead (ConfigurationOAuthUISettings.cs:5-18). The class accepts either signal. Generic OIDC providers follow the same two shapes under OAuth:Oidc:<Name>: a server lists a section whose ClientId is set, a WASM client lists a section flagged Enabled (class doc, lines 12-17).
      • [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] assesses what configuration reaches the browser. The WASM path carries availability flags only, never the client id, and the class shape is what makes that possible without a second implementation.
      • [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses duplication. One class, one rule per shape, every provider.
    • Walkthrough:
      • ReservedOidcNames (ConfigurationOAuthUISettings.cs:21-23) is a case-insensitive set of google, github, apple, complete, exchange and discover: the built-in provider names and the OAuth route segments, which a configured OIDC section may never shadow.
      • Four get-only auto-properties, GoogleEnabled, GitHubEnabled, AppleEnabled (lines 26, 29, 32) and OidcProviders (line 35, "in configuration order"), set in the constructor (line 37), which null-guards the configuration (line 39), takes the OAuth section (line 41), evaluates each built-in provider through the shared helper (lines 42-44) and reads the Oidc child section (line 45).
      • IsProviderEnabled(oauth, provider) (line 48) is the built-in rule: parse {provider}Enabled as a bool (line 50), and return true when that flag is set or when {provider}:ClientId is non-empty (line 51).
      • ReadOidcProviders(oidc) (line 54) keeps each child section whose key is not reserved and that is enabled (line 56), and projects it to an OidcProviderOption with the section key as Name, a trimmed DisplayName falling back to the key (line 59), and UsesDomains (lines 54-61). IsOidcProviderEnabled (line 63) is the same flag-or-client-id disjunction on Enabled and ClientId; UsesDomains (line 66) is true for a UsesDomains flag or any non-blank Domains entry.
      • Because the values are read once into properties, a render pass never re-walks configuration.
    • Why it's built this way: the flag-or-client-id disjunction is what lets the same type serve both hosts. The server side of the pairing is documented from the API package, which notes that the same OAuth:{Provider}:ClientId keys the API reads are what this class reads for its GoogleEnabled / GitHubEnabled answers (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authentication/ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:18). The federated-login design behind the flags is ADR-036.
    • Where it's used: MMCA.ADC registers it with AddSingleton (which replaces the framework's TryAddSingleton default regardless of ordering) on the Blazor Server head (MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web/Program.cs:86), the WASM client (MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:38) and MAUI (MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/MauiProgram.cs:96, whose comment at lines 77-79 explains that the MAUI registration goes before AddUIShared because that call TryAdds the default). The server head also projects the resolved flags to the WASM client through its /client-config endpoint (MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web/Program.cs:172-174); that projection carries the three built-in flags only, not an Oidc section.

    DefaultOAuthUISettings

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.OAuth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/DefaultOAuthUISettings.cs:7 · Level 1 · class (internal, sealed)

    • What it is: the framework's no-op IOAuthUISettings, which reports every provider as unavailable so an app that has not configured external login shows no social buttons.
    • Depends on: IOAuthUISettings only.
    • Concept reinforced, the Null Object as a registration default (the same move NullNotificationScopeProvider makes for notification scoping). [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] assesses whether a pattern removes branching: because a default is always registered, the login page injects the interface unconditionally and never tests whether one exists.
    • Walkthrough: the entire type is one line, internal sealed class DefaultOAuthUISettings : IOAuthUISettings; (DefaultOAuthUISettings.cs:7). It has no members because IOAuthUISettings gives all three properties false-returning default implementations; the class doc records the contract, that downstream apps override this registration to enable specific providers (lines 3-6).
    • Why it's built this way: internal because nothing outside the package should name it, and a semicolon body because the default interface members already say everything. It is registered with TryAddSingleton (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:245), so a host that registers first keeps its own, and a host that registers afterwards with AddSingleton wins the resolution.
    • Where it's used: resolved as IOAuthUISettings in every host that has not registered its own, which today is all of MMCA.Store's UI heads and MMCA.Helpdesk.

    OidcDiscoveryUIService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.OAuth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/OidcDiscoveryUIService.cs:11 · Level 2 · class (internal, sealed)

    • What it is: the framework's IOidcDiscoveryUIService over the API's anonymous GET auth/oauth/discover endpoint, through the named "APIClient" HttpClient (OidcDiscoveryUIService.cs:6-10).
    • Depends on: IOidcDiscoveryUIService, OidcDiscoveryResponse; externals IHttpClientFactory and System.Net.Http.Json.
    • Concept reinforced, a status code that is an answer versus one that is a failure. A 404 here means "no provider claims this domain", a normal outcome the page turns into a message, while a throttle or an outage must not be mistaken for that answer. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether a client maps the server's contract faithfully: this one maps exactly one status to null and lets every other failure throw (the HttpRequestException is documented at OidcDiscoveryUIService.cs:16).
    • Walkthrough: ApiClientName = "APIClient" (line 13). DiscoverAsync (line 17) null-guards the address (line 19), creates the named client (line 21), sends auth/oauth/discover?email=... with the address escaped through Uri.EscapeDataString (lines 22-24), returns null on 404 Not Found (lines 28-31, reason in the comment at 26-27), calls EnsureSuccessStatusCode (line 33) and deserializes the response body (line 34).
    • Why it's built this way: internal because hosts swap the interface, not this class, and a named client from IHttpClientFactory reuses the APIClient registration other UI services already go through, so the call needs no base address of its own (the URI is relative, line 23).
    • Where it's used: registered with TryAddScoped (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:207) and reached only through IOidcDiscoveryUIService from the Login page.

    ISecureTokenStore

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Tokens · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/ISecureTokenStore.cs:16 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: raw token persistence with no freshness semantics. It reads back exactly what was written and never triggers a refresh, which is what separates it from the storage contract callers actually consume, ITokenStorageService.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party. Implemented by MauiSecureTokenStore over OS SecureStorage; consumed by DirectApiTokenRefresher and by SecureStoreTokenStorageService.
    • Concept introduced, splitting storage from freshness to keep the graph acyclic. This interface exists for a dependency-graph reason that the source states in full (ISecureTokenStore.cs:4-9): ITokenStorageService, the layer callers consume, depends on ITokenRefresher; the refresher in turn depends on this raw store. The chain runs storage, then refresher, then raw store, with no loop. Collapse the two storage interfaces into one and the refresher would depend on the very acquisition that invoked it, which is a re-entrancy hazard at runtime, not just a diagram problem.
      • [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses whether a single interface has one reason to change. Here two responsibilities that look identical from the outside (read a token, write a token) are separated precisely because one of them is allowed to go to the network and the other is not.
      • [Rubric §11, Security] assesses where credentials rest. The remarks record that only hosts which persist tokens themselves implement it: MAUI backs it with OS SecureStorage, while the browser hosts hold the access token in memory and keep the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie, so they have no raw store to expose (ISecureTokenStore.cs:10-14).
    • Walkthrough: four members, all verbatim.
      • GetAccessTokenAsync() reads the stored access token or null (ISecureTokenStore.cs:19).
      • GetRefreshTokenAsync() does the same for the refresh token (line 22).
      • SetTokensAsync(accessToken, refreshToken) persists both, replacing whatever was there (line 25).
      • ClearTokensAsync() removes both, the logout path (line 28).
    • Why it's built this way: the interface is deliberately dumber than the one above it. Because it promises no freshness, an implementation can be a thin wrapper over a platform API with no policy, and the single-flight hydration policy lives once, higher up, in the storage services.
    • Where it's used: registered on the MAUI head only, services.AddScoped<ISecureTokenStore, MauiSecureTokenStore>() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/DependencyInjection.cs:117, with the rationale at lines 66-77). Injected into DirectApiTokenRefresher (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/DirectApiTokenRefresher.cs:26) and mocked directly in DirectApiTokenRefresherTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/DirectApiTokenRefresherTests.cs:31).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: no browser host implements it. Resolving it on a Blazor Server or WASM head is a DI failure by design, not an oversight.

    ITokenRefresher

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Tokens · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/ITokenRefresher.cs:17 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: a one-method contract for acquiring a fresh JWT access token, abstracting over the fact that each host holds its refresh credential somewhere completely different.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party. Implemented by SameOriginProxyTokenRefresher on the browser heads and DirectApiTokenRefresher on MAUI; consumed by WasmTokenStorageService, ServerTokenStorageService, SecureStoreTokenStorageService and AuthUIService.
    • Concept introduced, one contract over two materially different security models. The interface doc enumerates both (ITokenRefresher.cs:4-15): on the browser the refresh token lives in an HttpOnly cookie and rotation happens server-side behind the same-origin /auth/session/token endpoint, so the refresh token is never exposed to JS; on MAUI the refresh token sits in OS SecureStorage and is exchanged directly against the API's cross-origin auth/refresh.
      • [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether the strongest available mechanism is used per platform. A browser has an XSS surface and gets the cookie proxy; a native app has no DOM and gets direct token handling. The abstraction is what lets both be correct without a shared lowest common denominator.
      • [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] shows in the fact that the two implementations talk to two different origins (the UI host for one, the API for the other) behind one signature.
    • Walkthrough: a single member, Task<string?> AcquireAccessTokenAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (ITokenRefresher.cs:24). The nullable return is the whole error model: null means no valid session exists, whether the refresh credential is missing, expired, or revoked (lines 15-19). There is no exception path a caller has to know about.
    • Why it's built this way: null-rather-than-throw matches how the callers use it. Token storage calls this on a hot path (every outgoing request may hydrate) and "the session is gone" is an ordinary outcome, not an exceptional one. Modelling it as an exception would force a try around every hydrate.
    • Where it's used: registered per host, AddScoped<ITokenRefresher, SameOriginProxyTokenRefresher>() on the Blazor Server and WASM heads (MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI.Web/Program.cs:115, MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:45) and AddScoped<ITokenRefresher, DirectApiTokenRefresher>() on MAUI (MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI/MauiProgram.cs:97).

    TokenAcquisition

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Tokens · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/TokenAcquisition.cs:9 · Level 0 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the three-way outcome of a token-acquisition attempt: a token, a definitive "no session", or a transient failure. It is a sealed value holder with a private constructor (TokenAcquisition.cs:11), so the only ways to get one are its three factories.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party. Produced by ISessionAwareTokenRefresher implementations (SameOriginProxyTokenRefresher, DirectApiTokenRefresher) and read by WasmTokenStorageService.
    • Concept introduced, making "absent" and "unknown" different values. A nullable token collapses two very different facts: the server said there is no session, or the attempt failed and said nothing. Treating the second as the first makes a signed-in user look anonymous after a 429 or a dropped connection.
      • [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]: only the definitive NoSession lets storage skip repeat token POSTs, and the type, not an exception or a magic null, carries that distinction.
      • [Rubric §11, Security]: a revoked or reused refresh token is NoSession, but a 409 on a superseded token is Unavailable (DirectApiTokenRefresher.cs:85-88), so the stored pair is not cleared by a race.
    • Walkthrough:
      • NoSession (line 35), the static outcome for an answer that proves there is no session (the endpoint's 401); AccessToken is null and IsUnavailable is false.
      • Unavailable (line 38), for an attempt that failed without saying anything about the session; IsUnavailable is true, so the next read should try again (lines 43-47).
      • Acquired(accessToken) (line 52) calls ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace (line 54) and returns an outcome carrying the token, so a blank token can never masquerade as success.
      • AccessToken (line 41) is null for both non-success outcomes.
    • Why it's built this way: the two static singletons avoid allocation on the hot "no token" paths, and the private constructor keeps the invariant (a token implies not unavailable) unforgeable. Design rationale: ADR-051.
    • Where it's used: returned by TryAcquireAccessTokenAsync in both refreshers, and consumed in WasmTokenStorageService.HydrateAsync (WasmTokenStorageService.cs:212-214) and the handoff session services (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/SameOriginProxy/HandoffSessionServices.cs). Covered through WasmTokenStorageServiceTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/WasmTokenStorageServiceTests.cs).

    ITokenStorageService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Tokens · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/ITokenStorageService.cs:8 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the platform-agnostic token contract every other UI type depends on. Anything that needs a bearer token asks this, and never asks where the token is kept.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party. Implemented by WasmTokenStorageService, ServerTokenStorageService and SecureStoreTokenStorageService.
    • Concept introduced, the freshness-checking storage layer. It shares its four member signatures with ISecureTokenStore, and the difference is entirely in the promise: this one may go and acquire a token, the raw store may not. Reading the two interfaces side by side is the fastest way to understand the auth layering in this package.
      • [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] assesses whether presentation code depends on abstractions rather than platform APIs. Nothing above this line names SecureStorage, HttpContext, or a cookie.
      • [Rubric §11, Security] assesses the storage decision itself, and the doc makes it explicit: browser hosts hold the access token in memory and mirror the refresh token to an HttpOnly cookie, never localStorage; MAUI uses OS SecureStorage (ITokenStorageService.cs:3-7).
    • Walkthrough: GetAccessTokenAsync() (ITokenStorageService.cs:11), GetRefreshTokenAsync() (line 14), SetTokensAsync(accessToken, refreshToken) called after a successful login or refresh (line 17), and ClearTokensAsync() for logout (line 20).
    • Why it's built this way: four methods is the smallest surface that covers the whole client auth lifecycle, and keeping it free of any freshness parameter means the policy (skew, single-flight) belongs to the implementation, where it can differ per host.
    • Where it's used: injected into AuthDelegatingHandler, JwtAuthenticationStateProvider, AuthUIService, AuthenticatedServiceBase (which uses it for the direct-token path that bypasses the delegating handler, MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Api/AuthenticatedServiceBase.cs:65) and NotificationHubService for the SignalR access-token provider. Test hosts substitute StubTokenStorageService and NullTokenStorageService (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Gallery/Stubs/NullTokenStorageService.cs:8).

    JwtTokenInfo

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Tokens · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/JwtTokenInfo.cs:9 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: one static predicate, IsFresh, that answers whether a cached access token is still worth using or whether the caller should go and re-acquire one.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party. Externals: System.IdentityModel.Tokens.Jwt (JwtSecurityTokenHandler) and DateTime.UtcNow.
    • Concept introduced, unvalidated client-side token inspection. Reading a JWT without checking its signature looks alarming until you see what the answer is used for: it decides whether to call the refresher, nothing else. The class doc states the boundary plainly, no signature validation because the API validates every request (JwtTokenInfo.cs:5-7).
      • [Rubric §11, Security] assesses where trust decisions are made. A forged token that passed this check would still be rejected by the API on the first call, so the client-side read is an optimization, not an authorization.
      • [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses avoidable round trips. Without this check every outgoing request would have to hydrate; with it, a live token short-circuits the whole refresh path.
    • Walkthrough: IsFresh(string? token, TimeSpan skew) (JwtTokenInfo.cs:16) runs four guards and returns false on all of them, so every uncertain case biases toward refreshing:
      • a null, empty, or whitespace token (lines 18-21);
      • a token JwtSecurityTokenHandler.CanReadToken rejects, meaning it is not a readable JWT (lines 23-27);
      • otherwise it reads the token and compares ValidTo > DateTime.UtcNow + skew (line 31), so the skew is a proactive margin: the token is called stale slightly before it truly expires;
      • and a parse blowing up as ArgumentException or FormatException is caught and reported as not fresh (lines 33-36).
    • Why it's built this way: a static pure function of two arguments is trivially testable and has no lifetime to manage, and the deliberate fail-to-false makes every failure mode converge on the one safe action (refresh). The exception filter is narrow on purpose: only the two malformed-input types are swallowed, so a genuinely unexpected failure still surfaces.
    • Where it's used: WasmTokenStorageService.GetAccessTokenAsync with a 30-second skew (WasmTokenStorageService.cs:31,73), and the same pattern in ServerTokenStorageService (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Services/ServerTokenStorageService.cs:55).

    TokenHydrationWarmup

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Tokens · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/TokenHydrationWarmup.cs:26 · Level 1 · class (static, partial)

    • What it is: a one-method boot-time warm-up that reads the access token once through ITokenStorageService, so the first hydration overlaps the app's first render instead of delaying whichever API call happens to go out first.
    • Depends on: ITokenStorageService (resolved, not injected, so the call is optional at the call site) and Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.ILoggerFactory, both pulled from the host's root IServiceProvider (TokenHydrationWarmup.cs:37,42,46).
    • Concept introduced, a fire-and-forget warm-up that cannot fault. [Rubric §23, Front-End Performance] assesses avoidable delay on first render; this type exists because hydration used to run inline on whichever APIClient call the user made first. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] applies to the swallow-and-log shape: because the call is discarded (_ = TokenHydrationWarmup.WarmAsync(...)) rather than awaited, an unhandled fault here would surface as an unobserved task exception rather than anywhere useful, so the method is written to never throw. On the anonymous path a failed warm-up is expected (there is no session to hydrate), so the failure logs at Debug, not Warning (TokenHydrationWarmup.cs:52).
    • Walkthrough
      • WarmAsync(IServiceProvider services) (TokenHydrationWarmup.cs:37) null-guards services (line 38).
      • It resolves the logger before the try (line 41), with the comment noting that this keeps the handler resolution itself from being the thing that throws.
      • Inside the try, it resolves ITokenStorageService and calls GetAccessTokenAsync(), discarding the result (line 45): the point is the side effect (populating the in-memory token or the single-flight hydration), not the value.
      • A catch (Exception ex) (line 48, CA1031 suppressed with a comment explaining the design) logs through the source-generated LogWarmupFailed (lines 54, 59-60) and returns normally.
