    • Why it's built this way: a static partial class with a [LoggerMessage]-generated logging method keeps the warm-up allocation-light and dependency-free at the call site: it takes the root provider rather than a constructor-injected service, because it runs once at startup before any component tree exists to inject into.
    • Where it's used: MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:95, called and discarded (_ = TokenHydrationWarmup.WarmAsync(host.Services)) right after MmcaCultureBootstrap.SetBrowserCultureAsync and before host.RunAsync(); the surrounding comment (Program.cs:90-94) records the cost it replaces, about 2.4s added to the first cold-start APIClient call under the old inline hydration. Covered by TokenHydrationWarmupTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/TokenHydrationWarmupTests.cs:13), which exercises the success path (line 21), a storage failure (line 33) and a provider with no registered storage service (line 45).

    ISessionAwareTokenRefresher

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Tokens · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/ISessionAwareTokenRefresher.cs:12 · Level 1 · interface

    • What it is: an ITokenRefresher that can say why it returned no token. It adds one method that reports a TokenAcquisition instead of a bare nullable string.
    • Depends on: ITokenRefresher (base interface) and TokenAcquisition (the return type). Implemented by SameOriginProxyTokenRefresher and DirectApiTokenRefresher; consumed by WasmTokenStorageService and ServerTokenStorageService (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Services/ServerTokenStorageService.cs).
    • Concept introduced, a capability interface instead of a changed contract. The base Task<string?> answer cannot separate a definitive "no session" from a transient failure, and a caller that caches the absence of a session needs exactly that difference. Rather than break every ITokenRefresher implementation, the richer method lives on a derived interface that callers probe for at runtime (WasmTokenStorageService.cs:210).
      • [Rubric §1, SOLID] (open for extension, closed for modification): the original contract is untouched and implementers opt in.
      • [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses redundant work: knowing "no session" is definitive is what lets storage skip repeat token POSTs for a short grace.
    • Walkthrough: a single member, Task<TokenAcquisition> TryAcquireAccessTokenAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (ISessionAwareTokenRefresher.cs:17). Its documented result is "the acquired token, a definitive 'no session', or a transient failure" (line 16), and it does not throw for those cases.
    • Why it's built this way: see ADR-051. A refresher that does not implement it (for example the handoff one) keeps the previous reading, where null means "no session" (WasmTokenStorageService.cs:217-220).
    • Where it's used: the two refreshers above implement it, and WasmTokenStorageService.HydrateAsync type-tests for it (WasmTokenStorageService.cs:210). Covered by DirectApiTokenRefresherTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/DirectApiTokenRefresherTests.cs).

    ISessionAwareTokenStorage

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Tokens · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/ISessionAwareTokenStorage.cs:12 · Level 1 · interface

    • What it is: an ITokenStorageService that can report a session it held has ended on the server, and that can be told the API refused a token it handed out. It adds two members: the SessionEnded event (ISessionAwareTokenStorage.cs:18) and RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync, which carries a default implementation (line 37).
    • Depends on: ITokenStorageService (base interface); the "ended" signal is the definitive TokenAcquisition.NoSession outcome. Implemented by WasmTokenStorageService (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/WasmTokenStorageService.cs:29), ServerTokenStorageService (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Services/ServerTokenStorageService.cs:53) and the MAUI SecureStoreTokenStorageService (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/SecureStoreTokenStorageService.cs:59); consumed by JwtAuthenticationStateProvider (the event) and AuthDelegatingHandler (the renewal).
    • Concept introduced, a session can end without this client signing out. Revoking from another device ("Sign out everywhere") or deleting the account ends the server session while this shell still believes it is signed in. The next refresh answers a DEFINITIVE "no session", and the interface doc records the symptom it fixes: without the signal the shell stayed signed in behind 401s (ISessionAwareTokenStorage.cs:3-11).
      • [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] assesses whether auth state follows its source of truth. The storage is the first component to learn the session is gone, so it pushes that fact to the auth-state owner rather than waiting for a render to poll it.
      • [Rubric §1, SOLID]: the same capability-interface move as ISessionAwareTokenRefresher. The base contract is unchanged, and a storage that does not implement this behaves as before (line 10). The second member goes one step further: it is a default interface method returning null (line 37), so a storage written before it keeps compiling and behaves as before (lines 34-35).
    • Concept extended, an API 401 can end the session too. A refresh is the only place the first member learns a session is gone, and a still-fresh token never triggers one. The remarks record the gap: a locked user's fresh token kept the shell signed in behind "you are not signed in" errors until it expired (ISessionAwareTokenStorage.cs:32-34). RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync closes it by letting the HTTP pipeline report the refused token back to the storage that issued it.
    • Walkthrough:
      • event EventHandler? SessionEnded (ISessionAwareTokenStorage.cs:18). Its contract (lines 14-17): raised once, only when a refresh answered a definitive "no session" for a session this storage held, and the stored access token is already cleared when it fires. A transient refresh failure never raises it (line 9).
      • Task<string?> RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync(string rejectedAccessToken) (line 37). Its contract (lines 20-28): when the storage still holds the rejected token it discards it and attempts ONE refresh through the same single-flight a stale token takes; a definitive "no session" then clears the stored tokens and raises SessionEnded, and an acquired token replaces the rejected one. A token the storage no longer holds (already replaced, or never held by this instance) changes nothing. It returns the token the storage holds afterwards, or null (line 30).
    • Why it's built this way: an event, not a polled flag, because the consumer must react the moment the hydrate lands; and the renewal goes through the storage's own single-flight rather than a separate refresh, so a burst of 401s for one token costs one refresh. See ADR-051 for the client token lifecycle this extends.
    • Where it's used: JwtAuthenticationStateProvider type-tests its injected storage for it in the constructor and subscribes (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:50-53, same DI scope and lifetime as the storage, per the comment at line 49); its OnSessionEnded handler forgets the list-page state and calls NotifyUserLogout (lines 145-151). AuthDelegatingHandler reports a 401 to the storage that owns the bearer: ReportRejectedAsync falls back to a type test of the handler's own storage (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:318-320) and calls RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync (line 328), skipping a token that is itself the product of a renewal (lines 312-316). AuthenticatedServiceBase reads the same capability as StorageRenewsRejectedTokens, so a replaying caller does not refresh a second time (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Api/AuthenticatedServiceBase.cs:102). SessionEnded is raised by WasmTokenStorageService.HydrateAsync (WasmTokenStorageService.cs:243), by ServerTokenStorageService (ServerTokenStorageService.cs:314) and by SecureStoreTokenStorageService.RaiseSessionEnded (SecureStoreTokenStorageService.cs:238). Pinned by WhenTheStorageReportsTheSessionEnded_NotifiesAnonymous and WhenTheStorageReportsTheSessionEnded_ForgetsTheListPageStateAndNotifiesAnonymous (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/JwtAuthenticationStateProviderTests.cs:137,152); the renewal contract by the shared ApiUnauthorized_* cases (MMCA.Common/Tests/Shared/UI/TokenStorageServiceTestsBase.cs:327,347,378) and end to end by SessionBearerRenewalTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Api/SessionBearerRenewalTests.cs:53).

    SameOriginProxyTokenRefresher

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Tokens · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/SameOriginProxyTokenRefresher.cs:16 · Level 2 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the browser ISessionAwareTokenRefresher, used by both Blazor Server and WebAssembly. It asks a JS helper to POST the same-origin /auth/session/token endpoint and reports what comes back as a TokenAcquisition.
    • Depends on: ISessionAwareTokenRefresher (the contract), TokenAcquisition and IJSRuntime, plus the mmcaAuthSession helper in MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/wwwroot/mmca-auth-cookie.js:32, whose getToken issues the fetch (line 35).
    • Concept introduced, the BFF hop. The refresh token never enters this process. The browser sends its HttpOnly cookies with credentials:'same-origin', the UI host validates or refreshes server-side, and only the access token comes back over the wire (SameOriginProxyTokenRefresher.cs:5-10). The server half is SessionCookieEndpoints, which maps POST /auth/session/token (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/SessionCookies/SessionCookieEndpoints.cs:69).
      • [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] assesses whether a long-lived credential is reachable from scripts. It is not: an XSS on this page can steal an access token that expires in minutes, not the refresh token behind it.
      • [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] shows in the origin choice. The call goes to the UI host, not the API, so it stays same-origin and needs no CORS or cross-site cookie policy.
    • Walkthrough: two methods. AcquireAccessTokenAsync(cancellationToken) (SameOriginProxyTokenRefresher.cs:19) is a shim returning (await TryAcquireAccessTokenAsync(...)).AccessToken. TryAcquireAccessTokenAsync (line 23) invokes mmcaAuthSession.getToken through interop (line 27) and maps a blank result to TokenAcquisition.NoSession, anything else to Acquired (line 28). The remarks (lines 11-15) record the script contract: it answers null only for the endpoint's 401 and throws for any other failure (a 429, a 5xx, a network error), which is what lets this method tell the two apart. The four interop-unavailable exception types JsFetchSessionCookieSync filters on are caught inline (line 30) and reported as Unavailable, with the comment saying none of these says anything about the session and that the server-side cookie path covers the interop-less phases (lines 32-34).
    • Why it's built this way: a proxy hop instead of a direct API call is the decision recorded in ADR-022, including the SameSite=Lax plus Sec-Fetch-Site check that hardens the refresh endpoint. The three-way outcome (see ADR-051) lets token storage tell "no session" from "interop not ready or endpoint failing", so a transient failure is not remembered as anonymous; the plain string? shim still satisfies the ITokenRefresher contract.
    • Where it's used: registered on both browser heads (MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI.Web/Program.cs:115 and MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:45); consumed indirectly by WasmTokenStorageService and ServerTokenStorageService. Covered by SameOriginProxyTokenRefresherTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/SameOriginProxyTokenRefresherTests.cs:14).

    SecureStoreTokenStorageService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Tokens · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/SecureStoreTokenStorageService.cs:55 · Level 2 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the MAUI head's ITokenStorageService, declared as the ISessionAwareTokenStorage capability (SecureStoreTokenStorageService.cs:59). It is the freshness-checking layer over a persistent ISecureTokenStore, the device counterpart of WasmTokenStorageService (class doc, lines 7-12).
    • Depends on: ISecureTokenStore and ITokenRefresher (required constructor parameters, lines 56-57); optionally IDeviceMetadataReporter and ILogger<SecureStoreTokenStorageService> (lines 58-59); JwtTokenInfo for the freshness check, ISessionAwareTokenRefresher through a runtime type test (line 251), DeviceMetadataReporting for the backfill report; externals System.Threading.Lock, Interlocked and Volatile.
    • Concept introduced, process-wide single-flight for a scoped service. The single-flight hydration itself is taught at WasmTokenStorageService; what is new here is its scope. The refresh slot, the token version and the session-ended handler list are static (lines 63-76), and the class doc gives the reason (lines 30-38): the service is scoped, and the AuthDelegatingHandler built by IHttpClientFactory resolves its own instance in its handler scope. Per-instance state let the handler scope and the component scope each rotate the same refresh token, and the second rotation reads as reuse and revokes the session (BR-206); a per-instance event fired on the handler's instance while the auth state listened on the component's. A device runs one user session per process, so one slot is the right scope.
      • A definitive "no session" clears the stored pair. A token on a device can be hours or days old, and a dead pair left in the store made every read re-post a refresh the server could only refuse: the class doc records the 2026-10-17 conference-day loop of 6 to 31 refresh 401s a minute per device (lines 14-22). Clearing the pair ends that, because the next read finds no pair and the refresher answers without a request (line 22).
      • [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] assesses where shared state lives and who may share it. The three statics are deliberate, and that is enforced: StateManagementConventionTests lists them as the only allowed mutable statics of the class, with the rationale that only AddCommonMauiTokenStorage() registers it, so no Blazor Server circuit can share them (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Ui/StateManagementConventionTests.cs:21-34).
      • [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses how failures are told apart. Only a definitive "no session" for a held pair clears it; a transient failure (TokenAcquisition.Unavailable, a 409 superseded included) keeps the pair for the next attempt (lines 20-22, enforced at lines 262-265).
    • Walkthrough:
      • ExpirySkew, 30 seconds (SecureStoreTokenStorageService.cs:61), the proactive margin. Statics: HydrateSync and SessionEndedSync (lines 63, 65), the two Locks; _hydrateInFlight (line 67), the shared hydrate task; _tokenVersion (line 74), bumped by every set and clear so a sign-in that lands mid-refresh wins over the "no session" answer read before it (M234, lines 69-73); _processSessionEnded (line 76), the process-wide handler list. Per instance: _subscriptions (line 78), the handlers this instance added.
      • SessionEnded (line 81) is a custom event accessor: add and remove (lines 83-109) write the static list under SessionEndedSync and record the handler in _subscriptions, so an event raised by the handler scope's instance reaches the listener subscribed on the component scope's.
      • GetAccessTokenAsync() (line 113) returns the stored token when it is fresh (lines 115-119); otherwise it joins or starts the process-wide hydrate (line 127), awaits it (line 132) and clears the slot only if it still holds that task (line 136). After the slot is cleared, never inside the hydrate, a refreshed token triggers the once-per-process device report (lines 139-144): the report authenticates through the same APIClient pipeline, whose bearer read must find the fresh token instead of joining the refresh it follows.
      • RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync(rejectedAccessToken) (line 156) throws on a blank token (line 158), returns the stored token unchanged when it is not the rejected one (lines 160-164), and otherwise runs the same single-flight hydrate (lines 166-173). Concurrent 401s for one token therefore share one refresh, since a second rotation would read as reuse (remarks, lines 150-155).
      • GetRefreshTokenAsync() (line 178) passes through to the store; SetTokensAsync (line 181) and ClearTokensAsync (line 188) bump _tokenVersion (lines 183, 190) and delegate.
      • Dispose() (line 195) removes from the static list every handler this instance added (lines 199-202), so a disposed scope's subscriber is not kept alive by the static event.
      • JoinOrStartHydrate (line 215) publishes or reads the slot under HydrateSync with ??= (line 219); ClearHydrateIfCurrent (line 227) clears it only on ReferenceEquals (line 231), the same guard against dropping a newer hydrate (lines 223-226). RaiseSessionEnded (line 238) snapshots the handler list under the lock and invokes it outside it (lines 243-246).
      • HydrateAsync() (line 249): a refresher that is not session-aware keeps the previous behavior, its null passed through and the stored pair left alone (lines 251-256). Otherwise it captures the version and whether a refresh token is held (lines 258-259), calls TryAcquireAccessTokenAsync (line 261), and returns early on an acquired token, an unavailable answer or no held pair (lines 262-265). If the version moved meanwhile, a sign-in or sign-out owns the store and it returns null without touching it (lines 267-272). Only then does it clear the store, bump the version and raise SessionEnded (lines 274-276).
    • Why it's built this way: the store underneath (ISecureTokenStore) is deliberately policy-free, so the freshness check, the single-flight and the session-end decision live once, here. The refresh must never read this storage again: the class doc records that DirectApiTokenRefresher posts through the APIClient pipeline and opts out with AuthDelegatingHandler.SkipBearer, because the handler would otherwise await the very hydrate that is waiting for the refresh (lines 24-28). The token lifecycle is ADR-051.
    • Where it's used: registered on the MAUI head, services.AddScoped<ITokenStorageService, SecureStoreTokenStorageService>() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/DependencyInjection.cs:118, documented at lines 102-103), on top of MauiSecureTokenStore. Covered by SecureStoreTokenStorageServiceTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/SecureStoreTokenStorageServiceTests.cs:18), including the cleared pair with one SessionEnded (line 37), the kept pair on an unavailable refresh (line 56), a sign-in mid-refresh (line 86), Dispose (line 108), the cross-instance signal (line 124) and an API 401 ending the session (line 155); the device backfill by SecureStoreDeviceBackfillTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/Devices/SecureStoreDeviceBackfillTests.cs:17).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: unlike the browser storage there is no anonymous grace window; after a clear the next read relies on the refresher answering without a request (class doc, line 22). The RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync path never runs the device report, which only GetAccessTokenAsync triggers (lines 141-144). Because the statics are process-wide, every test class that drives it joins the SecureStoreTokenStorageCollection (SecureStoreTokenStorageServiceTests.cs:17,233), which serializes them: two such classes in parallel would join each other's in-flight refresh (lines 228-230).

    WasmTokenStorageService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Tokens · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/WasmTokenStorageService.cs:26 · Level 2 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the WebAssembly ITokenStorageService, declared as the ISessionAwareTokenStorage capability (WasmTokenStorageService.cs:29). The access token lives in memory only and is hydrated on demand from the HttpOnly cookies; there is no localStorage anywhere in it.
    • Depends on: ISessionCookieSync and ITokenRefresher (constructor parameters, WasmTokenStorageService.cs:26-29), plus JwtTokenInfo for the freshness check; optionally ISessionAwareTokenRefresher (a runtime type test in HydrateAsync, line 210); externals System.Threading.Lock and TimeProvider.
    • Concept introduced, single-flight hydration. Several callers can ask for a token in the same instant: the AuthDelegatingHandler on an outgoing request, the JwtAuthenticationStateProvider during a render, and NotificationHubService's access-token provider. Without coordination each would start its own refresh, and the last one to finish would overwrite the others' token. The fix is to share one in-flight Task, and the source is explicit that the lock, not a ??=, is what makes it single (lines 83-86).
      • Remembering "no session" for a short grace. A visitor with no session would otherwise cost one same-origin token POST per API call. After a hydrate returns a DEFINITIVE "no session", the service answers null from memory for AnonymousGrace, 15 seconds (line 34), checked in GetAccessTokenAsync (lines 78-81). A transient failure is never remembered, and SetTokensAsync resets the window so a login right after anonymous browsing does not wait it out (lines 145-146).
      • A login or logout wins over a hydrate already in flight (M234). _tokenVersion (line 48) is bumped by SetTokensAsync and twice by ClearTokensAsync. HydrateAsync captures it before the acquisition and, if it moved by the time the answer arrives, discards that stale answer together with its grace (lines 206, 222-225).
      • A held session that ends on the server signs the shell out (A-34). _sessionHeld (line 55) records whether this client holds a session. When a session-aware refresher answers a definitive "no session" while it is set, the service raises SessionEnded (line 58) so the auth state goes anonymous (class doc, lines 18-21). A plain refresher's null still starts the grace but is not proof enough to sign a held session out (lines 204-205).
      • [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] assesses ownership of shared per-circuit state; the in-memory token and its in-flight hydration are exactly that.
      • [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses redundant work: a burst of concurrent callers costs one network round trip, not one each.
      • [Rubric §11, Security] assesses at-rest exposure. The refresh token is never held client-side, the comment at line 139 saying it lives only in the HttpOnly cookie.
    • Walkthrough:
      • ExpirySkew, 30 seconds (WasmTokenStorageService.cs:31), the proactive margin handed to JwtTokenInfo.IsFresh; AnonymousGrace, 15 seconds (line 34).
      • _hydrateSync (line 36), the Lock; _timeProvider (line 37), the injected clock (system clock when null); _accessToken (line 39), the in-memory token; _hydrateInFlight (line 40), the shared hydration task; _anonymousUntil (line 41), the end of the current grace; _tokenVersion (line 48), the counter that lets a login or logout invalidate an in-flight hydrate; and the volatile _sessionHeld (line 55), set by a login and by every hydrate that acquired a token, cleared by a logout and when the session is found ended, and left alone by a transient failure (lines 50-54). SessionEnded (line 58) is the ISessionAwareTokenStorage event.
      • A second, two-argument constructor (line 66) chains to the primary one with a null clock, so code compiled against the original signature keeps binding.
      • GetAccessTokenAsync() (line 71) returns the cached token immediately when it is fresh (lines 73-76). If there is no token and the grace has not elapsed it returns null without any network call (lines 78-81). Otherwise it takes the lock only long enough to publish or read the in-flight task (lines 88-92), which is safe because HydrateAsync reaches its first await immediately so nothing slow runs under the lock (lines 83-86). It then awaits the shared task (line 96) and, in a finally, clears _hydrateInFlight only if it is still the same task (ReferenceEquals, line 104). That guard is the subtle half: an unguarded clear can drop a newer hydrate started after this one completed, splitting the next set of callers all over again (lines 100-101).
      • RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync(rejectedAccessToken) (line 118), the ISessionAwareTokenStorage renewal: it throws on a blank token (line 120), then under _hydrateSync returns the current token when it is not the rejected one (lines 125-128); otherwise it drops the token from memory, ends any grace and joins or starts the same in-flight hydrate (lines 130-133). AwaitHydrateAsync (line 176) awaits that task and clears the slot with the same ReferenceEquals guard (line 188), so concurrent 401s for one token share one refresh, and a definitive "no session" raises SessionEnded through HydrateAsync (remarks, lines 113-117).
      • GetRefreshTokenAsync() (line 140) returns null unconditionally, an honest answer rather than a stub: in the browser there is nothing to return.
      • SetTokensAsync(accessToken, refreshToken) (line 142) bumps _tokenVersion (line 145), resets _anonymousUntil (line 146), stores the access token in memory (line 147), sets _sessionHeld (line 148) and seeds the HttpOnly cookies through ISessionCookieSync.SyncAsync (line 153); the comment records that the refresh token transits JS only for that same-origin POST (lines 149-152). A false from the cookie write throws InvalidOperationException (lines 153-156), after the in-memory token is set, so AuthUIService reports Auth.TokenStorageUnavailable instead of a login that silently signs out at the first access-token expiry, when no cookie exists to refresh from.
      • ClearTokensAsync() (line 159) bumps _tokenVersion, nulls the field and clears _sessionHeld (lines 161-163), clears the cookies (line 167), then bumps the version a second time and nulls the field again (lines 172-173). The second bump covers a hydrate that started during the clear, captured the first version and read the session the clear was still removing: its answer is discarded if in flight, and dropped if it already landed (lines 169-171). Clearing is best-effort by contract, so a false from ClearAsync is discarded; the comment points a caller that needs proof the session ended at IAuthUIService.RevokeAllSessionsAsync (lines 164-166). A logout therefore never raises SessionEnded.
      • HydrateAsync() (line 196) captures _tokenVersion first (line 206), then branches on the refresher's capability. When it is an ISessionAwareTokenRefresher (line 210) it calls TryAcquireAccessTokenAsync, keeps AccessToken in a local, reads IsUnavailable and computes definitiveNoSession as a null token that is not unavailable (lines 212-215); otherwise it falls back to ITokenRefresher.AcquireAccessTokenAsync, where a null means "no session" for the grace but never counts as definitive (line 219). If the version moved meanwhile it returns the current _accessToken and publishes nothing (lines 222-225); otherwise it stores the answer (line 227). Only a null token that is not unavailable starts the grace (lines 229-232), so a 429, a 5xx or unavailable interop never makes a signed-in user look anonymous. Finally, an acquired token sets _sessionHeld (lines 234-237); a definitive "no session" while _sessionHeld is set clears it and raises SessionEnded, the token already gone from memory (lines 238-244). See TokenAcquisition.
    • Why it's built this way: the class doc records that it was hoisted out of the app WASM clients because it carries no app-specific state, and names its Blazor Server sibling ServerTokenStorageService in MMCA.Common.UI.Web. The two share the skew constant, the Lock, and the same single-flight shape; the server one adds an HttpContext branch for the prerender pass, and both implement ISessionAwareTokenStorage. The cookie-only storage model is ADR-022; the token lifecycle is ADR-051. The MAUI head's counterpart is SecureStoreTokenStorageService, which keeps the same single-flight but process-wide, over a persistent store.
    • Where it's used: registered on the WASM clients, AddScoped<ITokenStorageService, WasmTokenStorageService>() (MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:52, MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:51). Covered by WasmTokenStorageServiceTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/WasmTokenStorageServiceTests.cs:16), which inherits the shared TokenStorageServiceTestsBase cases: the concurrency path (MMCA.Common/Tests/Shared/UI/TokenStorageServiceTestsBase.cs:73), the failed cookie write as a throw (line 181) and the API-401 renewal (lines 327, 347, 378). SessionBearerRenewalTests drives the renewal end to end through the real pipeline (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Api/SessionBearerRenewalTests.cs:53).

    DirectApiTokenRefresher

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Tokens · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/DirectApiTokenRefresher.cs:40 · Level 3 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the MAUI ISessionAwareTokenRefresher (and so an ITokenRefresher). It reads the token pair out of OS SecureStorage, exchanges it against the API's cross-origin auth/refresh endpoint, and writes the rotated pair back, reporting the outcome as a TokenAcquisition.
    • Depends on: ISecureTokenStore (deliberately, not ITokenStorageService), AuthDelegatingHandler (for its SkipBearer request option), RefreshTokenRequest and AuthenticationResponse from MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth; externals IHttpClientFactory and System.Net.Http.Json.
    • Concept introduced, direct token handling where there is no DOM. The class doc justifies the choice: MAUI has no browser and thus no XSS surface, so holding a refresh token client-side and posting it is acceptable there in a way it is not in a browser (DirectApiTokenRefresher.cs:8-10). This is the counterpart to SameOriginProxyTokenRefresher, and reading the two together is the clearest statement of the framework's per-platform threat model.
      • [Rubric §11, Security] assesses per-platform credential handling, exactly as above.
      • [Rubric §1, SOLID], dependency direction: the second doc paragraph is unusually explicit (lines 12-18). Every operation it performs is a raw read or write, so it takes the raw store; taking ITokenStorageService instead would close the loop and let a refresh re-enter the acquisition that started it.
      • The same cycle through the HTTP pipeline. The third doc paragraph (lines 19-24) names the indirect route back into that loop: the APIClient carries AuthDelegatingHandler, which reads the storage service for a bearer. The refresh POST therefore sets AuthDelegatingHandler.SkipBearer (line 67), so the anonymous refresh call never reaches the storage instance that is awaiting it. The handler honors the option by passing the request through untouched (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:44,187).
      • A 409 is transient, never "no session". The fourth doc paragraph (lines 26-33) explains Auth.RefreshSuperseded: the presented token was rotated by another request inside the server's reuse grace. Clearing the pair on that answer would let a stolen-and-rotated token live for the full refresh lifetime, so the stored pair is left untouched and the next attempt presents it again.
      • Only a refusal is "no session". The fifth doc paragraph (lines 34-39) narrows NoSession to a refusal of the presented token (400, 401, 403). Every other failure (a 408, a 429, a 5xx during a revision swap, a dropped connection, an unrequested timeout) is Unavailable, as SameOriginProxyTokenRefresher reports it, because the caller treats "no session" as a sign-out and clears the stored pair.
    • Walkthrough: AcquireAccessTokenAsync(cancellationToken) (DirectApiTokenRefresher.cs:47) is an expression-bodied shim over TryAcquireAccessTokenAsync (line 52) that returns only .AccessToken, which keeps the plain ITokenRefresher contract intact. The Try method is a straight line of early returns, each producing a TokenAcquisition rather than an exception:
      • read both tokens from the store (lines 54-55), and return NoSession when either is blank (lines 57-60), so a never-logged-in device costs one storage read and no network call;
      • create the named "APIClient" (ApiClientName, line 45), build an HttpRequestMessage POSTing a RefreshTokenRequest carrying both tokens as JsonContent to the relative auth/refresh (lines 62-66), mark it SkipBearer (line 67), and send it inside a try (lines 69-82);
      • return Unavailable when the send throws HttpRequestException (line 76) or an OperationCanceledException the caller did not request, meaning an HttpClient.Timeout (lines 78-82), then hold the response in a using var (line 84);
      • on HttpStatusCode.Conflict (lines 86-89) delegate to ReadSupersededOutcomeAsync (line 112), which re-reads the store: if another refresh in this process already stored a different non-blank pair it returns Acquired with that access token, otherwise Unavailable with the pair left as it was (lines 114-121);
      • on any other non-success status (lines 91-96) return NoSession only for 400, 401 or 403, which is how a revoked or reused refresh token arrives, and Unavailable for the rest;
      • deserialize an AuthenticationResponse and return NoSession when the access token came back blank (lines 98-102);
      • persist the rotated pair through ISecureTokenStore.SetTokensAsync and return TokenAcquisition.Acquired with the new access token (lines 104-105).
    • Why it's built this way: the rotation-on-refresh shape it participates in is ADR-097, which made refresh sessions hashed, rotating and per device: writing the returned pair back is not an optimization, it is required, because the old refresh token is dead after the exchange. An explicit HttpRequestMessage rather than PostAsJsonAsync is what gives the call an Options bag to carry SkipBearer. The using var httpClient (line 62) and the relative Uri both lean on the named client configured once in AddUIShared, which also attaches the delegating handler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:152,174).
    • Where it's used: registered on the MAUI heads, AddScoped<ITokenRefresher, DirectApiTokenRefresher>() (MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI/MauiProgram.cs:98, MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/MauiProgram.cs:177). Covered by DirectApiTokenRefresherTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/DirectApiTokenRefresherTests.cs:17), which stubs the store and the HTTP handler (lines 25-36) and asserts the SkipBearer mark on the refresh POST (line 62).

    CultureDelegatingHandler

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Culture · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Culture/CultureDelegatingHandler.cs:13 · Level 0 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: a one-method DelegatingHandler that stamps the active UI culture onto every outgoing API call as an Accept-Language header, so validation and error text come back from the backend in the language the user selected.
    • Depends on: no first-party types. Externals: System.Net.Http.DelegatingHandler, System.Globalization.CultureInfo, and System.Net.Http.Headers.StringWithQualityHeaderValue. It rides the same named "APIClient" pipeline as AuthDelegatingHandler.
    • Concept introduced, culture as a transport header rather than only a cookie. [Rubric §27, Internationalization] assesses whether locale is carried end to end instead of being applied only at the rendering edge; this handler is the piece that closes that loop for server-produced strings. The class comment (CultureDelegatingHandler.cs:7-11) states the reason plainly: the cross-origin Gateway does not carry the ASP.NET culture cookie through to the services, so a cookie-only design would render the page in Spanish while the API answered in English. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven Design] also applies, because this is a concern every service call needs and no service call implements: it is attached once in the HttpClient pipeline instead of at each call site.
    • Walkthrough
      • The only member is the SendAsync override (CultureDelegatingHandler.cs:16).
      • It reads CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture.Name (CultureDelegatingHandler.cs:20) and does nothing when that is blank (CultureDelegatingHandler.cs:21), so an unresolved culture sends no header rather than an empty one.
      • When there is a value it calls AcceptLanguage.Clear() before Add(...) (CultureDelegatingHandler.cs:23-24); the clear matters because a retried request object would otherwise accumulate a second language entry.
      • It returns base.SendAsync(request, cancellationToken) directly (CultureDelegatingHandler.cs:27) rather than awaiting it, so the handler adds no async state machine to the hot path.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-027 makes multi-locale a whole-stack concern. Registering the behavior as a message handler means the culture travels on calls made by code that has never heard of localization. It is registered transient in DependencyInjection (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:143) and appended to the "APIClient" pipeline after the auth handler (DependencyInjection.cs:174-175).
    • Where it's used: every request through the "APIClient" named client, which is every call made by EntityServiceBase<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType>, ChildEntityServiceBase, ApiUserPreferenceReader and ApiUserPreferenceWriter.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: it reads whatever ambient UI culture the head has already established. On a Blazor WebAssembly head that is set by MmcaCultureBootstrap before the host runs; the handler itself makes no attempt to resolve or validate a culture.

    ICultureApplier

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Culture · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Culture/ICultureApplier.cs:14 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the one-method contract for "switch the language and put the user back where they were", written as an abstraction because the mechanism differs per head.
    • Depends on: nothing. Implemented by EndpointCultureApplier (the Blazor Web default) and by MauiCultureApplier in the device-capability layer.
    • Concept introduced, a terminal call. [Rubric §18, UI Architecture] assesses whether host-specific mechanics are hidden behind contracts the components can share; this interface is the clearest example in the UI package. The doc comment (ICultureApplier.cs:3-13) spells out both halves of the contract: a Blazor Web head round-trips the server /culture/set endpoint so the cookie, the SSR prerender and the WASM runtime all agree, while a MAUI Blazor Hybrid head has no ASP.NET pipeline and switches the process culture in place. Because each implementation owns landing the user back on the return path (a redirect on the web, a WebView reload on a hybrid head), callers must treat ApplyAsync as terminal and do no navigation of their own. [Rubric §25, Navigation & Information Architecture] applies for the same reason: navigation ownership is part of the contract rather than an afterthought at each call site.
    • Walkthrough
      • ApplyAsync(string culture, string returnPath, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (ICultureApplier.cs:27) is the whole surface.
      • Two documented behaviors belong to the contract rather than to any one implementation: a culture outside SupportedCultures.All is ignored by the underlying mechanism rather than throwing (ICultureApplier.cs:19-22), and an empty returnPath falls back to "/" (ICultureApplier.cs:23-25).
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-027. Hard-coding the endpoint navigation into the culture switcher component would have made that component unusable on MAUI, where the URL matches no route and the Blazor Router renders the not-found page. The interface lets one shared component serve both heads.
    • Where it's used: injected by the shared CultureSwitcher component, which persists the choice first and then treats the applier call as the last thing it does (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Globalization/CultureSwitcher.razor:6 and CultureSwitcher.razor:44-48), and by the login page when reconciling a returning user's stored culture (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor:15 and Login.razor:239-244).

    LoginRefusal

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/TwoFactor/LoginRefusals.cs:9 · Level 0 · enum (internal)

    • What it is: the four next steps a refused password sign-in can ask of the sign-in page (LoginRefusals.cs:8): Other (show the message, LoginRefusals.cs:12), SecondFactorRequired (the password was proved and the account has a second factor, so ask for the code, LoginRefusals.cs:15), SecondFactorInvalid (the code did not verify, so keep the code step and ask again, LoginRefusals.cs:18) and EmailNotConfirmed (offer to resend the confirmation link, LoginRefusals.cs:21).
    • Depends on: nothing. It is the return type of LoginRefusals.Classify; the mapping from error codes lives in LoginRefusals, which introduces the concept.
    • Where it's used: Login.HandleRefusalStep (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor.cs:123) switches on it: both second-factor values show the code step and clear the previous code (Login.razor.cs:126-131), only SecondFactorRequired counts as fully handled with no message (Login.razor.cs:131), and EmailNotConfirmed records the trimmed address for the resend prompt (Login.razor.cs:134-137). See Login.

    EndpointCultureApplier

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Culture · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Culture/EndpointCultureApplier.cs:18 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the Blazor Web implementation of ICultureApplier. It force-navigates to the server's GET /culture/set endpoint, which writes the culture cookie and redirects the user back to where they were.
    • Depends on: ICultureApplier (implemented) and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.NavigationManager. It pairs with the server endpoint mapped by MapCultureEndpoint() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationExtensions.cs:103, the MapGet("/culture/set", ...) at WebApplicationExtensions.cs:121) and with MmcaCultureBootstrap on the WASM side.
    • Concept introduced, why the full page reload is deliberate. [Rubric §27, Internationalization] assesses whether a locale switch is coherent across every rendering path; the class comment (EndpointCultureApplier.cs:8-10) says the force-load is load-bearing, because the server has to re-render SSR under the new cookie and the WASM runtime has to re-read it on startup, which keeps prerender and hydration on the same culture. A soft, client-only switch would leave the two disagreeing and show a locale flash on the next full load.
    • Walkthrough
      • ApplyAsync (EndpointCultureApplier.cs:21) rejects a null or whitespace culture up front with ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace (EndpointCultureApplier.cs:23).
      • It falls back to "/" for an empty return path (EndpointCultureApplier.cs:25) and builds the URL with Uri.EscapeDataString on both values (EndpointCultureApplier.cs:26), so a return path containing a query string survives round-tripping.
      • It then calls navigation.NavigateTo(url, forceLoad: true) (EndpointCultureApplier.cs:30) and returns Task.CompletedTask (EndpointCultureApplier.cs:31): the method is synchronous in substance and Task-shaped only because the interface must also fit asynchronous heads.
      • The inline comment (EndpointCultureApplier.cs:28-29) notes that validating the culture is the endpoint's job: an unsupported value lands the user back on the same page unchanged rather than failing.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-027. The class comment (EndpointCultureApplier.cs:11-15) also records the boundary of its validity: a head with no ASP.NET pipeline would route /culture/set through the Blazor Router, match no page and render the not-found page, which is exactly why MAUI heads register their own applier after AddUIShared.
    • Where it's used: registered as the default with TryAddScoped<ICultureApplier, EndpointCultureApplier>() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:227), with the comment above it (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:223-226) recording that a hybrid head overrides it afterwards. The MAUI replacement is MauiCultureApplier.

    MmcaCultureBootstrap

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Culture · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Culture/MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:14 · Level 1 · class (static)

    • What it is: the Blazor WebAssembly culture bootstrap. It reads the same ASP.NET culture cookie the server used for SSR prerender and sets the WASM runtime's default thread cultures before the host starts running.
    • Depends on: SupportedCultures from the Shared layer and the culture.js module in the package's wwwroot. Externals: IJSRuntime and CultureInfo.
    • Concept introduced, closing the prerender/hydration culture gap. [Rubric §27, Internationalization] assesses whether every rendering path resolves the same locale; the class comment (MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:7-13) states the outcome this buys: the interactive client renders in the same language the server prerendered, with no locale flash and no prerender/hydration mismatch. [Rubric §23, Front-End Performance] applies too, because the alternative (letting the client discover the culture after first render) costs a visible re-render of the whole page.
    • Walkthrough
      • Two overloads of SetBrowserCultureAsync. The one-argument form (SetBrowserCultureAsync(IJSRuntime jsRuntime), MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:25) forwards with allowPseudoLocale: false, so the pseudo locale is never accepted through it. The real work is in SetBrowserCultureAsync(IJSRuntime jsRuntime, bool allowPseudoLocale) (MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:41), null-guarded at MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:43. A Development host passes builder.HostEnvironment.IsDevelopment() as the flag, because the server accepts the pseudo locale only in Development (MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:28-40).
      • It imports ./_content/MMCA.Common.UI/culture.js under an await using (MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:46-47), so the module reference is released as soon as the one call is done: unlike the long-lived services, this runs once at startup and has no reason to hold it.
      • The import and the getCulture call sit inside a #pragma warning disable BL0016 / restore pair (MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:45 and MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:49). The suppression comment gives the reason: the code runs in the WASM Program.cs before the host starts, so there is no circuit, and an interop failure must reach that caller rather than silently boot in the default culture. Nothing here catches the exception.
      • It calls getCulture (MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:48), whose JS side parses the .AspNetCore.Culture cookie's uic= segment and returns null when the cookie is absent or unparseable (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/wwwroot/culture.js:4).
      • The returned value is accepted when SupportedCultures.IsSupported says so, or when allowPseudoLocale is true and SupportedCultures.IsPseudoLocale matches; anything else falls back to SupportedCultures.Default (MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:51-53). The predicate is at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Globalization/SupportedCultures.cs:35, the pseudo-locale check at SupportedCultures.cs:76, the "qps-Ploc" constant at SupportedCultures.cs:28, the allowlist at SupportedCultures.cs:18, and the "en-US" default at SupportedCultures.cs:12.
      • It then assigns only CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentCulture and CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentUICulture (MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:55-56), never CurrentCulture/CurrentUICulture directly: setting the defaults makes every subsequently created thread inherit the culture, which is what a later switch needs in order to take effect.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-027. The cookie is deliberately non-HttpOnly for exactly this reader, a decision recorded in the suppression comment on the server side (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationExtensions.cs:112, written at WebApplicationExtensions.cs:121), which names MmcaCultureBootstrap.SetBrowserCultureAsync as the consumer. The doc comment (MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:11-12) also pins the call ordering: it must run after builder.Build() and before host.RunAsync().
    • Where it's used: both Blazor Web clients call the two-argument overload exactly as documented, passing builder.HostEnvironment.IsDevelopment() so hydration keeps the pseudo locale the server prerendered: MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:86 and MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:71. Its MAUI counterpart is MauiCultureInitializer.

    Subscription

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/TwoFactor/MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:54 · Level 1 · class (private sealed, nested)

    • What it is: the handle MultiFactorRequiredSignal returns from Subscribe: one subscriber, which on disposal removes itself only while it is still the current one for its storage (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:53).
    • Depends on: ITokenStorageService (the key it belongs to) and the enclosing class's Subscriptions table. Implements IDisposable.
    • Concept introduced: none of its own; the weak-keyed signal is taught at MultiFactorRequiredSignal.
    • Walkthrough
      • It holds the storage only through a WeakReference<ITokenStorageService> (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:56), so the handle a component keeps never pins an ended scope's storage, and the callback in a nullable Action? field (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:57).
      • Invoke (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:59) calls the callback when one is still set.
      • Dispose (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:61) first nulls the callback (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:63), so a raise that already fetched this handle becomes a no-op. It then removes the table entry only when the storage is still alive and the entry is this very instance (ReferenceEquals, MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:64-68): disposing a subscription a later Subscribe replaced leaves the successor in place.
    • Where it's used: only through MultiFactorRequiredSignal.Subscribe, whose caller is MultiFactorRequiredListener (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/MultiFactorRequiredListener.cs:41).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the name is shared with unrelated webhook and broker-transport Subscription identifiers elsewhere in Common; this one is private to the signal class and has no other caller.

    ViewerTimeZone

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Culture · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Culture/ViewerTimeZone.cs:22 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: a scoped service that learns the viewer's browser time zone once and converts the UTC instants the API serializes onto the clock the person actually reads. Until the zone is known it reports UTC (ViewerTimeZone.cs:36).
    • Depends on: LazyJsModule (held as _module, built over the host's IJSRuntime in the constructor, ViewerTimeZone.cs:30) and the time-zone.js module named at ViewerTimeZone.cs:24. Implements IAsyncDisposable.
    • Concept introduced, rendering instants on the viewer's clock. [Rubric §27, Internationalization] assesses whether dates are shown the way the reader expects, not the way the server stores them. A server-side ToLocalTime() would use the server's zone; this service asks the browser instead.
    • Walkthrough
      • Zone (ViewerTimeZone.cs:36) defaults to TimeZoneInfo.Utc; IsResolved (ViewerTimeZone.cs:42) stays false while JS interop is unavailable, so a later call can retry.
      • EnsureResolvedAsync (ViewerTimeZone.cs:54) returns early when already resolved, then imports the module and invokes getTimeZone (ViewerTimeZone.cs:64-65). JS side: MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/wwwroot/time-zone.js:6 returns the Intl.DateTimeFormat zone id, or null when the browser cannot say.
      • Failure handling is split by whether a retry could help. InvalidOperationException (SSR prerender, no interop yet), JSDisconnectedException and OperationCanceledException return false without marking resolved (ViewerTimeZone.cs:67-80); a JSException means the browser answered with an error, so the zone id becomes null and resolution is final (ViewerTimeZone.cs:81-85).
      • Once the browser has answered (successfully or not) it sets IsResolved, assigns Zone through the private ResolveZone, and returns true (ViewerTimeZone.cs:87-89). It returns true even when the zone stays UTC, because the first resolution is what turns Format output from the empty placeholder into a time, so the caller always re-renders once. ResolveZone (ViewerTimeZone.cs:128) falls back to UTC for a missing or unknown id.
      • ToViewerTime (ViewerTimeZone.cs:100) reads Utc and Unspecified kinds as UTC (a deserialized value often arrives unspecified) and normalizes Local first, then calls TimeZoneInfo.ConvertTimeFromUtc. Format (ViewerTimeZone.cs:118) returns string.Empty while IsResolved is false (prerender, and the first interactive render before EnsureResolvedAsync ran); once resolved it formats the converted value with CultureInfo.CurrentCulture, default format "g".
      • DisposeAsync (ViewerTimeZone.cs:122) forwards to the module wrapper.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-027 treats locale as a per-viewer concern. Returning a boolean from EnsureResolvedAsync keeps the service free of render coupling: the page calls it from OnAfterRenderAsync on its first render and decides whether to call StateHasChanged. Swallowing prerender interop failures lets the same component render on the server and then fill in after hydration; rendering an empty placeholder until then, rather than a UTC fallback, means a UTC time never paints only to jump to the viewer's clock a moment later.
    • Where it's used: registered with TryAddScoped<ViewerTimeZone>() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:231) and injected by NotificationList.razor.cs:30, NotificationInbox.razor.cs:37 and Sessions.razor.cs:35 under MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/ and by Components/Auth/UserSessionsTable.razor.cs:32, plus ADC pages such as MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Pages/Points/MyPoints.razor.cs. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Culture/ViewerTimeZoneTests.cs.

    MultiFactorRequiredSignal

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/TwoFactor/MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:19 · Level 2 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: an in-process signal that carries "the API refused this session for want of a second factor" from the API client's message handler to the page that should react to it (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:6-12).
    • Depends on: ITokenStorageService (the key) and its nested Subscription. Externals: ConditionalWeakTable<TKey, TValue>.
    • Concept introduced, a signal keyed by the token owner, not by DI scope. The handler that sees the refused response runs in the IHttpClientFactory handler scope, not the component's, so a scoped event service would reach the wrong subscriber. The class keys the signal by the token storage that attached the bearer (the same owner AuthDelegatingHandler reports a 401 to), and the subscriber is the listener rendered in that storage's scope (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:8-11). [Rubric §19, State Management] assesses whether cross-component state has one clear owner and lifetime; here the lifetime is the storage instance itself: the ConditionalWeakTable key means an ended circuit or scope is never kept alive by a subscription (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:14-15). [Rubric §11, Security] applies because the signal is how a step-up demand from the API turns into a prompt instead of a silent failure.
    • Walkthrough
      • Subscriptions (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:21) is the static ConditionalWeakTable<ITokenStorageService, Subscription>: one subscriber per storage.
      • Subscribe(ITokenStorageService, Action) (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:27) null-guards both arguments (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:29-30), creates the handle and stores it with AddOrUpdate (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:33), so a later subscription replaces an earlier one (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:15-17), and returns it as an IDisposable (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:34).
      • HasSubscriber(owner) (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:40-41) lets the handler skip all body inspection when nothing listens.
      • Raise(owner) (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:45) invokes the subscriber when there is one (MultiFactorRequiredSignal.cs:47-50) and is otherwise a no-op.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-051 makes the token storage the unit that owns a session on the client; keying the signal by that same instance keeps the 403 path aligned with the 401 renewal path.
    • Where it's used: AuthDelegatingHandler.ReportMultiFactorRequiredAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:231) resolves the owner of the refused bearer, returns early unless HasSubscriber is true and the response is Problem Details (AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:240-243), buffers the body, and calls Raise when it carries the multi-factor-required code (AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:246-250). MultiFactorRequiredListener subscribes (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/MultiFactorRequiredListener.cs:41). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/TwoFactor/MultiFactorRequiredSignalTests.cs.

    ITwoFactorUIService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorUIService.cs:16 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the client contract for the signed-in account's own two-factor authentication against auth/two-factor: status, enrollment, recovery codes and turning it off (ITwoFactorUIService.cs:6-9).
    • Depends on: Result and the shared response contracts TwoFactorStatusResponse, TwoFactorSetupResponse and TwoFactorRecoveryCodesResponse.
    • Concept introduced, a separate interface so existing implementations keep compiling. [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses interface segregation among other things; the remarks say this is a separate interface rather than new IAuthUIService members precisely so a consumer's own IAuthUIService implementation keeps compiling (ITwoFactorUIService.cs:11-12). [Rubric §24, Forms/Validation/UX Safety] applies to the write contract: every write is sent once and never retried, because enrollment mints a fresh secret per call, a code is accepted once per time step, and a regenerated set replaces the previous one (ITwoFactorUIService.cs:12-14).
    • Walkthrough
      • GetStatusAsync (ITwoFactorUIService.cs:21): whether the second factor is on and how many recovery codes are left.
      • BeginEnrollmentAsync (ITwoFactorUIService.cs:29): the API mints a secret and returns the shared key and provisioning URI; the factor is not on yet.
      • ConfirmEnrollmentAsync(code) (ITwoFactorUIService.cs:35): turns the factor on and returns the recovery codes, shown once.
      • RegenerateRecoveryCodesAsync(code) (ITwoFactorUIService.cs:41) and DisableAsync(code) (ITwoFactorUIService.cs:47): both proved with a live authenticator or recovery code.
      • Every member returns Result/Result<T> carrying the API's own refusal on failure.
    • Where it's used: implemented by TwoFactorUIService and registered by TwoFactorUIModule (AddTwoFactorUI(), MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/DependencyInjection.cs:27); injected by TwoFactorAccount and TwoFactorEnrollmentPanel. The UI gallery supplies a stub (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Gallery/Stubs/StubTwoFactorUIService.cs).

    LoginRefusals

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/TwoFactor/LoginRefusals.cs:29 · Level 3 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the refusal-code classification and notice mapping shared by the sign-in page and the two-factor account page, kept out of their code-behind files (LoginRefusals.cs:24-28).
    • Depends on: LoginRefusal, AuthErrorCodes, Result and the LocalizedErrorMessage extension on it. Externals: IStringLocalizer.
    • Concept introduced, match the code, never the wording. [Rubric §27, Internationalization] assesses whether behavior survives translation; the class comment states the rule: refusals are matched on the error code, never on the message, which is localized and may change (LoginRefusals.cs:26-27). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] applies because the error code is the contract between API and UI.
    • Walkthrough
      • Constants: TwoFactorEnabledReason "two-factor-enabled" (LoginRefusals.cs:32) and TwoFactorRequiredReason "two-factor-required" (LoginRefusals.cs:35), the reason query values the two-factor page sends to the sign-in page; and RecentSignInRequiredCode "Authentication.TwoFactorRecentSignInRequired" (LoginRefusals.cs:41), spelled here because the UI references the shared contracts only (LoginRefusals.cs:37-40).
      • Classify(Result) (LoginRefusals.cs:46) returns Other unless there is exactly one error (list pattern [var error], LoginRefusals.cs:50-52), then maps TwoFactorRequired, TwoFactorInvalid and EmailNotConfirmed to their steps (LoginRefusals.cs:55-60).
      • HasCode(result, code) (LoginRefusals.cs:68-69) is an ordinal match over every error.
      • ReasonNoticeKey(reason) (LoginRefusals.cs:77) maps the two reasons to Auth.Login.TwoFactorEnabledNotice and Auth.Login.TwoFactorRequiredNotice and ignores anything else (LoginRefusals.cs:79-81), so an arbitrary query value cannot select text.
      • Describe(result, localizer, fallbackKey) (LoginRefusals.cs:93) picks words in three tiers: the resource named by a single error code when it exists (LoginRefusals.cs:98-104, because the API's message is an English sentence), then the API message localized when it can be, then the fallback key (LoginRefusals.cs:107).
    • Where it's used: Login classifies with it (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor.cs:125); TwoFactorAccount sends both reasons and uses HasCode/Describe (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAccount.razor.cs:225, TwoFactorAccount.razor.cs:305, TwoFactorAccount.razor.cs:356, TwoFactorAccount.razor.cs:362); TwoFactorEnrollmentPanel does the same for enrollment (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorEnrollmentPanel.razor.cs:101 and TwoFactorEnrollmentPanel.razor.cs:108).

    TwoFactorUIService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorUIService.cs:24 · Level 4 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the HTTP implementation of ITwoFactorUIService over the auth/two-factor endpoints (TwoFactorUIService.cs:10-12).
    • Depends on: AuthenticatedServiceBase (base class), ITokenStorageService, HttpResultExecutor, ProblemDetailsResultReader and TwoFactorCodeRequest. Externals: IHttpClientFactory.
    • Concept introduced: none new; it follows the authenticated-service shape of MachineClientAdminService (TwoFactorUIService.cs:14-18): the bearer comes from the component's own token storage so a 401 renews the right session, responses are read through ProblemDetailsResultReader with the API's error codes intact, and transport faults become failures through HttpResultExecutor. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses whether retries are applied only where safe; here only the status read is retried (TwoFactorUIService.cs:18-19). [Rubric §11, Security] applies too: neither the secret nor a recovery code is logged or cached, they live only in the returned value (TwoFactorUIService.cs:19-20).
    • Walkthrough
      • Endpoint is "auth/two-factor" (TwoFactorUIService.cs:29).
      • GetStatusAsync (TwoFactorUIService.cs:32) is the only call wrapped in RetryPolicy.ExecuteAsync (TwoFactorUIService.cs:37).
      • BeginEnrollmentAsync (TwoFactorUIService.cs:47) POSTs enrollment with no body (TwoFactorUIService.cs:52-53).
      • ConfirmEnrollmentAsync (TwoFactorUIService.cs:61-62) and RegenerateRecoveryCodesAsync (TwoFactorUIService.cs:65-66) share the private PostCodeAsync (TwoFactorUIService.cs:92), which rejects a blank code (TwoFactorUIService.cs:94) and posts a trimmed TwoFactorCodeRequest, reading back the recovery codes (TwoFactorUIService.cs:100-106).
      • DisableAsync (TwoFactorUIService.cs:69) applies the same blank-code guard (TwoFactorUIService.cs:71) and posts to disable, reading a non-generic Result (TwoFactorUIService.cs:77-82).
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-094 sets the client data-access shape the authenticated services share; ADR-051's token-owner tracking is why the bearer comes from the injected storage rather than a shared client.
    • Where it's used: registered as TryAddScoped<ITwoFactorUIService, TwoFactorUIService>() by AddTwoFactorUI() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/DependencyInjection.cs:27). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorUIServiceTests.cs.

    IPublicLinkBuilder

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Navigation · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/IPublicLinkBuilder.cs:9 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: a one-method abstraction that turns an app-relative path into an absolute, publicly shareable URL (IPublicLinkBuilder.cs:9-13). It exists so share sheets, copy-link buttons and QR payloads produce a URL that still works once it leaves the app.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party. BCL Uri and string. Implemented by NavigationPublicLinkBuilder in this package and by MauiPublicLinkBuilder on the hybrid head.
    • Concept introduced, head-agnostic absolute link building. [Rubric §18, UI Architecture] assesses whether shared components stay host-agnostic instead of branching on the host they run in, and [Rubric §25, Navigation & Information Architecture] assesses whether outbound links are built from one authority rather than string-concatenated per call site. The doc comment (IPublicLinkBuilder.cs:3-8) states the problem exactly: web heads can derive a shareable origin from the browser, but the MAUI head cannot, because its internal origin is the WebView's virtual host. Encoding that virtual origin into a QR code or a shared link would produce a URL nobody outside the app can open. One interface with two implementations moves the head-specific knowledge to the composition root and lets the pages stay identical on every head.
    • Walkthrough
      • A single member, Uri BuildAbsolute(string relativePath) (IPublicLinkBuilder.cs:13). It returns a Uri rather than a string, so callers that need text do the ToString() themselves, and the doc comment gives /sessions/42 as the shape of the argument (IPublicLinkBuilder.cs:11).
      • The default binding resolves the path against NavigationManager.BaseUri (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/NavigationPublicLinkBuilder.cs:25), after rejecting a blank path (NavigationPublicLinkBuilder.cs:23).
      • The hybrid binding resolves against the PublicSite:BaseUrl key pinned in the head's embedded configuration (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/Services/MauiPublicLinkBuilder.cs:17 and MauiPublicLinkBuilder.cs:28-32), and throws InvalidOperationException at construction when the key is missing, so a misconfigured head fails at startup instead of shipping unusable links.
    • Why it's built this way: the default is registered with TryAddScoped (DependencyInjection.cs:161) and the comment above it (DependencyInjection.cs:157-160) records the override rule: the hybrid head calls AddCommonMauiPublicLinkBuilder() after AddUIShared (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/DependencyInjection.cs:152-153, invoked at MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/MauiProgram.cs:156) and the last registration wins. That is the same head-override composition convention ADR-042 establishes for the device capability layer.
    • Where it's used: the shared SharePageButton component (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Sharing/SharePageButton.razor:4 and SharePageButton.razor:43), the shared QrCodeButton component (QrCodeButton.razor:1 and QrCodeButton.razor:79), and app pages such as ADC's speaker QR page (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/Pages/Speakers/SpeakerQr.razor.cs:26 and SpeakerQr.razor.cs:62). A bUnit test pins the default registration to the browser-origin builder (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Navigation/NavigationPublicLinkBuilderTests.cs:59).

    BackNavigationResult

    • Concept introduced, the interop return contract. This record is also the wire shape of a single JS interop call: nav-interop.js's tryGoBack() returns an object that deserializes straight into it (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/MauiBackNavigationBridge.cs:48), so the C# type and the JS return value are one contract.

Handled is true when the WebView's history stack contained a previous entry and history.back() fired (MauiBackNavigationBridge.cs:9-13); AtRoot is true when no previous entry exists, and the doc comment records that MAUI hosts typically exit the app on Android when that is reported (MauiBackNavigationBridge.cs:14-18).

    ReturnUrlProtector

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Navigation · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/ReturnUrlProtector.cs:9 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: a pure sanitizer for returnUrl query parameters: it accepts only same-origin relative paths and replaces anything else with a safe fallback, closing the open-redirect hole in post-login and post-action redirects.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; System.Uri (BCL) supplies the final relative-URI parse guard.
    • Concept introduced, open-redirect defense. [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] assesses whether user-controlled navigation targets are validated before use. An open redirect lets an attacker craft /login?returnUrl=https://evil.com so the victim lands on an attacker site after authenticating, a classic phishing amplifier. Sanitize rejects every off-host form rather than trying to enumerate attacks, and the ordered guards read as a documented threat model.
    • Walkthrough: Sanitize(string? candidate, string fallback = "/") (ReturnUrlProtector.cs:18) runs a sequence of cheap, regex-free checks (a regex here would invite ReDoS), each returning fallback on failure:
      • null or empty (lines 20-23);
      • must start with /, which rules out scheme-prefixed absolutes such as http:// and javascript: (lines 25-30);
      • the second character must not be / or \, which browsers read as the start of an authority component and would send the user off-host (lines 32-37);
      • no backslash anywhere, since some browsers normalize \ to / (the source names "/\\evil.com" becoming //evil.com in Chrome, lines 39-44);
      • no control characters, which are header-injection, response-splitting and cookie-smuggling vectors (lines 46-51);
      • and finally it must parse as a well-formed relative URI (Uri.TryCreate(..., UriKind.Relative), lines 53-57). Only a candidate that survives all six is returned unchanged (line 59).
    • Why it's built this way: a static pure function whose only input is the candidate is trivially unit-testable across every attack vector, and calling it centrally means no page hand-rolls its own redirect validation.
    • Where it's used: login and post-authentication redirects sanitize the returnUrl they read from the query string; NavigationHistoryService.GoBackAsync also runs its fallback path through it (NavigationHistoryService.cs:82), so even the "safe" branch cannot be turned into a redirect vector.

    AuthEmailPrefill

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Navigation · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/AuthEmailPrefill.cs:11 · Level 0 · class (internal, static)

    • What it is: a two-method helper that hands an email address from one shared auth page to the next through the navigation's history state rather than the URL, so a page can open with the address already typed (AuthEmailPrefill.cs:5-10).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party. Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.NavigationManager and NavigationOptions (ASP.NET Core Blazor, AuthEmailPrefill.cs:1).
    • Concept introduced, history state as a private side channel. [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] assesses whether sensitive values stay out of places they leak from. A query string such as /login?email=... is written into the address bar, browser history, server request logs and the Referer header of any outbound request; NavigationOptions.HistoryEntryState travels with the history entry and appears in none of those, which is exactly the reason the class doc gives (AuthEmailPrefill.cs:6-7). [Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] reads the other side: the user is not asked to retype an address the app already holds.
    • Walkthrough
      • Two private prefixes tag the state string (AuthEmailPrefill.cs:13-14): "mmca-auth:existing-account:" and "mmca-auth:prefill:". The prefix carries one extra bit, whether the address was just refused because it already holds an account.
      • NavigateWithEmail(navigation, path, email, existingAccount = false) (AuthEmailPrefill.cs:23-27) calls NavigateTo(path, new NavigationOptions { HistoryEntryState = prefix + email }).
      • Read(navigation, out bool existingAccount) (AuthEmailPrefill.cs:33-52) reads navigation.HistoryEntryState, returns null when there is none (:38-41), sets existingAccount and strips the prefix when the existing-account tag matches (:43-47), strips the plain prefix otherwise (:49-51), and returns null for any state it did not write. Both comparisons are StringComparison.Ordinal. NonEmpty (:54) turns a blank remainder into null, so a page never prefills an empty string over its own default.
    • Why it's built this way: the prefix check means a history entry written by some other code is ignored rather than misread as an address, and keeping the class internal holds the convention to the shared auth pages that read and write it. No ADR records the choice; the rationale is the class doc (AuthEmailPrefill.cs:5-10).
    • Where it's used: Register lands a duplicate address on sign-in with existingAccount: true (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Register.razor:268) and sends the pending address to sign-in (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Register.razor.cs:79); Login reads it (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor.cs:182) and hands the typed address to /forgot-password (Login.razor.cs:211), which reads it back (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/ForgotPassword.razor:82). bUnit tests drive the round trip (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Pages/Auth/SignInLinks/LoginSignInLinkTests.cs:47, MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Pages/Auth/RegistrationPending/RegisterPendingTests.cs:83).
    • Caveats: history state lives only on the history entry; a fresh URL typed or opened in a new tab carries no state, and the page falls back to an empty field.

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Navigation · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/IForbiddenReExecutionDetector.cs:17 · Level 0 · interface

[Rubric §25, Navigation, Routing & Information Architecture] reads the result: a signed-in user who lacks a permission sees Access Denied, not a misleading Page Not Found.

MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Pages/NotFoundTests.cs covers both branches, and HttpContextForbiddenReExecutionDetectorTests covers the server implementation.
