    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Preferences · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/IUserPreferenceWriter.cs:9 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the write half of cross-device UI preferences. It persists the signed-in user's culture and theme choice to the backend so the choice follows them to their next browser or device.
    • Depends on: nothing. Implemented by ApiUserPreferenceWriter; the read half is IUserPreferenceReader.
    • Concept introduced, best-effort persistence over a local source of truth. [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] assesses where state lives and which copy wins; the doc comment (IUserPreferenceWriter.cs:3-8) answers both. The cookie and localStorage remain the runtime channel, this interface is a roaming convenience, and a failed or skipped persist must never break the in-page switch. Implementations must no-op for anonymous users. A null field means "leave unchanged" (IUserPreferenceWriter.cs:11-13), which is what lets the theme toggle and the culture switcher share one method without either clobbering the other's value.
    • Walkthrough
      • SaveAsync(string? culture, string? theme, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (IUserPreferenceWriter.cs:18). Both value arguments are nullable by design, per the null-means-unchanged rule stated at IUserPreferenceWriter.cs:15-16.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-027 and ADR-028. Keeping it an interface is what lets a host with no auth/preferences endpoint (the Helpdesk seed is the named example at ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:11-12) simply not register it: the callers resolve it with GetService<T> and skip the persist when it is absent.
    • Where it's used: the theme toggle resolves it optionally and saves only the theme (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/ThemeToggle.razor:23-27); the culture switcher does the same for culture before handing off to the applier (CultureSwitcher.razor:38-42).

    OfflineWriteOptions

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteOptions.cs:4 · Level 0 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: the optional per-write settings a caller passes to IOfflineWriteQueue.EnqueueAsync: the idempotency key, the row version the write was based on, and a coalesce key.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party at compile time; its values are copied onto PendingWrite.
    • Concept introduced: nothing new here; the queue it configures is taught under OfflineWriteQueue. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] applies in the small: the idempotency key is what makes a replayed write safe to send twice.
    • Walkthrough
      • IdempotencyKey (OfflineWriteOptions.cs:7): null means the queue generates a new GUID in "N" form (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:140).
      • BasedOnRowVersion (OfflineWriteOptions.cs:11), a byte[]? carrying the EF rowversion in its wire shape, with a CA1819 suppression justified as the same exemption DTOs get (line 10). The replay sends it as If-Match through PendingWrite.IfMatch.
      • CoalesceKey (OfflineWriteOptions.cs:14): pairs writes that cancel each other out, used by IOfflineWriteQueue.CancelPendingAsync.
    • Why it's built this way: an options record with init members keeps EnqueueAsync to one optional parameter, so a caller that needs none of the three passes nothing. ADR-144 (Website/docs-src/adr/144-offline-writes-and-delta-reads.md) records the offline-write design.
    • Where it's used: ADC's SessionBookmarkUIService sets IdempotencyKey and CoalesceKey for a create and only CoalesceKey for a delete (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Bookmarks/SessionBookmarkUIService.cs:202,207).

    OfflineWriteOutcome

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteOutcome.cs:4 · Level 0 · enum

    • What it is: how a queued offline write left the queue: Completed, Conflict, Rejected or Expired (OfflineWriteOutcome.cs:7,10,13,16).
    • Depends on: nothing.
    • Concept introduced: nothing new; it is the vocabulary of the settle step taught under OfflineWriteQueue.
    • Walkthrough
      • Completed: the replay succeeded. Conflict: the server refused because the item changed (for example a 412). Rejected: any other permanent refusal. Expired: the write was older than OfflineWriteQueueOptions.MaxAge and was discarded unsent.
      • There is deliberately no "transient" member: a transient failure keeps the write queued, so it never settles. The queue's private Classify returns OfflineWriteOutcome? and uses null for that case (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:263).
    • Why it's built this way: an Expired write has no handler result at all (OfflineWriteSettledEventArgs.Result is null for it), so a bare Result could not describe every way a write leaves the queue; the enum names each terminal state for the subscriber. See ADR-144.
    • Where it's used: carried by OfflineWriteSettledEventArgs, which Common's OfflineWriteNotifier component subscribes to (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Capabilities/OfflineWriteNotifier.razor:46) and by ADC's bookmark replay tests.

    OfflineWriteQueueOptions

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueueOptions.cs:4 · Level 0 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the options-pattern settings of OfflineWriteQueue: where the queue is stored, how old a write may get, and how many writes it holds.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; bound through Microsoft.Extensions.Options.
    • Concept introduced: nothing new. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] applies: the MaxAge default is tied to the server's idempotency window, so the queue never replays a write the server could no longer deduplicate.
    • Walkthrough
      • StorageKey (OfflineWriteQueueOptions.cs:7), default "mmca.offline-writes": the single local store key the whole queue lives under.
      • MaxAge (OfflineWriteQueueOptions.cs:14), default TimeSpan.FromHours(24). The doc comment (lines 9-13) states the reason: 24 hours is the window in which the server replays an idempotency key, so an older write could otherwise run twice. Older writes settle as OfflineWriteOutcome.Expired.
      • MaxPendingWrites (OfflineWriteQueueOptions.cs:17), default 200: beyond it an enqueue fails with OfflineWrites.QueueFull (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:152,176).
    • Why it's built this way: mutable set properties so AddOfflineWriteQueue(configure) can apply an Action<OfflineWriteQueueOptions> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:417-425). See ADR-144.
    • Where it's used: injected as IOptions<OfflineWriteQueueOptions> into OfflineWriteQueue (OfflineWriteQueue.cs:85); configured by DependencyInjection.

    UserPreferences

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Preferences · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/UserPreferences.cs:9 · Level 0 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: the two-field result of reading a user's stored UI preferences, their culture and their theme.
    • Depends on: nothing. Returned by IUserPreferenceReader and its implementation ApiUserPreferenceReader.
    • Concept introduced: nothing new. It reuses the null-means-unset convention introduced by IUserPreferenceWriter: the doc comment (UserPreferences.cs:3-6) states that a null field means the user never chose that preference, so the request default or the OS preference applies. [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] applies in the small, because "no stored value" and "stored value that happens to be the default" stay distinguishable, which is what lets the login reconciliation skip a redundant culture round-trip.
    • Walkthrough
      • A positional record with two members, Culture and Theme, both string? (UserPreferences.cs:9). There is no factory and no validation: the values are whatever the backend returned.
    • Why it's built this way: a positional record is the smallest thing that deserializes cleanly from the auth/preferences payload and compares by value.
    • Where it's used: returned by ApiUserPreferenceReader, including its static Empty instance (ApiUserPreferenceReader.cs:26); consumed by the login page's preference reconciliation (Login.razor:228-247).

    UserPreferencesRequest

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Preferences · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:39 · Level 0 · record (private sealed, nested)

    • What it is: the request body the writer PUTs to auth/preferences, the same culture and theme pair in the write direction.
    • Depends on: nothing. It is declared inside ApiUserPreferenceWriter and used only there.
    • Concept introduced: nothing new; it is the wire-facing twin of UserPreferences. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] applies in the small: the request type is kept separate from the response type even though the two currently have identical members, so the directions can diverge without a breaking change, and it is declared private so it never becomes part of the package's public surface.
    • Walkthrough
      • private sealed record UserPreferencesRequest(string? Culture, string? Theme) (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:39). It is instantiated once, inline in the PutAsJsonAsync call (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:103).
    • Why it's built this way: nesting it privately keeps a serialization detail from leaking into the package API, and a positional record needs no mapper.
    • Where it's used: only in ApiUserPreferenceWriter.SaveAsync (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:101-104).

    IUserPreferenceReader

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Preferences · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/IUserPreferenceReader.cs:9 · Level 1 · interface

    • What it is: the read half of cross-device preferences. It fetches the signed-in user's stored culture and theme, used at login to reapply a returning user's choices on a new device.
    • Depends on: UserPreferences (its return type); implemented by ApiUserPreferenceReader. The write half is IUserPreferenceWriter.
    • Concept introduced: nothing new; it mirrors the best-effort contract the writer introduced. The doc comment (IUserPreferenceReader.cs:3-8) pins the failure mode: implementations return an empty UserPreferences (both fields null) for anonymous users or on any error, so a failed read never blocks login. [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] applies, since this is the moment the roaming copy is reconciled against the local one.
    • Walkthrough
      • GetAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) returning Task<UserPreferences> (IUserPreferenceReader.cs:13). There is no failure channel in the signature at all, which is the contract making itself unmistakable.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-027 and ADR-028. A Result<T> here would invite a caller to surface an error the user cannot act on during a login they just completed successfully.
    • Where it's used: injected by the login page (Login.razor:14) and read once in ApplyStoredPreferencesAndNavigateAsync (Login.razor:228-230), which applies the theme through ThemeService (Login.razor:232-235) and the culture through ICultureApplier (Login.razor:243), skipping the culture round-trip when the stored value already matches the current one (Login.razor:237-238).

    PendingWrite

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/PendingWrite.cs:12 · Level 1 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: one entry of the offline write queue, exactly as it is persisted to the device's local store: what to replay, with which payload, for which user, and how often it has failed.
    • Depends on: ConcurrencyETag (formats IfMatch, line 47); System.Text.Json (JsonSerializerOptions.Web, [JsonIgnore]).
    • Concept introduced: nothing new beyond the queue taught under OfflineWriteQueue. [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] applies: the record is the durable state, so everything a later replay needs (including the user it belongs to) travels inside it rather than in memory.
    • Walkthrough
      • Identity and routing: Id (PendingWrite.cs:15) and Kind (line 18), the handler key, for example Engagement.Bookmark.Create.v1.
      • Replay safety: IdempotencyKey (line 21) so a write the server already ran is not run twice, and BasedOnRowVersion (line 25), a byte[]? with a CA1819 suppression justified by the record being persisted locally, not a domain type (line 24).
      • Payload: PayloadJson (line 28), serialized with JsonSerializerOptions.Web, and the generic ReadPayload<TPayload>() (line 52) that deserializes it with the same options.
      • Scoping and bookkeeping: CoalesceKey (line 31), UserScope (line 34, the signed-in user's id or null for an anonymous user), EnqueuedOn (line 37) and Attempts (line 40), the count of transient replay failures so far.
      • IfMatch (line 47) is computed, not stored ([JsonIgnore], line 46): the weak ETag of BasedOnRowVersion via ConcurrencyETag.Format, or null when no row version was given.
    • Why it's built this way: required + init members keep an entry immutable; the queue changes Attempts with a with expression (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:430-442). Storing the payload as JSON text keeps the list one homogeneous type in the local store whatever the payload type. See ADR-144.
    • Where it's used: built by OfflineWriteQueue.EnqueueAsync (OfflineWriteQueue.cs:136), handed to every IOfflineWriteHandler, and carried by OfflineWriteSettledEventArgs. ADC's BookmarkCreateReplayHandler and BookmarkDeleteReplayHandler read it.

    IOfflineWriteHandler

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/IOfflineWriteHandler.cs:9 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the per-kind replay strategy. A module registers one handler per write kind; the queue hands it a PendingWrite and gets back the server's answer.
    • Depends on: PendingWrite, Result.
    • Concept introduced: nothing new; the queue that drives it is taught under OfflineWriteQueue. [Rubric §1, SOLID] applies: the framework queue knows no endpoint, and each module adds a write kind by adding a handler, not by editing the queue.
    • Walkthrough
      • Kind (IOfflineWriteHandler.cs:12): the key the handler answers to, for example Engagement.Bookmark.Create.v1.
      • ReplayAsync(PendingWrite, CancellationToken) returning Task<Result> (line 23). The doc comment (lines 14-19) fixes the contract: send the write with its IdempotencyKey (and IfMatch when set), and report the answer as a Result. A transport failure, a timeout, or an unexpected, too-many-requests or unauthorized error keeps the write for a later replay; a conflict or any other failure discards it.
    • Why it's built this way: returning a Result rather than an outcome lets a handler reuse the normal HTTP-to-Result path, and the queue alone decides what counts as transient (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:263-283).
    • Where it's used: registered with AddOfflineWriteHandler<THandler>() as a scoped TryAddEnumerable entry (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:437-440); implemented in ADC by BookmarkCreateReplayHandler (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Bookmarks/BookmarkCreateReplayHandler.cs:24) and BookmarkDeleteReplayHandler (BookmarkDeleteReplayHandler.cs:19).
    • Caveats: when two handlers share a Kind, the first one registered wins (OfflineWriteQueue.cs:100 uses TryAdd).

    OfflineWriteSettledEventArgs

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteSettledEventArgs.cs:9 · Level 3 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the payload of IOfflineWriteQueue.WriteSettled: which write left the queue, how, and with what handler result.
    • Depends on: PendingWrite, OfflineWriteOutcome, Result; derives from EventArgs.
    • Concept introduced: nothing new.
    • Walkthrough: a primary-constructor class (OfflineWriteSettledEventArgs.cs:9) exposing Write (line 12), Outcome (line 15) and Result (line 18), which is null for OfflineWriteOutcome.Expired because an expired write is never sent.
    • Why it's built this way: the standard EventHandler<TEventArgs> shape, raised by OfflineWriteQueue.SettleAsync only after the store no longer holds the write (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:424-428).
    • Where it's used: Common's OfflineWriteNotifier (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Capabilities/OfflineWriteNotifier.razor:46) and ADC's SessionBookmarkReplayTests.

    ApiUserPreferenceWriter

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Preferences · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:30 · Level 4 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the default IUserPreferenceWriter. It PUTs the culture/theme choice to auth/preferences through the shared "APIClient", and it declines to make the call at all when the request is already known to be doomed.
    • Depends on: IUserPreferenceWriter (implemented), ITokenStorageService, JwtTokenInfo and the nested UserPreferencesRequest. Externals: IHttpClientFactory and System.Net.Http.Json.
    • Concept introduced, best-effort writes still have a cost. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether the system's own traffic keeps its signals meaningful; the class comment (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:21-26) makes the argument explicitly. Because the caller never learns the write failed, a doomed request cannot help the user and still lands in failed-request telemetry, and at low traffic one 401 per theme or culture toggle is enough on its own to trip a failed-request alert rule. Both guards below therefore exist for the alerting story, not the user's story. [Rubric §11, Security] also touches this: the writer never inspects the token's claims itself: it asks JwtTokenInfo whether one is usable, then attaches it as the Authorization: Bearer header of the request message (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:113), the same explicit per-request bearer the reader attaches.
    • Walkthrough
      • The primary constructor takes IHttpClientFactory and ITokenStorageService (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:30-32). ExpirySkew is 30 seconds and is documented as matching the token-storage skew so this class agrees with the layer that does the refreshing (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:34-35). _rejectedToken (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:47) holds the token the API last refused, for the lifetime of this scoped writer.
      • Saves are serialized in call order. SaveAsync (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:66) is not async: under a System.Threading.Lock gate (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:37,68) it chains the new save onto _lastSave (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:50), stores the new task as the latest, and returns it (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:70-72). The remarks (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:59-65) give the reason: a theme toggle followed quickly by a language switch used to send two concurrent PUTs, and the switcher force-reloads as soon as its own save returns, so the reload either cut off the theme PUT (WASM) or the two raced on the user row's concurrency token and the server kept the old theme. Serializing means the switcher's existing await also drains the earlier save.
      • SaveAfterAsync (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:76) waits for the previous save with WaitAsync(PreviousSaveWait, cancellationToken) under ConfigureAwaitOptions.SuppressThrowing (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:80-81), so a fault, timeout or cancellation of the earlier save only ends the wait (comment, ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:78-79). PreviousSaveWait is an internal init property defaulting to 5 seconds (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:56), bounded so a hung earlier request delays the next save, and the culture reload behind it, by a few seconds at most (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:52-55). It then calls PutAsync (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:83).
      • PutAsync (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:86) reads the access token (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:88), then applies guard one: JwtTokenInfo.IsFresh(token, ExpirySkew) (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:93, the helper at MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/JwtTokenInfo.cs:16). The comment (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:90-92) notes that IsFresh also covers null and unreadable tokens, which makes this the anonymous-user guard as well.
      • Guard two compares the current token against _rejectedToken with StringComparison.Ordinal (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:101); the comment (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:98-100) explains why expiry alone is not enough, since a token can be unexpired and still rejected (revoked session, rotated signing key, a user the API now treats as gone).
      • The call itself is a hand-built PUT HttpRequestMessage with a JSON body, sent through SendAsync, to the relative auth/preferences (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:108-118), and a 401 Unauthorized latches _rejectedToken (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:120-123). Just before SendAsync it calls AuthDelegatingHandler.TrackTokenOwner(token!, tokenStorageService) (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:117, the helper at MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:68). The comment (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:115-116) gives the reason: the handler's own token storage is a different instance, so it is told which storage this bearer came from, and a 401 then renews (or ends) this session rather than the handler's. The helper records the owner weakly and only when it is an ISessionAwareTokenStorage (AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:70), so AuthDelegatingHandler can route the 401; the comment names CreateAuthenticatedClientAsync as the path that already does the same.
      • Both HttpRequestException (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:125) and TaskCanceledException (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:129) are swallowed, each with a comment noting that the cookie already holds the choice for this device.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-027 and ADR-028 make the local cookie the runtime channel and this write a roaming extra. Storing the rejected token rather than setting a boolean latch is the deliberate detail (ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:41-46): a fresh sign-in produces a different token, so writing resumes with no reset step and no staleness of its own.
    • Where it's used: registered with TryAddScoped in DependencyInjection (MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:240); resolved optionally by the theme toggle (ThemeToggle.razor:23-27) and the culture switcher (CultureSwitcher.razor:38-42). Pinned by ApiUserPreferenceWriterTests, including the ordering and the bounded wait (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceWriterTests.cs:146,173).

    ApiUserPreferenceReader

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Preferences · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceReader.cs:22 · Level 4 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the default IUserPreferenceReader. It GETs auth/preferences with the signed-in user's bearer token and hands back the culture and theme the user chose on some other device, or empty preferences when there is nothing to read.
    • Depends on: IUserPreferenceReader (the contract, ApiUserPreferenceReader.cs:24), UserPreferences (the two-nullable-field record it returns, constructed at line 26), ITokenStorageService (primary-constructor parameter, line 24), JwtTokenInfo (the freshness check, line 39); IHttpClientFactory and System.Net.Http.Json (BCL) for the named "APIClient".
    • Concept introduced, a best-effort read that cannot fail its caller. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven Design] assesses whether a secondary concern is prevented from changing the outcome of the primary operation. Applying a stored preference is a nicety attached to login; a network hiccup while reading it must not turn a successful sign-in into an error page. This class encodes that as a type-level promise: GetAsync returns UserPreferences rather than a Result, and there is no path out of it that reports a failure. That is the posture ADR-096 records for side effects generally (Website/docs-src/adr/096-best-effort-side-effects.md), applied on the read side. [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] also applies, in a small but real way: the class refuses to spend a round trip on a token it can already see is stale.
    • Walkthrough
      • Two statics carry the whole configuration. Empty is a single shared new UserPreferences(null, null) (line 26), so the failure paths allocate nothing, and ExpirySkew is TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30) (line 29) with a comment stating why the value is duplicated here: it must agree with the token-storage layer that does the refreshing, or the two would disagree about when a token is still usable.
      • GetAsync(CancellationToken) (line 32) reads the access token (line 34) and gates on JwtTokenInfo.IsFresh(token, ExpirySkew) (line 39). The comment (lines 36-38) spells out the two cases this covers: an expired or unreadable token buys a guaranteed 401, and IsFresh also covers the anonymous (null) case. Both return Empty (line 41).
      • The request is built by hand: resolve the named "APIClient" (line 46), which already carries the culture and auth handlers (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:174-175), then an HttpRequestMessage GET to the relative URI auth/preferences with the token it already read set as the Authorization: Bearer header on that request (lines 47-48). The reader sets it itself because in Blazor Server AuthDelegatingHandler resolves in a separate DI scope whose token store is empty, which would send the read anonymous; the handler leaves an existing header alone, so WASM and MAUI see no change (class doc comment). Before sending it calls AuthDelegatingHandler.TrackTokenOwner(token!, tokenStorageService) (line 52, the helper at MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:68); the comment (lines 50-51) explains that the handler's own storage is another instance, so it is told which storage this bearer came from and a 401 renews (or ends) this session. SendAsync (line 53) is followed by a non-success short-circuit to Empty (lines 54-57), and only then ReadFromJsonAsync<UserPreferences> (line 59).
      • Null-coalescing on the deserialized value (line 60) means a body of literal null is the same as no preference.
      • Two catch blocks, HttpRequestException (line 62) and TaskCanceledException (line 66), both return Empty. Note what is not caught: anything else, including a JsonException from a malformed body, still escapes, so a contract break is loud while a transport failure is quiet.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-027 (Website/docs-src/adr/027-multi-locale-i18n.md) and ADR-028 make the stored culture and theme a per-user server-side value so the choice follows a user between devices, and login is the one moment where reading it is worth a round trip. Catching narrowly and returning a shared empty record is what makes the reconciliation safe to await unconditionally in the login flow. It is the read half of a pair: ApiUserPreferenceWriter is the write half, and the two are registered together (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:240-241).
    • Where it's used: registered by AddUIShared with TryAddScoped (DependencyInjection.cs:241) and injected by exactly one page, the framework's login page (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor:14). Its ApplyStoredPreferencesAndNavigateAsync calls GetAsync, applies a stored theme through ThemeService, and, when the stored culture differs from the current one, hands the rest of the navigation to ICultureApplier, which owns the head-specific switch (Login.razor:228-248).
    • Caveats: the reader is pinned by ApiUserPreferenceReaderTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceReaderTests.cs) and ServerSignInPreferenceReadTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Tests/Services/ServerSignInPreferenceReadTests.cs), alongside its sibling writer's ApiUserPreferenceWriterTests. Because TaskCanceledException is caught unconditionally, a caller that cancels its own token receives Empty rather than an OperationCanceledException, which is the opposite of the convention HttpResultExecutor enforces elsewhere in this package; the single caller passes no token (Login.razor:230), so the difference is invisible in current use.

    IOfflineWriteQueue

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/IOfflineWriteQueue.cs:11 · Level 4 · interface

    • What it is: the contract of the opt-in durable offline write queue: queue a write now, replay it when the device is back online, and tell subscribers how each write settled.
    • Depends on: PendingWrite, OfflineWriteOptions, OfflineWriteSettledEventArgs, Result.
    • Concept introduced: the queue itself is taught under OfflineWriteQueue; this is its surface. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] applies: the interface lets a UI service accept a write while offline instead of failing it.
    • Walkthrough
      • IsAvailable (IOfflineWriteQueue.cs:18): false only with the default NullLocalCacheStore; a host that calls AddBrowserDeviceCapabilities (Blazor Server and WebAssembly) or the MAUI capabilities has a store (doc comment, lines 13-17). See NullLocalCacheStore.
      • Two events: WriteSettled (line 21), raised once per write that left by a replay after the store no longer holds it, and PendingChanged (line 24), raised after every persisted change.
      • EnqueueAsync<TPayload>(kind, payload, options, cancellationToken) (line 33) returns Result<PendingWrite>: the queued write, or the OfflineWrites.Unavailable / OfflineWrites.QueueFull failure (doc, line 32).
      • GetPendingAsync (line 38) lists the current user's writes oldest first; CancelPendingAsync(coalesceKey) (line 44) removes every write of the current user with that key (ordinal) without raising WriteSettled.
      • ReplayAsync (line 52) returns the number of writes that settled, and does nothing (returns 0) when the store is unavailable, the device is offline, or another replay is running (lines 46-49).
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-144 (Website/docs-src/adr/144-offline-writes-and-delta-reads.md). Failures a caller can act on (no store, queue full) come back as a Result; replay outcomes, which arrive later, come back as events.
    • Where it's used: registered scoped by AddOfflineWriteQueue (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:419), which no framework code calls (doc comment, line 413); injected into ADC's SessionBookmarkUIService (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Bookmarks/SessionBookmarkUIService.cs:40) and drained by Common's OfflineWriteNotifier (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Capabilities/OfflineWriteNotifier.razor:54).

    OfflineWriteQueue

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:47 · Level 5 · class (sealed, partial)

    • What it is: the default IOfflineWriteQueue. It keeps the whole queue as one List<PendingWrite> under one key of the device's ILocalCacheStore, scoped per signed-in user, and replays it through per-kind IOfflineWriteHandlers on reconnect, on demand, and on its own backoff timer.
    • Depends on: ILocalCacheStore, IConnectivityStatusService, IOfflineWriteHandler, OfflineWriteQueueOptions, PendingWrite, OfflineWriteOutcome, HttpResultExecutor (its transport and timeout error codes), Error and ErrorType. Externals: AuthenticationStateProvider, TimeProvider, IOptions<T>, ILogger<T>, System.Text.Json.
    • Concept introduced, a durable client-side outbox for writes. A write the user makes while offline is persisted on the device with an idempotency key, then replayed in order once the device is online. It is the client-side counterpart of the server outbox idea (ADR-003): durability first, delivery later, and idempotency so a delivery that happens twice is harmless. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses whether the system degrades gracefully when a dependency is down; here a lost network becomes a delayed write rather than a failed one. [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] applies because the queue's state is the device store, re-read on every change rather than cached. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] applies through the three [LoggerMessage] warnings (OfflineWriteQueue.cs:549-556).
    • Walkthrough
      • Retry timing constants: InitialRetryDelay 5 seconds (OfflineWriteQueue.cs:50) and MaxRetryDelay 5 minutes (line 53). Fields include an ordinal handler dictionary (line 57), a SemaphoreSlim(1, 1) _gate (line 62) for store edits, and a Lock _scheduleSync for the timer.
      • The constructor (line 79) indexes handlers by Kind with TryAdd, so the first registered wins (line 100), and subscribes to ConnectivityChanged (line 103). IsAvailable is the store's own flag (line 113).
      • EnqueueAsync (line 122) fails with OfflineWrites.Unavailable when there is no store (line 133), builds the PendingWrite (line 136, a new "N" GUID when no idempotency key was given, line 140, and the current user as UserScope), and adds it through MutateAsync unless MaxPendingWrites is reached (line 152), else OfflineWrites.QueueFull (line 176). When the kind has a handler it bumps _replayableEnqueues and schedules a retry (lines 162-171).
      • GetPendingAsync (line 180) and CancelPendingAsync (line 193) filter by the current user's scope; InScope (line 254) orders oldest first.
      • ReplayAsync (line 211) returns 0 unless the store is available, the device is online and no other replay holds the Interlocked.CompareExchange flag (line 213). Its finally always calls CompletePass (line 231), so a pass that threw still schedules the next attempt.
      • ReplayPassAsync (line 293) walks a snapshot: it skips an entry that left the store since the snapshot (line 307, so a write cancelled meanwhile is not sent), expires one older than MaxAge unsent (line 312), keeps an entry whose kind has no handler in this app (line 319), and otherwise calls the handler. A thrown handler exception is logged, counts an attempt and stops the pass (lines 335-341); a Result goes through Classify (line 343).
      • Classify (line 263) maps success to Completed, any transient error to null (keep and stop), any ErrorType.Conflict to Conflict, and everything else to Rejected. IsTransient (line 280) is the transport or timeout code of HttpResultExecutor, or ErrorType.Unexpected, TooManyRequests or Unauthorized; the transient check runs first.
      • Backoff: CompletePass (line 361) resets the delay to the initial value after a pass that settled something and otherwise doubles it via NextDelay (line 285) up to the 5-minute cap, reschedules when a replayable write was queued during the pass, and cancels the timer otherwise. ScheduleRetryLocked (line 383) keeps at most one one-shot timer on the injected TimeProvider, and never while offline or disposed; a per-schedule token object lets OnRetryTimer (line 405) ignore a stale callback.
      • Persistence: MutateAsync (line 449) re-reads the list, applies the edit and writes it back under the semaphore, then raises PendingChanged; SettleAsync (line 424) removes the entry and then raises WriteSettled; CountAttemptAsync (line 430) bumps Attempts.
      • OnConnectivityChanged (line 501) cancels the timer when the device goes offline and starts a background replay, not awaited, when it comes back; ReplayInBackgroundAsync (line 522) catches and logs every fault so no unobserved task escapes. Dispose (line 237) removes the timer and unsubscribes.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-144 (Website/docs-src/adr/144-offline-writes-and-delta-reads.md). One list under one key with a read-edit-write under one semaphore means concurrent callers of the same instance never lose a write; the class remarks say plainly that two instances over one store (two tabs, two circuits) are not coordinated (OfflineWriteQueue.cs:14-20). User scoping means one device can hold writes for several accounts, and signing out clears the local store and the queue with it (remarks, line 44).
    • Where it's used: registered scoped, together with TimeProvider.System and the options, by AddOfflineWriteQueue (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:417-429); exercised by OfflineWriteQueueTests and OfflineWriteQueueRetryTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Offline/) and by ADC's bookmark tests. ADC's SessionBookmarkUIService is the one consumer.
    • Caveats: the scope is "scoped" because the browser connectivity service and store it reads are scoped (DependencyInjection.cs:407-408), so each Blazor Server circuit has its own queue instance over the same browser store, which is exactly the uncoordinated two-instances case the remarks name.

[Rubric §20, Design System & Theming] assesses whether visual tokens are centralized rather than scattered as literals; here the whole palette lives in exactly one C# class, and the theme carries no hex literal of its own. [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance & Documentation] assesses whether necessary duplication is monitored: C# cannot read CSS at build time, so the brand colors must exist in both BrandColors and app.css, and BrandColorTokenTests in MMCA.Common.UI.Tests asserts the two stay in sync so the copy cannot silently drift (BrandColors.cs:6-8). The contrast reasoning for LightWarning and DarkError is deliberately not here: their summaries point at MMCATheme, where the math sits beside the assignment (lines 56, 116, 122).
    • Walkthrough: public const string fields in four commented groups.
      • The primary triad: Primary = "#1565C0" (line 13), PrimaryDark = "#0D47A1" (line 16), PrimaryLight = "#42A5F5" used for accents and dark-mode contrast (line 19). The secondary triad: Secondary = "#00796B" (line 26, with the contrast rationale immediately above it at lines 21-25), SecondaryDark = "#00695C" (line 29), and SecondaryLight = "#4DB6AC" (line 32).
      • Shared chrome, identical in both palettes (line 34): ChromeBackground = "#1A2035" for the app bar and sidebar (line 37), ChromeText = "#FFFFFF" (line 40), and ChromeTextMuted = "#FFFFFFB3", white at 70% alpha for sidebar text and icons (line 43).

Note DarkInfo and PrimaryLight share #42A5F5, and DarkTextSecondary and DarkActionDefault share #B0BEC5: each keeps its own name so a role can change without dragging the other.

Keeping every palette value in one class means a rebrand or a contrast fix touches one file plus the mirrored CSS, and the theme reads as a mapping of roles to names rather than a wall of hex.

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Theme · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/IInitialThemeModeSource.cs:16 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: an optional hook that lets a head tell the theme providers the stored Day/Dark mode without JavaScript, so the first render already has the right palette instead of light-then-dark (ADR-028). Its one member, bool? IsDarkMode (line 21), is true for dark, false for light, and null when nothing is stored yet, which leaves the first render unchanged.
    • Depends on: nothing.
    • Concept introduced, an optional capability probed with GetService. [Rubric §20, Design System, Theming & UI Consistency] covers theming that works from the first paint. The provider asks the container for the interface and treats absence and null identically (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/MmcaThemeProviders.razor:43-50), so web heads register nothing and still behave as before, while the JS path in OnAfterRenderAsync stays the source of truth for them.
    • Why it's built this way: the MAUI head can read its stored mode synchronously from device preferences, which a Blazor circuit cannot do with a cookie before the first render. A nullable bool keeps "unknown" distinct from "light".
    • Where it's used: implemented by MauiInitialThemeModeSource (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/Theme/MauiInitialThemeModeSource.cs:12) and registered as a singleton (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/DependencyInjection.cs:69); consumed by MmcaThemeProviders.razor:47; pinned by MmcaThemeProvidersInitialModeTests.

    ThemeInterop

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Theme · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/ThemeInterop.cs:9 · Level 0 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: a one-method guard, TryAsync(Func<Task>) (ThemeInterop.cs:18), that runs a best-effort JS interop call and returns false instead of throwing when it fails.
    • Depends on: Microsoft.JSInterop exception types (JSException, JSDisconnectedException) and InvalidOperationException (BCL).
    • Concept introduced, theme interop failure must not escape the component lifecycle. [Rubric §18, UI Architecture & Component Design] covers resilient component lifecycles. The filter catches exactly three cases: the asset is missing or the browser call failed (JSException), the circuit was torn down mid-call (JSDisconnectedException), and interop is unavailable on this renderer (InvalidOperationException, a prerender race or disposed dispatcher). Any other exception still propagates.
    • Why it's built this way: theming is cosmetic, so a failed cookie read or write degrades to "the page keeps its current mode" rather than killing the circuit from the root layout.
    • Where it's used: MmcaThemeProviders.razor:62,90 and ThemeToggle.razor:22 (all under MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/). No dedicated test file; it is exercised through the provider and toggle component tests.

    TwoFactorPageRequirement

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:14 · Level 0 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the authorization requirement behind the policy the two-factor account page declares instead of a bare [Authorize]. Its one member is the policy name, PolicyName = "mmca:two-factor-pages" (TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:17).
    • Depends on: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.IAuthorizationRequirement (ASP.NET Core). The doc comment names TwoFactorPageGate and TwoFactorPageAuthorizationHandler (TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:5-13).
    • Concept introduced: none new. This is the two-factor copy of the "signed in, unless the page is hidden for this host" policy first taught at NotificationPageRequirement; the doc comment says the notification pages' policy follows the same rule (TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:10-11). [Rubric §25, Navigation & IA] assesses whether a route answers consistently with what the host actually offers: a host that never registered the two-factor UI answers the page with a 404 rather than a sign-in challenge for a page that does not exist for it (TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:6-10).
    • Walkthrough: a marker class with no state; the requirement means "an authenticated caller, exactly as [Authorize] asks, except when the host never called AddTwoFactorUI(), in which case every caller passes" (TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:6-9). The decision itself lives in TwoFactorPageAuthorizationHandler.
    • Why it's built this way: authorization runs before the router, so a plain [Authorize] would send an anonymous visitor of a host without the feature to sign-in for a page that will then 404. Letting the request through to the router hands the answer to TwoFactorPageGate.
    • Where it's used: AddUIShared registers the policy unconditionally, so the page's attribute resolves in every host (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:94-100); the TwoFactorAccount page references it with [Authorize(Policy = TwoFactorPageRequirement.PolicyName)] (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAccount.razor:4). Pinned by TwoFactorRoutesTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/TwoFactor/TwoFactorRoutesTests.cs:26).

    ThemeService

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Theme · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/ThemeService.cs:23 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the single owner of the Day/Dark preference (ADR-028). It holds the current mode for the circuit, persists a change through a small JS module to a cookie plus localStorage, and raises an event so every subscriber re-renders together.
    • Depends on: LazyJsModule (single-flight importer for its JS module, ThemeService.cs:26); Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSRuntime (ASP.NET Core, primary-constructor parameter at line 23); an optional IInitialThemeModeSource, the second primary-constructor parameter, defaulting to null (line 23); the asset it imports, MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/wwwroot/theme.js, which owns the cookie and localStorage access (theme.js:5,23,33). IAsyncDisposable (BCL) is implemented so the module reference is released with the circuit.
    • Concept introduced, one scoped service as the theme's single source of truth. [Rubric §20, Design System, Theming & UI Consistency] assesses whether theming is a first-class, centrally owned concern rather than per-page CSS toggling. Here exactly one scoped service holds IsDarkMode (line 32); the toggle button, the MudThemeProvider wrapper and, on MAUI, the native chrome all read from it and all subscribe to OnChange (line 38). Nothing else stores a copy. [Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow] is the same fact viewed as state: an event-plus-property service is the framework's pattern for cross-component UI state that is not routed, and the cost of that pattern is unsubscription discipline in every consumer.
    • Concept introduced, JS interop is not available during prerender. [Rubric §18, UI Architecture & Component Design] covers the render-mode contract a Blazor component must respect (ADR-056, Website/docs-src/adr/056-blazor-render-mode-strategy.md). Reading a cookie or localStorage requires a live browser, so InitializeAsync can only run after the first interactive render; the class documents that requirement on itself (ThemeService.cs:11-14) rather than guarding it internally, and the component that owns the lifecycle calls it from OnAfterRenderAsync(firstRender) (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/MmcaThemeProviders.razor:59-69).
    • Walkthrough
      • ModulePath is the _content/MMCA.Common.UI/theme.js static-web-asset path (line 25), wrapped in a LazyJsModule field (line 26). Two components resolving the same scoped service therefore share one import rather than racing two.
      • IsDarkMode (line 32) and IsInitialized (line 35) are public with a private setter: subscribers read the state, only this class writes it. OnChange (line 38) is a plain EventHandler?. IsDarkMode is seeded from the constructor's initialModeSource?.IsDarkMode ?? false (line 32), so on a head with a native store (MAUI registers one) every reader, the app-bar toggle's icon and label among them, starts in the mode the page is painted in rather than light until initialization runs (doc comment, lines 17-22); a web head passes no source and starts at false.
      • InitializeAsync() (line 44) is idempotent by an early return on IsInitialized (lines 46-49). It imports the module (line 51), asks get for the stored value (line 53), and resolves the mode: a stored value wins by an ordinal case-insensitive compare against "dark" (lines 54-55), otherwise it falls back to the OS setting through systemPrefersDark (line 56), which reads prefers-color-scheme (theme.js:33-35). Only then does it set IsInitialized and raise OnChange (lines 59-60), so the first notification carries the resolved answer, not the default.
      • InitializeAtStartupAsync(bool?) (line 72, internal) is the entry point MmcaThemeProviders calls on first render, passing the mode of an optional IInitialThemeModeSource it resolved in OnInitialized (MmcaThemeProviders.razor:50,69). A null falls through to InitializeAsync; a known native value takes InitializeFromNativeAsync (lines 75-92), which is also idempotent on IsInitialized (lines 77-80), adopts the value, sets IsInitialized and raises OnChange (lines 82-84), and only then reseeds the cookie and localStorage through set (lines 88-90), so a stale WebView value can neither win now nor be mirrored back over the native one. The reseed is last on purpose: a failure leaves the native value in force and surfaces to the caller's best-effort guard (comment, lines 86-87).
      • Each of the three JS calls that can fail sits inside a #pragma warning disable BL0016 block whose justification names why the failure must propagate rather than be caught here: the caller observes it through ThemeInterop (lines 52-57, 89-91, 101-103).
      • SetDarkModeAsync(bool) (line 96) persists first, through set (line 102), then writes the field (line 104) and notifies (line 105): a failed import or JS call leaves IsDarkMode and every subscriber on the mode that is actually stored (comment, ThemeService.cs:98-99). The JS side writes a non-HttpOnly cookie with a one-year max-age and samesite=lax and mirrors it to localStorage, guarding the mirror in a try because private browsing can refuse storage (theme.js:23-31). The cookie is deliberately readable by the server, which is how SSR can paint the right theme on the first response (theme.js:1-2).
      • ToggleAsync() (line 109) is SetDarkModeAsync(!IsDarkMode), the entire body of the app-bar toggle's click handler.
      • DisposeAsync() (line 114) forwards to the module wrapper, which is where the guarded release of a torn-down circuit's IJSObjectReference lives.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-028 (Website/docs-src/adr/028-dark-theme-mode.md) requires the preference to survive a reload and to be visible to the server for a no-flash first paint, which is why the value goes to a cookie and localStorage rather than to component state, and why the service holds no MudTheme of its own: it publishes a boolean and lets the theme providers decide what that means visually. Not gating InitializeAsync on RendererInfo is also deliberate and pinned: the prerender test uses the get invocation as proof that the first render ran at all (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Theme/MmcaThemeProvidersPrerenderTests.cs:29-33).
    • Where it's used: registered by AddUIShared as scoped (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:221) and consumed by MmcaThemeProviders, which subscribes in OnInitialized, initializes on first render and unsubscribes on dispose (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/MmcaThemeProviders.razor:56,69,147), by ThemeToggle (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/ThemeToggle.razor:2,7), by the MAUI head's NativeThemeSync, which mirrors the in-app choice onto the native chrome (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/Components/NativeThemeSync.razor:17,41,52), and by the login flow, which applies a returning user's stored theme (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor:393). Hosts that compose their own DI register it directly, for example MMCA.Helpdesk (MMCA.Helpdesk/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Helpdesk.UI.Web/Program.cs:23). Behavior is pinned through the two components that drive it, MmcaThemeProvidersTests and ThemeToggleTests, and end to end by DarkModeE2ETests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.E2E.Tests/Layout/DarkModeE2ETests.cs:54).
    • Caveats: no test file in MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services is named for this type; its behavior is covered only through those components, so a change to InitializeAsync surfaces as a component-test failure rather than a direct one. OnChange is a plain event with no weak-reference handling, so a subscriber that fails to unsubscribe outlives its component for the life of the circuit; both in-framework subscribers unsubscribe on dispose and both have a test asserting it. SetDarkModeAsync sets IsDarkMode only after the JS write succeeds, so a failed set throws out of the call with the in-memory mode, the persisted mode and the subscribers still in agreement and no OnChange raised. The native-first path orders it the other way on purpose: InitializeFromNativeAsync adopts the native value and raises OnChange before the set reseed, so a failed reseed throws with the in-memory mode already the native one. The exception is not swallowed here: the callers that must not take down the circuit wrap the call in ThemeInterop (ThemeToggle.razor:22).

Keeping it opt-in and off by default means a host adopting nothing sees no change to its document.     • Where it's used: called only by MmcaThemeProviders, after its first interactive render (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/MmcaThemeProviders.razor:76) and after every theme change (MmcaThemeProviders.razor:127).
