Externals: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http (IHttpContextAccessor, HttpContext), Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR (HubMetadata), BCL Lock, TimeProvider, Interlocked, Volatile, Task, TimeSpan, EventHandler, InvalidOperationException.
    • Concept introduced, the two-world token store (SSR request versus interactive circuit). A Blazor Web page runs twice: first as a server-side prerender inside a live HTTP request, where an HttpContext exists and JS interop does not, and then as a stateful circuit whose HttpContext is not null but is only the request that opened the hub connection, sent before any sign-in on that circuit and never updated, so its cookie is stale by construction (class doc, lines 29-41). One store has to serve both worlds, and this class decides which source of truth applies in TryAnswerFromCookie (lines 325-353, called at line 109), which looks at whether an HttpContext exists and whether memory has yet become authoritative.
      • Cookie-first answer (TryAnswerFromCookie, lines 325-353): when an HttpContext exists and memory is not yet authoritative, the request's HttpOnly cookie is read via cookieTokenReader.ReadAccessToken() (line 334). On a page request being prerendered (not IsHubConnection, line 338) the cookie wins outright, because the middleware may have just refreshed it in place on this navigation. On the request that opened the Blazor Server hub connection (IsHubConnection, lines 360-362, recognized by SignalR HubMetadata or a WebSocket request) the cookie is only the session the circuit started with: a cookie token there marks the session as held (lines 347-350), and the cookie answers only when absent or still fresh (JwtTokenInfo.IsFresh, line 352); an expired one is never handed back, since it would 401 every call for the life of the circuit, and the refresher re-acquires instead.
      • Interactive circuit (lines 114-152): the token lives in the _accessToken field (line 63). If JwtTokenInfo.IsFresh(_accessToken, ExpirySkew) (line 115) says it survives the 30-second skew (line 55), it is returned as is; otherwise it is re-acquired, unless a recent definitive "no session" answer is still remembered (the anonymous grace, below).
      • [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] assesses how credentials are held in the browser. This is a deliberate XSS-hardening design: the long-lived refresh token stays in an HttpOnly cookie unreachable from script, the access token exists only in circuit memory and is never persisted, and the refresh token transits JS exactly once, for the same-origin POST that seeds the cookies at login, as protected handoff ciphertext when the same-origin API proxy is enabled (SetTokensAsync, comment lines 211-215).
      • [Rubric §11, Security] assesses the wider auth model; this store is one edge of the browser session-cookie design (ADR-022) and of the client token lifecycle (ADR-051), the piece that decides where a bearer token is read on each side of the prerender boundary.
      • Login fails loudly, logout stays best-effort. The two cookie writes are deliberately asymmetric. SetTokensAsync throws InvalidOperationException("The session cookie could not be written.") when SyncAsync returns false (lines 216-219), after the in-memory token is already set, so AuthUIService reports Auth.TokenStorageUnavailable instead of a login that looks successful and then silently signs out at the first access-token expiry, when no cookie exists to refresh from (comment above the sync call). ClearTokensAsync discards the boolean (_ = await sessionCookieSync.ClearAsync(), line 233), because logout is best-effort by contract (IAuthUIService.LogoutAsync never fails); a caller that needs proof the session ended uses IAuthUIService.RevokeAllSessionsAsync (comment above it).
      • Anonymous grace, so a signed-out visitor costs one token round trip, not one per API call. AnonymousGrace is a 15-second static readonly TimeSpan (line 58). When a hydrate returns no token and the refresher did not report itself unavailable, HydrateAsync sets _anonymousUntil = now + AnonymousGrace (line 302); GetAccessTokenAsync then answers null from memory while _accessToken is null and the clock is before _anonymousUntil (line 120). SetTokensAsync resets _anonymousUntil (line 207) so a login right after anonymous browsing does not wait out the grace, and a session created in another tab is seen within the window (class doc, lines 19-28). Only a DEFINITIVE answer starts it: a refresher implementing ISessionAwareTokenRefresher reports a 429, a 5xx, a dropped connection or unavailable interop as unavailable (comment, lines 267-274), so the next read hydrates again instead of treating a signed-in user as anonymous; a refresher without that capability keeps the earlier reading, where null means "no session" (lines 286-289).
      • Session ended on the server, so the circuit signs out (A-34). The volatile _sessionHeld flag (line 85) records whether the circuit holds a session: it is set by a login (line 210), by a hydrate that acquired a token (lines 305-308), by a hub-connection cookie that carried one (lines 347-350) and by a rejected-token renewal (line 186), and cleared by a logout (line 229). When a hydrate gets a definitive "no session" (definitiveNoSession, line 284, only possible from an ISessionAwareTokenRefresher whose answer is null and not unavailable) while _sessionHeld is true, it clears the flag and raises SessionEnded (lines 309-315, event declared at line 88). A plain refresher's null still starts the grace but is not proof enough to sign a held session out (comment, lines 273-274), and a transient failure leaves the flag alone (field doc, lines 81-84).
      • A 401 renews the rejected token once. A still-fresh token can be refused by the API (a locked account, a revoked session), and without a renewal path the circuit would stay signed in behind 401s until the token expired (ISessionAwareTokenStorage.cs:31-36). AuthDelegatingHandler reports the rejected token to RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:328); this store drops it and runs one hydrate through the same single-flight a stale token takes, so a definitive "no session" ends the session exactly as an expired token's refresh does (remarks, lines 155-162).
    • Walkthrough
      • The primary constructor (lines 48-53) takes IHttpContextAccessor, CookieTokenReader, ISessionCookieSync, and ITokenRefresher, and a nullable TimeProvider. A public four-argument constructor (from line 98) chains to it with timeProvider: null, kept so code compiled against the original signature keeps binding. The type is sealed and carries no app-specific state, which is why it could be hoisted out of the app Blazor Web hosts (class doc, lines 16-17).
      • Fields: ExpirySkew (line 55, a static readonly TimeSpan of 30 seconds), AnonymousGrace (line 58, 15 seconds), the Lock _hydrateSync (line 60, the .NET 9+ dedicated lock object), _timeProvider (line 61, timeProvider ?? TimeProvider.System), the in-memory _accessToken (line 63), _hydrateInFlight (line 64, the shared acquisition task), _anonymousUntil (line 65, the end of the remembered "no session" answer), _tokenVersion (line 72, bumped by every login and logout so a stale hydrate can be recognized), the volatile _memoryIsAuthoritative (line 78, set once this instance has stored, cleared or hydrated a token, which only happens on the circuit, so from then on memory wins over the connection request's stale cookie) and the volatile _sessionHeld (line 85). The public SessionEnded event (line 88) implements the ISessionAwareTokenStorage member.
      • GetAccessTokenAsync (lines 107-152): the cookie-first branch (TryAnswerFromCookie, line 109), the freshness check (line 115), the anonymous-grace short-circuit (line 120), then the single-flight guard. _hydrateInFlight ??= HydrateAsync() executes inside lock (_hydrateSync) (lines 130-134) and the resulting task is copied to a local before the lock is released, because two callers could otherwise each start a hydrate and the later completion would overwrite the other's token; HydrateAsync reaches its first await immediately, so nothing slow runs under the lock. The finally (from line 140) clears _hydrateInFlight only when it is still reference-equal to the task this caller awaited (line 146), so a newer hydrate started after this one completed is not dropped, which would split the next set of callers again.
      • RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync(string rejectedAccessToken) (lines 163-192): throws on a null or blank argument (line 165), then, under _hydrateSync (lines 168-189), works out which token the store holds: the cookie's while an HttpContext exists and memory is not authoritative, otherwise _accessToken (lines 171-172). A held token that differs from the rejected one (already replaced, or never held here) is returned unchanged (lines 173-176), and so is a rejection during the SSR prerender, where no JS interop exists to refresh with (lines 178-181). Otherwise it nulls the token, clears _anonymousUntil, marks memory authoritative so the stale cookie never answers again, marks the session held (lines 183-186), joins or starts the shared hydrate (lines 187-188), and awaits it through AwaitHydrateAsync (line 191).
      • GetRefreshTokenAsync (lines 194-201): returns cookieTokenReader.ReadRefreshToken() (line 199) whenever an HttpContext exists, the live request during SSR and, on the circuit, the hub-connection request whose cookie can be as stale as the class remarks describe; otherwise null. The refresh token is never held in memory. It wraps the value in Task.FromResult rather than being async.
      • SetTokensAsync (lines 203-220): bumps _tokenVersion (line 206), resets _anonymousUntil (line 207), caches the access token in memory, marks memory authoritative (line 209) and the session held (line 210), then awaits sessionCookieSync.SyncAsync(accessToken, refreshToken) and throws when it reports failure (lines 216-219).
      • ClearTokensAsync (lines 222-240): bumps _tokenVersion (line 224), nulls the in-memory token, marks memory authoritative (line 228) so a logout is not undone by the connection request's cookie, clears _sessionHeld (line 229) so the logout itself never raises SessionEnded, awaits sessionCookieSync.ClearAsync() with its result explicitly discarded (line 233), then bumps the version a second time (line 238) and nulls the token again, so a hydrate that started during the clear and read the session being removed has its answer discarded, or dropped if it already landed.
      • AwaitHydrateAsync(Task<string?> inFlight) (lines 247-263): the renewal path's copy of the guarded await, clearing _hydrateInFlight under the lock only when it is still reference-equal to the awaited task (line 257).
      • HydrateAsync (lines 265-318): snapshots _tokenVersion (line 275), then, when the refresher is an ISessionAwareTokenRefresher, calls TryAcquireAccessTokenAsync() (line 281) and keeps the token, the IsUnavailable flag and the derived definitiveNoSession (line 284); otherwise it calls AcquireAccessTokenAsync() (line 288). If the version moved while the acquisition was in flight (a login or logout landed), the stale answer and its grace are discarded and the current _accessToken is returned (lines 291-294). Otherwise the token is cached, memory is marked authoritative (line 298), a null token with unavailable false starts the grace (lines 300-303), and the session-held bookkeeping runs (lines 305-315): a token marks the session held, a definitive "no session" for a held session raises SessionEnded. Every await on the hydrate path uses ConfigureAwait(false) (lines 138, 251, 281, 288), the library posture the cookie-write awaits do not take.
    • Why it's built this way: Blazor Server's split lifecycle breaks the naive "read a token from storage" store, which would either fail during prerender (no JS) or leak the refresh token to script if it used localStorage. Branching on HttpContext presence and keeping the refresh token cookie-only resolves both. The locked single-flight is the correction of a real concurrency defect in the simpler ??= version, and it is worth reading as a small case study in why "good enough" atomicity on a circuit is not good enough; the 401 renewal reuses that same single-flight rather than opening a second refresh path. Surfacing a failed cookie write at login, while tolerating one at logout, puts the failure where the user can still act on it. The 15-second anonymous grace trades a short staleness window for not paying a token round trip on every API call of a signed-out visitor, and it never remembers a transient failure. SessionEnded exists so a session that ended on the server does not leave the circuit rendering as signed in; only a definitive answer for a session the circuit actually held raises it, so neither an anonymous visitor nor a transient outage signs anyone out. See ADR-022.
    • Where it's used: registered as the scoped ITokenStorageService by AddCommonServerTokenStorage() in the MMCA.Common.UI.Web DependencyInjection (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/DependencyInjection.cs:41-50); consumer hosts call that instead of shipping their own copy, and BlazorWebHostExtensions calls it for every host built with AddMmcaBlazorWebHost (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Hosting/BlazorWebHostExtensions.cs:134). The same call registers BrowserOriginHandler on the "APIClient" pipeline (lines 47-48). JwtAuthenticationStateProvider subscribes to SessionEnded when the registered storage is session-aware (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:52, handler OnSessionEnded at line 145) to sign the circuit out. Pinned by ServerTokenStorageServiceTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Tests/Services/ServerTokenStorageServiceTests.cs).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the cookie names, lifetimes, and the /auth/session/token and /auth/session/handoff endpoints themselves are not in this file; they live in the MMCA.Common.API session-cookie plumbing and the same-origin proxy referenced by the doc comment (lines 9-47).

    AppLockInertBackground

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Capabilities · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Capabilities/AppLockInertBackground.cs:15 · Level 1 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the small JS-interop helper that makes everything outside the app-lock overlay inert while BiometricGate is locked, and lifts that again on unlock. It wraps one lazily imported module, ./_content/MMCA.Common.UI/app-lock.js (ModulePath, AppLockInertBackground.cs:18), and remembers whether its last apply landed (IsApplied, :23).
    • Depends on: IJSRuntime (primary constructor, :15), ElementReference, IAsyncDisposable, and the internal LazyJsModule import wrapper (:20). The JS side exports inertOutside and release (wwwroot/app-lock.js:12, :32).
    • Concept introduced, a modal that blocks the page behind it, not only the Tab key. [Rubric §21, Accessibility] assesses whether a modal surface really is the only thing a keyboard or assistive-technology user can reach. A focus trap keeps Tab inside the panel, but programmatic focus and a screen reader's virtual cursor can still reach the page underneath; the script header (app-lock.js:1-8) records that the inert attribute removes that page from both, while leaving the lock root itself live. It also leaves an element that was already inert alone and never releases it later, so the helper never undoes someone else's inert.
    • Walkthrough
      • ApplyAsync(ElementReference lockRoot) (AppLockInertBackground.cs:28-44) imports the module through GetOrImportAsync (:32), calls inertOutside with the overlay wrapper (:33) and only then sets IsApplied (:34). JSDisconnectedException (circuit gone) and JSException (the browser refused) are both swallowed (:36-43): the comment at :42 notes the focus trap still holds Tab inside the panel when the inert call fails.
      • ReleaseAsync() (:48-69) returns at once when nothing was applied (:50-53), clears IsApplied before the call (:55), invokes release (:59) and tolerates the same two exceptions (:61-68).
      • DisposeAsync() (:72-87) releases, then disposes the module (:76-77), again tolerating a disconnected circuit or a shutdown-time interop race (:79-86).
    • Why it's built this way: every call is best effort and never throws, which is what lets BiometricGate call it from OnAfterRenderAsync, from unlock and sign-out, and fire and forget its disposal from a synchronous Dispose(bool) (BiometricGate.razor.cs:103-108). Keeping IsApplied means a release with nothing applied costs no interop call at all.
    • Where it's used: only BiometricGate, which creates it lazily through its InertBackground property (BiometricGate.razor.cs:48); pinned through BiometricGateTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Components/Capabilities/BiometricGateTests.cs).

    InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner>

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Lists · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Lists/InfiniteScrollObserver.cs:17 · Level 1 · class (internal sealed, generic)

    • What it is: the one place that talks to infinite-scroll.js for the two infinite-scroll components. It owns a per-instance observer id, a lazily imported JS module, the DotNetObjectReference back to its owner, and an IsObserving flag (lines 25-40). Its owner (a component exposing a [JSInvokable] callback) constructs it as new InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner>(JS, this) and calls ObserveAsync, UnobserveAsync and DisposeAsync from its lifecycle.
    • Depends on: IJSRuntime, ElementReference, DotNetObjectReference<TOwner>, IAsyncDisposable, and the internal LazyJsModule import wrapper (line 35). Nothing else first-party; consumed by InfiniteScrollSentinel and MobileInfiniteScrollList<TItem> (the TOwner constraint is class, line 18).
    • Concept introduced, one JS-interop lifecycle shared by two components. [Rubric §23, Front-End Performance] (assesses whether observers are attached on demand and detached so they stop costing anything) and [Rubric §18, UI Architecture]. Before the extraction each component carried its own copy of the import, attach, detach and dispose code; the helper makes a fix to one race a fix to both.
    • Walkthrough:
      • ObserveAsync(ElementReference sentinel) (lines 48-78) awaits _module.GetOrImportAsync() (line 52), a single-flight import: Blazor does not serialize OnAfterRenderAsync, so a second call can start while the first import is in flight, and an unguarded ??= would import twice and leak the overwritten instance (comment, lines 32-34). If the owner was disposed while the import was in flight, the late module is released and no observer is attached that nobody would ever detach (lines 54-62). Otherwise it creates the DotNetObjectReference once (line 66), calls observe with the reference, the element and the id (line 67), and sets IsObserving (line 68). JSDisconnectedException and JSException are both swallowed (lines 70-77): the list simply stops at the pages already loaded.
      • UnobserveAsync() (lines 82-104) returns unless the module is imported and an observer is attached (line 84), calls unobserve with the id (line 92), tolerates both exceptions, and clears IsObserving (line 103).
      • DisposeAsync() (lines 107-133) guards re-entry with _disposed (lines 109-114), unobserves and disposes the module (lines 118-119), tolerates both exceptions, and disposes the DotNetObjectReference in a finally (line 131) so the .NET side is released even if JS already went away.
    • Why it's built this way: the observe path is where the two components had drifted apart (one tolerated JSException, one did not); a single internal class with the guarded import fixes the leak and the dispose-during-import race once.
    • Where it's used: InfiniteScrollSentinel.razor.cs (lines 35, 59-60, 78-80) and MobileInfiniteScrollList.razor.cs; exercised through InfiniteScrollSentinelTests.

    ViewAsBanner

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/ViewAsBanner.razor.cs:23 · Level 1 · class (partial component)

    • What it is: the banner the shared layout shows while a support user is viewing the app as another account (ADR-137, Website/docs-src/adr/137-read-only-view-as-support-access.md). It names the viewed account, counts down the time left on the view-as token, and ends the session when the countdown reaches zero. MainLayout.razor:87 renders it unconditionally; it renders its content only when the principal is a view-as principal.
    • Depends on: the cascading Task<AuthenticationState> (ViewAsBanner.razor.cs:36), IStringLocalizer<SharedResource> (SharedResource, :38), IJSRuntime (:39), the IsViewAs extension on ClaimsPrincipalExtensions (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:137), and ComponentLifetimeExtensions for LifetimeToken() (ViewAsBanner.razor.cs:104, :134). Externals: PeriodicTimer, CancellationTokenSource.
    • Concept introduced, a time-boxed elevated session that ends itself. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether delegated or impersonated access is visible to the person using it and bounded in time. The banner reads the remaining lifetime straight from the token's exp claim, so the countdown shows the same deadline the server enforces, and it calls the end endpoint itself once that deadline passes rather than waiting for the next refused request.
    • Walkthrough
      • ApiPathPrefix (ViewAsBanner.razor.cs:34) is the same-origin proxy prefix, /api when unset (:134).
      • Remaining(ClaimsPrincipal?, DateTimeOffset) (:48-58) is public and static, so it is testable without rendering: it parses exp as invariant Unix seconds (:50-51), returns null when the claim is missing or unreadable (:53), and clamps a past expiry to TimeSpan.Zero (:56-57).
      • OnParametersSetAsync (:70-76) sets _viewAs from IsViewAs() (:73), takes the display name from Identity.Name or the ClaimTypes.Name claim (:74), and turns the remaining time into an absolute _expiresAt (:75).
      • OnAfterRender (:79-87) starts a one-second PeriodicTimer on the first render, only for a view-as principal and only when RendererInfo.IsInteractive (:82); the comment (:81) records that a prerender shows the starting value only. FormatRemaining (:89-98) renders the time left as mm:ss (:97), never negative.
      • TickAsync (:100-122) re-renders every tick (:106) and, once _expiresAt has passed, dispatches EndAsync and stops (:107-111). Cancellation and an ObjectDisposedException between ticks both end the loop quietly (:114-121).
      • EndAsync (:124-141) is guarded by _ending (:126-131) and calls the mmcaViewAs.end script with {prefix}/auth/view-as/end (:134). A JSException, JSDisconnectedException, InvalidOperationException or OperationCanceledException resets _ending (:136-140): the comment records that the page is reloading or the circuit is gone and the overlay expires on its own.
      • DisposeAsync (:61-67) cancels the token source, disposes the timer and the source.
    • Why it's built this way: computing the deadline once and re-rendering against the clock keeps the countdown honest across a slow render, and the guard on _ending keeps a late tick from posting the end request twice.
    • Where it's used: the shared MainLayout (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Layout/MainLayout.razor:87); pinned by ViewAsComponentTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Components/Auth/ViewAsComponentTests.cs).     BiometricGate

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Capabilities · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Capabilities/BiometricGate.razor.cs:18 · Level 2 · class (partial, component code-behind)

    • What it is: a hybrid-head app-lock gate. It locks the UI behind a biometric prompt whenever the app returns from the background having sat there longer than ReLockAfter, so a device handed to someone else, or simply left unattended, does not reopen straight into a signed-in session. While locked, the page behind the overlay is made inert and focus is held on the Unlock button.
    • Depends on: injected services resolved by the component (AppLifecycle's Resumed event with AppResumedEventArgs, Preferences (IDevicePreferences) read with DevicePreferenceKeys.AppLockEnabled, TokenStorage, AuthService (IAuthUIService, used only to sign out), Biometrics, Navigation, Logger, JS, the page's localizer L); AppLockInertBackground for the inert page behind the overlay (BiometricGate.razor.cs:32, :48); MudBlazor's MudButton for the focus target (_unlockButton, line 30).
    • Concept introduced, a discarded lifecycle task that cannot afford to throw. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether a re-auth control actually re-arms on every qualifying event, not just the first one. The class subscribes to AppLifecycle.Resumed on first render regardless of the current preference, because app lock can be switched on later in the same session (comment, lines 76-77), and every resume re-reads the preference. [Rubric §18, UI Architecture & Component Design] covers the handler shape itself: OnResumed (line 125) is a plain EventHandler<AppResumedEventArgs>, so it cannot be async; it fires ReLockAsync with an explicit discard, and the comment (lines 119-124) states why that discard is safe here: ReLockAsync observes its own failures with a catch-all, which avoids the async-void crash-the-process mode (VSTHRD100), and the catch-all comment (lines 160-161) records that nothing else would observe a failed re-lock.
    • Concept introduced, a precondition read that fails open before opt-in and closed after it. [Rubric §11, Security] also assesses which way a control fails when its own inputs are unreadable. ShouldLockAsync documents both halves (lines 166-171): if the AppLockEnabled preference itself cannot be read, nothing says the owner opted in, so the gate stays open rather than forcing a biometric prompt on a device that may have none enrolled; if the preference reads as on but the stored session cannot be read, the session state is unknown and the gate locks. Either way the method never throws, which matters because it runs from both the first render and the resume path.
    • Concept introduced, a lock that owns focus and the page behind it. [Rubric §21, Accessibility] assesses whether a modal surface is the only thing a keyboard or screen-reader user can reach. Every lock goes through EngageLock (lines 206-215), which sets _locked and queues both the focus move onto Unlock and the inert background, whichever path locked the gate (start-up or resume), so focus never stays on the page behind the overlay (field comment, lines 34-39).
    • Walkthrough
      • ReLockAfter (lines 25-26) is a [Parameter] TimeSpan defaulting to 30 seconds; the comment (lines 20-24) explains the default is deliberately short, a device handed off is usually away from its owner longer than a glance at a notification.
      • State: _lockRoot is the overlay wrapper the inert boundary is measured from (line 31), _inertBackground the lazily created helper behind the InertBackground property (lines 32, 48), and _focusUnlockPending and _inertPending the two flags acted on after render (lines 40, 46).
      • OnAfterRenderAsync(firstRender) (lines 51-89): first focuses the Unlock button if _focusUnlockPending and the button reference now exists (lines 53-57), because that flag can only be acted on once the locked branch has actually rendered. Then, if _inertPending and still locked, it applies the inert background to _lockRoot (lines 59-62) and releases it again at once when an unlock landed while the call was in flight (lines 64-68). On firstRender it subscribes to AppLifecycle.Resumed (lines 78-79), then calls ShouldLockAsync and, if it returns true, calls EngageLock and awaits UnlockAsync (lines 81-88).
      • ReLockAsync (lines 127-164) returns early if already locked or if the background duration was under ReLockAfter (line 131), otherwise dispatches the check, EngageLock and unlock sequence through InvokeAsync (lines 136-146). It catches ObjectDisposedException and InvalidOperationException as expected teardown races (lines 148-155), and a general Exception last under a scoped CA1031 suppression, logged rather than rethrown (lines 156-163).
      • ShouldLockAsync (lines 172-204) wraps the preference read in its own try (lines 175-185): a failure is logged as a warning and returns false. A preference that is off also returns false (lines 187-190). Otherwise a second try (lines 192-203) returns whether a refresh token is still stored, nothing to protect without a session, and a failure there is logged and returns true (line 202). Both catch-alls carry a scoped CA1031 suppression naming their disposition.
      • UnlockAsync (lines 217-238) calls Biometrics.AuthenticateAsync with a localized prompt reason; success clears _locked and both pending flags and lifts the inert background through ReleaseBackgroundAsync (lines 219-224); failure re-queues _focusUnlockPending for the next render (line 234). Both paths call StateHasChanged under a BL0012 suppression, because UnlockAsync also runs from OnAfterRenderAsync and ReLockAsync, where nothing re-renders automatically (lines 225-227, 235-237).
      • FocusUnlockAsync (lines 244-258) tolerates JSDisconnectedException (circuit gone) and InvalidOperationException (prerendering, or the element already removed).
      • SignOutAsync (lines 264-272) calls AuthService.LogoutAsync() (line 266), clears _locked and both pending flags, releases the inert background, and navigates to /login. The doc (lines 260-263) states why it is the app's own logout and never a bare token clear: clearing the tokens alone left Blazor's auth state signed in and the previous session's read cache and offline snapshots on the device.
      • ReleaseBackgroundAsync (lines 274-276) releases only when a helper exists, otherwise returns a completed task.
      • Dispose(bool) (lines 93-110) unsubscribes from AppLifecycle.Resumed if subscribed, guarded so it is safe to call more than once, then fires and forgets the helper's DisposeAsync so a gate torn down while locked does not leave the page behind it inert (lines 103-109); the public Dispose() (lines 113-117) forwards to it and suppresses finalization.
    • Why it's built this way: the re-lock decision is driven entirely by wall-clock background duration rather than any UI state, so it behaves the same whether the app was backgrounded for a phone call or for the rest of the day. Catching broadly inside ReLockAsync but narrowly inside FocusUnlockAsync reflects the difference between an operation whose caller cannot observe a failure at all (the lifecycle event) and one whose failure just means "skip the focus this time". The two catches inside ShouldLockAsync resolve in opposite directions on purpose: before opt-in the safe default is "no lock", after opt-in it is "lock". Routing every lock through EngageLock keeps the start-up and resume paths from drifting apart on focus and inertness.
    • Where it's used: MMCA.ADC's DeviceUIModule (MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/DeviceUIModule.cs) and App.xaml.cs (MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/App.xaml.cs); referenced by TermsAcceptanceGate (TermsAcceptanceGate.razor.cs); pinned by BiometricGateTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Components/Capabilities/BiometricGateTests.cs). Its place in the UI module shell is described in ADR-067 (Website/docs-src/adr/067-ui-module-shell-composition.md).

    InfiniteScrollSentinel

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Lists · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Lists/InfiniteScrollSentinel.razor.cs:21 · Level 0 · class (partial component)

    • What it is: a bottom-of-list marker that raises OnVisible when it scrolls near the viewport, so the hosting page can fetch and append its next page. It owns the IntersectionObserver and nothing else: the item markup, the fetch, and the accumulated list stay with the page.
    • Depends on: IJSRuntime, ElementReference, and MudBlazor's MudProgressCircular in the markup; first-party, only InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner>, which owns the shared JS module _content/MMCA.Common.UI/infinite-scroll.js (wwwroot/infinite-scroll.js). It is a sibling of MobileInfiniteScrollList<TItem>, which drives the same JS module.
    • Concept introduced, the observer as a child component so disposal is correct. [Rubric §23, Front-End Performance] (assesses render and network cost: paging on demand instead of loading everything, and detaching observers so they stop costing anything), [Rubric §21, Accessibility] (assesses whether dynamic content changes are announced without hijacking focus) and [Rubric §18, UI Architecture]. The design point recorded in the doc comment (lines 14-19) is a lifecycle one: a page deriving from DataGridListPageBase<TDto> cannot hook async disposal because its DisposeAsync is not virtual, whereas a child component is disposed by the renderer the moment the host stops rendering it. Rendering the sentinel only while more pages exist therefore makes "detach the observer" a rendering decision rather than a bookkeeping one, and a filter reset that refills the list gets a fresh instance with a fresh observer.
    • Walkthrough:
      • Parameters: OnVisible (line 26), IsLoading (line 29) which renders the inline progress row, and LoadingLabel (line 32), the localized accessible name for that row.
      • State (lines 34-41): the _sentinelRef element reference (line 34), the _observer field (line 35, an InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner> that now owns the observer id, the imported JS module, the DotNetObjectReference and the observing flag), _wasLoading (line 40, the previous render's IsLoading), and _disposed (line 41).
      • OnSentinelVisible() (lines 47-49) is the [JSInvokable] callback. Its name is fixed by the shared JS module, which calls it by string (lines 43-46). It returns immediately when disposed, otherwise marshals onto the renderer with InvokeAsync before invoking OnVisible.
      • OnAfterRenderAsync (lines 52-63) attaches the observer on the first render, and re-attaches it on the render where a load has just finished: loadJustFinished is _wasLoading && !IsLoading && _observer?.IsObserving == true (line 54), _wasLoading is then updated (line 55), and either condition lazily creates the observer helper (line 59) and calls ObserveAsync(_sentinelRef) (line 60). The reason is recorded on the field (lines 37-39): an IntersectionObserver reports threshold crossings only, so a sentinel that is still inside the viewport when the appended page arrives would never fire again and the list would stall until the user scrolled away and back. Re-observing creates a fresh observer, which delivers a fresh initial entry.
      • The module import, the DotNetObjectReference, the observe/unobserve calls and the swallowed JSDisconnectedException/JSException live in the shared helper, not here; see InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner>.
      • DisposeAsync (lines 67-82) suppresses finalization, guards re-entry with _disposed (lines 71-74), and delegates teardown to _observer.DisposeAsync() when one was created (lines 78-80), so the detach, the module release and the DotNetObjectReference disposal happen in the helper.
      • The markup (Components/InfiniteScrollSentinel.razor:4-13) is a single div carrying the element reference, with the progress row rendered only while IsLoading. That row is role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-busy="true" (line 9), matching PageLoadingState's politeness so a screen reader hears that more items are loading without the announcement interrupting reading.
      • The JS side is deliberately tiny: observe disconnects any prior observer for the id, creates an IntersectionObserver with rootMargin: '200px' and invokes OnSentinelVisible on intersection (wwwroot/infinite-scroll.js:3-14); unobserve disconnects and forgets the id (lines 16-22). The 200px margin is what makes the next page start loading slightly before the sentinel is on screen, and the disconnect-before-create step is what makes the post-load re-attach above safe to call repeatedly with the same id.
    • Why it's built this way: extracting just the observer is what lets a page keep its own cards, empty state and error state and still get infinite scroll (lines 10-13). The alternative, folding the behavior into the list component, would force any page that wants infinite scroll to also adopt that component's layout.
    • Where it's used: ADC's public speaker list renders it below the card grid while more pages exist, wiring OnVisible to its own loader and passing a localized loading label (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/Pages/Public/Speakers/PublicSpeakerList.razor:144-145, inside PublicSpeakerList). Covered by InfiniteScrollSentinelTests.

    SignInHistoryTable

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/SignInHistoryTable.razor.cs:22 · Level 2 · class (partial component)

    • What it is: a read-only table of an account's sign-ins, newest first, including ones that have ended. It takes the rows as a parameter and only formats them: a device label, an IP address, a status, and viewer-local times. It is the history counterpart of UserSessionsTable, which shows only the live sessions (ADR-097, Website/docs-src/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.md).
    • Depends on: SignInSummaryResponse (the row shape, SignInHistoryTable.razor.cs:30), SignInHistoryEntryKind (:72), SignInEndReasons (:82-87), ViewerTimeZone (:33), UserAgentSummary (:74), SharedResource for the IStringLocalizer (:32) and ComponentLifetimeExtensions for LifetimeToken() (:46).
    • Concept introduced, a status read from why a session ended. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether an account holder can see suspicious access. Each row's status comes from its end reason, so a refresh-token reuse, a session-cap eviction or an account deletion reads differently from an ordinary sign-out (DescribeStatus, :79-89). A view-as row (ADR-137) shows who looked, not a device of the account holder's (comment :70, :71-74).
    • Walkthrough
      • SignIns is an [EditorRequired] parameter defaulting to an empty list (:28-30).
      • OnAfterRenderAsync (:43-50) resolves the viewer's time zone on first render only, skips it once disposed, and calls StateHasChanged when the lookup resolved a zone (:46-49); the comment (:45) records that the zone is only readable once JS is available.
      • Row helpers: DescribeDevice returns the localized Auth.SignIns.ViewedBySupport text for a ViewAs row and otherwise UserAgentSummary.Describe(signIn.Device, signIn.UserAgent, L) (:71-74); DescribeIpAddress falls back to Auth.Sessions.IpUnknown when the address is blank (:76-77).
      • DescribeStatus (:79-89) maps a row with no end reason and no EndedAt to "Active", each SignInEndReasons constant (SignedOut, ReuseDetected, SessionCapExceeded, AccountDeleted, Expired) to its own localized text, and ViewAsEnded and any unknown reason to the generic "Ended" text (:87-88).
      • FormatInstant calls ViewerTime.Format (:91).
      • Disposal: IDisposable with an idempotent protected Dispose(bool) that cancels and disposes the CancellationTokenSource bounding the zone lookup (:36-40, :54-68).
    • Why it's built this way: the table owns no data fetching, so the account's own sessions page and the admin user-detail page share it, and the default arm of the status switch keeps a reason added on the server later rendering as "Ended" instead of blank.
    • Where it's used: the shared Sessions page (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Sessions.razor:125) and ADC's user detail page (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI/Pages/Users/UserDetail/UserDetail.razor:136); pinned by SignInHistoryTableTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Components/Auth/SignInHistoryTableTests.cs) and ADC's UserDetailTests.

    UserSessionsTable

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/UserSessionsTable.razor.cs:21 · Level 2 · class (partial component)

    • What it is: a read-only table of an account's live (signed-in) sessions, newest first. It takes the rows as a parameter and only formats them: a device label, an IP address and viewer-local times. The admin user-detail page feeds it from IUserAdminUIService.GetSessionsAsync (IUserAdminUIService<TUserDto>).
    • Depends on: RefreshSessionSummaryResponse (the row shape, UserSessionsTable.razor.cs:29), ViewerTimeZone (UserSessionsTable.razor.cs:32), UserAgentSummary (UserSessionsTable.razor.cs:69), SharedResource for the IStringLocalizer (UserSessionsTable.razor.cs:31) and ComponentLifetimeExtensions for LifetimeToken() (UserSessionsTable.razor.cs:45).
    • Concept introduced, times shown on the viewer's clock. [Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] covers presenting data the way the user will read it. The viewer's time zone is only readable once JS interop is available, so the component resolves it after the first render and re-renders once it is known (UserSessionsTable.razor.cs:42-49); until then the instants format on the default zone.
    • Walkthrough
      • Sessions is an [EditorRequired] parameter defaulting to an empty list (UserSessionsTable.razor.cs:27-29).
      • OnAfterRenderAsync runs the zone lookup on first render only, skips it once disposed, and calls StateHasChanged when the lookup resolved a zone (UserSessionsTable.razor.cs:42-49).

Its history counterpart SignInHistoryTable follows the same shape and the same device description.
    • Where it's used: ADC's user detail page (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI/Pages/Users/UserDetail/UserDetail.razor:112), and pinned by UserSessionsTableTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Components/Auth/UserSessionsTableTests.cs) and ADC's UserDetailTests.

    FieldRefusal

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:198 · Level 3 · record struct (private, nested in ChangePasswordCard)

    • What it is: a server message for one form field, held against the exact value it was raised for, so it clears itself the moment the user edits that field (doc comment, ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:194-197).
    • Depends on: Result (Result) and its Errors (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:202); the target and code of each error.
    • Concept introduced, a refusal bound to a value. [Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] assesses whether a server rejection is shown where the user can act on it. Holding the value beside the message means no timer or event is needed to dismiss a stale message: MessageFor compares the field's current value to the stored one and returns null once they differ.
    • Walkthrough
      • The positional record struct carries Value and Message (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:198); the default instance carries neither, so an unset refusal never matches.
      • From(result, field, value, matchCode) picks the first error whose target names the field or whose code equals matchCode, and returns default when there is none or its message is blank (:200-209).
      • MessageFor(value) returns the message only on an ordinal match with the stored value (:211-212).
      • TargetsField returns false for an empty target, then compares the last dotted segment of the error target to the field name, case-insensitively (:216-225). The segment start is found with AsSpan().LastIndexOf('.') (:223). The comment (:214-215) records why only the last segment counts: a validator over the request yields NewPassword, one over the command yields Request.NewPassword, in either casing once it crossed the wire.
    • Why it's built this way: it is a readonly record struct, so the two fields on the card (_currentPasswordRefusal, _newPasswordRefusal, ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:43-44) cost no allocation and compare by value.
    • Where it's used: only ChangePasswordCard: ShowFieldRefusalsAsync builds the two refusals (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:185-186) and the validators read them (:103, :121).

    MobileInfiniteScrollList<TItem>

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Lists · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Lists/MobileInfiniteScrollList.razor.cs:20 · Level 3 · class (generic partial component)

    • What it is: the mobile card list every list page falls back to on a narrow viewport. It owns the whole loop: an IntersectionObserver sentinel that asks for the next page, an accumulated item list rendered through a caller-supplied card template (with optional per-card actions beside it), a rendered-item cap that bounds DOM growth, generation-guarded supersession of in-flight fetches, and localized load-failure handling with a Retry button.
    • Depends on: Result and its generic form (the fetch delegate's return type), SharedResource through IStringLocalizer<SharedResource>, ResultUiExtensions.LocalizedErrorMessage, the EmptyState component, the ClickableCard component each row's card is wrapped in, and, through InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner>, the shared _content/MMCA.Common.UI/infinite-scroll.js module it shares with InfiniteScrollSentinel. Externals: IJSRuntime, DotNetObjectReference, CancellationTokenSource, MudBlazor primitives.
    • Concept introduced, generation-guarded supersession. [Rubric §19, State Management] (assesses whether concurrent updates to client state have a defined winner) and [Rubric §23, Front-End Performance]. The hard problem in an infinite list is not fetching, it is what happens when the user changes the filter while a fetch is in flight. Cancellation alone is not enough: the fetch delegate is consumer-supplied and may ignore its CancellationToken entirely, so a superseded call can still complete successfully and try to append rows to a list that was cleared. The answer here is a monotonically increasing _generation counter (line 72). A load snapshots it before awaiting (line 166) and discards its results if the value moved while it waited (line 182). The token cancellation is still issued (it stops work that does honor it), but the generation, not the token, is authoritative (comment, lines 179-181). The second half of the pattern is that the page counter is computed, not committed: targetPage = _currentPage + 1 (line 173) and _currentPage only advances on a successful, non-superseded completion (line 197), so a cancelled, failed or superseded fetch leaves nothing to compensate back and no page is ever re-requested (comment, lines 170-172).
    • Concept introduced, card actions beside the clickable area, not inside it. [Rubric §21, Accessibility] assesses whether interactive controls are nested inside other interactive controls. CardActionsTemplate (lines 29-37) renders a row's delete or edit buttons beside the card body rather than inside the element that carries the card's button role, so a clickable card that also holds actions is not axe nested-interactive and a tap on an action does not raise OnCardClick.
    • Walkthrough:
      • Injected services (lines 22-23: IJSRuntime and the localizer, no toast service) and parameters (lines 25-62). CardTemplate is an [EditorRequired] RenderFragment<TItem> (line 27); CardActionsTemplate is the optional RenderFragment<TItem>? for per-card controls (line 37). FetchPageResult (line 47), also [EditorRequired], is the fetch delegate in the shape every Result-returning UI service already has, (page, pageSize, cancellationToken) returning Result<(IReadOnlyList<TItem> Items, int TotalItems)>, which is IEntityService<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType>.GetPagedAsync minus the filter and sort arguments. PageSize defaults to 10 (line 49), EmptyIcon to SearchOff (line 55), MaxRenderedItems to 500 (line 62).
      • State (lines 64-94): _items, _totalCount, _currentPage, _generation, the four render flags (_isInitialLoad, _isLoadingMore, _hasMore, _loadError), _loadErrorMessage, the interop handles (_sentinelRef, _observer, the shared InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner> that owns the module, the DotNetObjectReference and the observer id, and _cts), _reobservePending (line 93) and _disposed.
      • OnInitializedAsync (lines 96-102) validates the delegate then loads page 1. ValidateFetchParameter (lines 109-116) throws an InvalidOperationException when FetchPageResult is null, deliberately before the load, so a misconfigured call site fails loudly instead of rendering as a load failure with a Retry button that can never succeed (lines 104-108).
      • OnAfterRenderAsync (lines 118-128) consumes and clears _reobservePending (lines 120-121), then attaches the observer only while more pages exist, there are items to scroll past and the initial load is done, either when none is observing yet (_observer?.IsObserving != true) or when a re-observe was queued (line 123). It lazily creates the shared InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner> (line 125) and calls ObserveAsync(_sentinelRef) (line 126); the helper tolerates JSDisconnectedException and JSException on both paths.
      • OnSentinelVisible() (lines 130-143), the [JSInvokable] entry point, returns a completed task when already loading, exhausted or disposed (lines 133-136), otherwise the InvokeAsync task that loads on the renderer's context and re-renders (lines 138-142).
      • LoadNextPageAsync(bool isInitial) (lines 145-237) is the core. It guards re-entry (lines 147-150), sets _isLoadingMore and clears the error state (lines 152-154), and, for a next-page load only, queues a render at once so the "Loading more items" status paints while the fetch is in flight, because a load started from a JS callback or the Retry button otherwise renders nothing until it ends (lines 156-162). It then snapshots the generation and publishes a fresh CancellationTokenSource (lines 164-168), computes targetPage (line 173), and awaits the delegate (line 177). After the await it checks disposal and generation (line 182), unwraps the Result with TryGetValue and routes a failure to SetLoadFailed (lines 187-193), and only then commits: advance the page (line 197), append the items through AppendNew and keep the count of new rows (line 199), record the total (line 200), set _hasMore from HasMoreAfter(appended) (line 201), which is where the DOM cap and the empty-append guard stop the loop, and call MarkReobserveAfterAppend(isInitial) (line 203). OperationCanceledException is swallowed as a normal supersession (lines 205-208); any other exception, caught under a scoped CA1031 suppression, raises the generic failure, again only for the current generation (lines 209-219). The finally (lines 220-236) is careful about ownership: only the current generation may clear _isLoadingMore (a superseding reset already cleared it and may have set it again), and only the still-current CancellationTokenSource is disposed here (ReferenceEquals, line 229), because a resetter that took one over already cancelled and disposed it.
      • AppendNew(IEnumerable<TItem> items) (lines 245-253) appends only the rows not already shown and returns how many were new. Offset paging plus an insert ahead of the window can repeat a row across pages, and rows are keyed by value (@key="item"), so a repeat would be two siblings with one key and a render error (lines 239-244). It filters lazily with _items.Contains while adding (line 250), so a row repeated inside the same page is caught too; records compare by value, the same equality @key uses. HasMoreAfter(int appended) (lines 261-262) is appended > 0 && _items.Count < _totalCount && _items.Count < MaxRenderedItems: besides the rendered-item cap it stops when a page added nothing new (an empty page, or a window shifted by a whole page), so the re-observed sentinel cannot re-request the same page forever; ResetAsync starts over (lines 255-260).
      • MarkReobserveAfterAppend(bool isInitial) (lines 268-274) sets _reobservePending after a non-initial append that left more pages. The IntersectionObserver reports threshold crossings only, so a sentinel still inside the viewport after the append would never fire again; re-observing creates a fresh observer, which delivers an initial entry with the current state (lines 90-92). This is the same stall InfiniteScrollSentinel guards against with its post-load re-attach.
      • SetLoadFailed(Result? failure) (lines 286-290) sets the inline error state and nothing else: no toast is raised, because the inline alert is announced on its own, rendered in place of the list for a failed first page or below it for a later page (lines 276-279). The message comes from failure?.LocalizedErrorMessage(L) (line 289); a raw exception passes null, because exception text is neither translatable nor safe to surface (lines 280-284), and the generic resource string is used instead.
      • CardCallback(TItem item) (lines 299-302) binds one row's click behavior for the markup below. When OnCardClick has a delegate it returns an EventCallback.Factory.Create wrapping the invoke; when it does not, it returns default, deliberately not EventCallback.Empty, because EventCallback.Empty wraps a no-op Action so its HasDelegate is still true and every card would present as interactive. default is the only value ClickableCard reads as "no handler wired", which is what lets it render a plain, non-focusable card instead of a keyboard control that does nothing (lines 292-298).
      • CardActions(TItem item) (line 308) binds one row to CardActionsTemplate, or returns null when the consumer supplied none, which keeps ClickableCard on its original one-element markup (lines 304-307). RetryAsync (line 310) is a plain LoadNextPageAsync(isInitial: false); the load queues its own render.
      • ResetAsync() (lines 316-354) is the public API a page calls when filters change. Order matters and is commented: bump the generation first so any in-flight fetch is already superseded (line 320), then cancel and dispose the stale token source (lines 322-329), then clear _isLoadingMore explicitly (lines 331-334, because the superseded load will not clear it), then reset the list and every flag (lines 336-342), detach the observer (lines 344-347), and reload from page 1 (lines 349-353).
      • DisposeAsync (lines 356-377) guards re-entry, cancels and disposes the token source (lines 367-371), then delegates to _observer.DisposeAsync() (lines 373-376), which detaches the observer, releases the JS module and disposes the DotNetObjectReference.
      • The markup (Components/Lists/MobileInfiniteScrollList.razor:1-64) renders one of four shapes: an indeterminate progress bar inside a role="status" live region on the initial load (lines 5-14), the load-failure alert when the first page itself failed (lines 15-20, because a failed first page is not an empty list), EmptyState when the list came back empty (lines 21-24), or a MudStack of ClickableCard wrappers around the caller's template, each keyed by item and wired to CardCallback(item) and CardActions(item) (lines 27-34). Below the cards it renders the sentinel div only while _hasMore, with a polite live-region spinner while a page loads (lines 36-49), and the same alert when a later page failed (lines 51-54). That alert is one RenderFragment, LoadFailedAlert, carrying role="alert" with the message and a Retry button (lines 58-63).
    • Why it's built this way: the component encapsulates the part of infinite scroll that is genuinely hard to get right (supersession, cancellation ownership, disposal, the DOM cap) and leaves the part that is app-specific (what a card looks like, where the data comes from) to parameters. The Result-returning delegate rather than a raw Task<List<T>> is what makes a localized failure message reachable without the component knowing any error catalogue.
    • Where it's used: the mobile branch of every page built on ListPageShell<TItem>, which renders it at Components/Lists/ListPageShell.razor:36 (the ADC conference admin lists such as SessionList.razor, SpeakerList.razor and RoomList.razor, and Store's CategoryList.razor, ProductList.razor and ShoppingCartList.razor). Pages that render it directly: ADC's PublicEventList.razor:25, PublicSessionListView.razor:6 and the check-in AttendeeSearchPanel.razor:28, and Store's MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.UI/Pages/Orders/OrderList.razor:39. Covered by MobileInfiniteScrollListTests. The list-shell placement is recorded in ADR-146 (Website/docs-src/adr/146-ui-page-bases-and-list-shell.md).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: MaxRenderedItems bounds the DOM but there is no virtualization, so 500 rendered cards remain in the DOM; whether that is acceptable on a given device is not determinable from source. A consumer fetch delegate that ignores its CancellationToken still runs to completion after a reset: the generation guard discards its results, but the request itself is not stopped.

    MultiFactorRequiredListener

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/MultiFactorRequiredListener.cs:24 · Level 3 · class (internal sealed component)

    • What it is: a markup-less layout component that sends the user to the two-factor page when the API refuses a request because the session lacks a second factor. TwoFactorUIModule contributes it to the layout through LayoutComponentTypes (TwoFactorUIModule.cs:28), so a host that opts into two-factor gets the redirect with no page changes (ADR-067, Website/docs-src/adr/067-ui-module-shell-composition.md).
    • Depends on: ComponentBase and IDisposable (MultiFactorRequiredListener.cs:24), ITokenStorageService (:28), NavigationManager (:30), MultiFactorRequiredSignal for the subscription (:41), ReturnUrlProtector (:81) and TwoFactorUIModule.AccountPath (:47, :83).
    • Concept introduced, a step-up redirect that cannot become an open redirect or a loop. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether a second-factor requirement is enforced consistently and whether a return URL can be abused. The listener sanitizes the current location through ReturnUrlProtector.Sanitize with / as the fallback before putting it in returnUrl (:81-83), and never redirects away from the two-factor page or the sign-in page (IsExempt, :46-48), so the refusal that brought the user there cannot bounce them again.
    • Walkthrough
      • OnInitialized (:40-41) subscribes through MultiFactorRequiredSignal.Subscribe(TokenStorage, OnRequired); Dispose (:33-37) disposes and clears the subscription.
      • OnRequired (:50) discards RedirectAsync, which dispatches Redirect through InvokeAsync and swallows ObjectDisposedException and InvalidOperationException, the two shapes of a circuit that ended between the refusal and the dispatch (:52-66).
      • Redirect (:68-84) does nothing outside an interactive renderer (:70-73), reads the base-relative path (:75), returns for an exempt path (:76-79), and navigates to {AccountPath}?required=true&returnUrl=... with the escaped, sanitized path (:81-83).
      • IsExempt (:46-48) is an ordinal, case-insensitive prefix match on the trimmed AccountPath and on login.
    • Why it's built this way: listening at the layout rather than in each page means every refused call, whichever page made it, takes the user to the same place, and the internal visibility keeps it a detail of the two-factor module rather than a component consumers place by hand.
    • Where it's used: registered by TwoFactorUIModule (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/TwoFactorUIModule.cs:28); pinned by MultiFactorRequiredListenerTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Components/Auth/MultiFactorRequiredListenerTests.cs), TwoFactorOptInRenderTests and TwoFactorUIModuleTests.

    ChangePasswordCard

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:23 · Level 4 · class (partial component)

    • What it is: the shared change-password form for a signed-in user: three password fields inside a MudForm, client-side length and confirmation checks, and a submit that calls the auth service and reports the outcome through toasts. A consumer app drops it into its profile page instead of re-implementing the form (ADC does so with a bare <ChangePasswordCard />, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI/Pages/Users/Profile/Profile.razor:83).
    • Depends on: IAuthUIService (@inject AuthService, ChangePasswordCard.razor:2), IToastService (ChangePasswordCard.razor:3), IStringLocalizer<ChangePasswordCard> (ChangePasswordCard.razor:4) with the plural helper StringLocalizerPluralExtensions, ResultUiExtensions for LocalizedErrorMessage (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:165), ComponentLifetimeExtensions for LifetimeToken() (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:149), PasswordComplexity and ChangePasswordRequest (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:30-31, :59, :120), AuthFieldMessages for the complexity message (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:122), and the nested FieldRefusal (:43-44). Externals: MudForm and MudTextField from MudBlazor.
    • Concept introduced, a form that reports the server's reason, not its own guess. [Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] assesses whether validation feedback is honest and where it is raised. Two layers are visible here. The client checks only what it can know cheaply: the new password meets MinLength (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:113-116), satisfies the shared PasswordComplexity rule the server's strong-password rules also evaluate (:118-122), and the confirmation matches (:125-128); the server still enforces its own rules (doc comment, ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:46-49). A server refusal is shown with the server's own message when it has one, falling back to a fixed ChangePassword.Failed text only when the failure carries none (comment ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:162-165). When the refusal names the current or the new password field, it is also shown under that field via FieldRefusal (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:166, :180-192).
    • Walkthrough
      • Parameters: MinLength defaults to 8, the framework's password policy minimum, and also feeds the helper text (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:51; ChangePasswordCard.razor:18). MaxLength is an int? that defaults to PasswordComplexity.MaximumLength, the bound the server's password rules enforce; null leaves the field unbounded (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:53-59); the razor falls back to the private NoMaxLength constant 524288, MudTextField's own default (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:25-26; ChangePasswordCard.razor:20). AdditionalActions (RenderFragment?) renders extra actions, such as a device-management link, after the submit button (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:66; ChangePasswordCard.razor:38).
      • Callbacks: OnChanged fires after success, once the toast has been shown (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:70); OnFailed carries the failed Result after the failure toast, and is not raised for a client-side validation failure, which the form itself reports (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:77).
      • Validators: all three return null for valid or empty input and leave the Required check to report a missing value (comment ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:100-102). ValidateCurrentPassword (:103) only echoes a server message held for the exact value still in the field. ValidateNewPassword (:106) checks length first, plural-aware through L.Plural (:115), then PasswordComplexity.Evaluate: a failing value gets AuthFieldMessages.PasswordComplexity (:122), a passing one gets any held server message (:121). The mismatch uses Validation.PasswordsDoNotMatch (:128), and the confirmation comparison is ordinal (:126).
      • SavePasswordAsync (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:130) opens with a re-entrancy guard before the first await: it returns when the @ref-set form is absent or a save is already running (:135), because a second click before the disabled render would resend the stale current password, which the server refuses and counts toward lockout (comment :132-134). It then sets _isSaving (:140) and, inside the try, validates the form and stops on invalid (:143-147) before calling AuthService.ChangePasswordAsync(current, new, _cts.LifetimeToken()) (:149). On success it resets the form, clears the three fields, toasts ChangePassword.Success and raises OnChanged (:151-158). On failure it toasts (:165), calls ShowFieldRefusalsAsync (:166) and raises OnFailed(result) (:167). A cancelled call is swallowed (:170-173), and _isSaving always clears in finally (:176).
      • ShowFieldRefusalsAsync (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:183) builds a FieldRefusal for the current-password field (matching the wrong-password code Auth.InvalidCurrentPassword, :32) and for the new-password field, then re-validates the form so the message lands under the field and in the summary (:185-191).
      • Disposal: the component implements IDisposable (ChangePasswordCard.razor:5). Dispose(bool) is idempotent, sets _disposed, then cancels and disposes the CancellationTokenSource (ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:88-98). The MudForm reference is not disposed here because the renderer owns it (comment ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:36).
    • Why it's built this way: the cancel-on-dispose token is what makes a navigation away, or an InteractiveAuto render-mode transition, harmless: the in-flight request is cancelled and the OperationCanceledException is expected (comment ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:172). Taking MinLength and MaxLength as parameters lets a consumer tighten the form without forking it, while the server remains the authority. Localization follows ADR-027 (Website/docs-src/adr/027-multi-locale-i18n.md).
    • Where it's used: ADC's profile page renders it (Profile.razor:83), and PasskeysPanel mirrors its card layout (Profile.razor:106). Its behavior is pinned by ChangePasswordCardTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Components/Auth/ChangePasswordCardTests.cs) and ChangePasswordCardErrorSummaryTests, and FormsConventionTestsBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Ui/FormsConventionTestsBase.cs:33) references it by its <ChangePasswordCard tag.

Every list page passes the same parameters into one shell, so a change to the header, the search row, the empty state or the pager reaches every list at once.     PasskeySignInButton

    MMCA.Common.UI · MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/PasskeySignInButton.razor.cs:25 · Level 4 · class (partial component)

    • What it is: the sign-in page's passkey entry point (the opt-in passkey sign-in of ADR-139, Website/docs-src/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.md). It offers a "sign in with a passkey" button and, where the browser supports it, starts passkey autofill so a saved passkey is suggested in the sign-in form without a click.
    • Depends on: IPasskeyUIService for the server half of the ceremony (PasskeySignInButton.razor.cs:40), IPasskeyCapability for the platform half (:42), PasskeySignInRequest (:133), ResultUiExtensions for LocalizedErrorMessage (:145), SharedResource (:44) and ComponentLifetimeExtensions for LifetimeToken() (:73).
    • Concept introduced, no server challenge until the browser can use it. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether an authentication ceremony issues only what it can redeem. Autofill checks IsAutofillAvailableAsync before asking the server for options, because the options store a server challenge that a browser without conditional mediation could never redeem (comment :71-72, :73). An explicit click cancels any running autofill first (:104) so the two ceremonies never overlap.
    • Walkthrough
      • Parameters: OnSignedIn is raised once the passkey signed the user in and the tokens are stored (:33-34); EnableAutofill defaults to true (:37-38).
      • OnAfterRenderAsync (:62-91) runs on the first render only, when autofill is enabled and the component is not disposed (:64): it checks support (:73), begins a sign-in flow (:78) and on success starts autofill with a callback that completes the flow on the renderer's context (:81-84). An OperationCanceledException is swallowed only when disposed (:87).
      • SignInAsync (:93-129) guards on _isBusy (:95), clears the error, cancels autofill (:104), begins a flow (:105) and shows the failure message when that fails (:106-110), then asks the platform for an assertion (:112); a null credential shows the localized Auth.Login.PasskeyCancelled text (:113-117), otherwise it completes the flow (:119). _isBusy clears in finally (:125-128).
      • CompleteAsync (:131-142) posts a PasskeySignInRequest(flowId, assertion) (:133); a failure sets the message and re-renders (:134-139), a success raises OnSignedIn (:141).
      • FailureMessage (:144-145) prefers the result's localized message and falls back to Auth.Login.PasskeyFailed.
      • DisposeAsync (:47-59) is idempotent, cancels and disposes the token source and cancels any running autofill (:57).
    • Why it's built this way: splitting the ceremony between a UI service (server) and a device capability (platform) lets the same button run in a browser and in a native head without a branch.
    • Where it's used: the shared sign-in page (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor:170).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: no test file references the type by name outside its defining file; its coverage, if any, runs through the sign-in page.

Most refusals show the server's own reason (the last-passkey rule, a name that is too long; comment :221-222), but a step-up refusal, code Passkeys.StepUpRequired restated as StepUpRequiredCode because UI references Shared only (:23-24), shows the localized Passkeys.SignInAgain text instead, the one refusal with an action the user can take (FailureMessage, :236-241).
